items.title: Journalism and AI: Who owns the news?
items.summary: Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on?

scraped.title: AI answers rely on journalism. Who gets paid?
scraped.description: Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on?
scraped.h1: Should AI companies pay for the journalism they use?
scraped.body_text:
Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on?

Millions of people now use AI chatbots as a source of news to find quick answers to questions about current events.

A 2026 survey by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, which questioned more than 90,000 people worldwide, found that 10% use AI chatbots for news on a weekly basis, a figure that is significantly higher among younger audiences.

Explaining what is happening in the world, why it matters, and what it means has traditionally been the work of journalism. Media organizations send reporters into the field, commission investigations and conduct research, producing stories that help audiences understand global events. But as more people turn to AI tools for information, the relationship between those producing journalism and those distributing it is changing.

"In the past, search engines like Google indexed our websites and directed users to their articles, generating traffic in return," Julia Becker, publisher of Funke Media Group, told a panel at the Global Media Forum (GMF) in Berlin. "But now that exchange has broken down."

"AI companies draw on our quality reporting to generate answers, yet the reporting itself often remains largely invisible by the end of this process," said DW Director General Barbara Massing in a keynote address at the forum.

Their remarks reflect a worry that is growing across the media industry. Publicly available news is copied and summarized by AI chatbots, while news organizations are becoming less and less able to rely on the money and visibility that used to come from distributing that work.

There has been growing concern about how copyrighted material is collected, used, and reproduced by artificial intelligence , and whether the companies that build those systems should pay the people and organizations that created the material.

Media houses are now pressing "Big Tech" companies to ask permission before using their work and to pay for it.

In October, German broadcasters ARD and RTL, along with the country's Federal Association of Digital Publishers and Newspaper Publishers (BDZV) and the Association of Private Media (VAUNET), called for stronger copyright protections for media companies.

In the US, lawsuits are adding pressure. The New York Times has sued internet company Brave Softwar for allegedly using its content without permission and getting around its paywall.

Meanwhile, legal institutions in the EU, including the European Court of Justice (ECJ) are examining whether AI-generated answers can themselves infringe copyright.

In February, a coalition of media organizations, including the Guardian , the BBC, and the Financial Times , called for rules that would give publishers more control over how AI systems copy and reproduce their content.

The problem goes beyond whether AI companies may use journalism. It also concerns how publishers and journalists can get paid when their work becomes part of the answers AI systems generate.

"AI systems shouldn't just use quality journalism. They should also pay for it," Massing said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Professor Martin Senftleben, who directs the Institute for Information Law at the University of Amsterdam, separates two ways AI companies use journalistic material: Training their models and generating responses to individual user questions.

Payment for training is a more complicated legal question, he said. The more urgent issue is what happens when an AI system uses journalism to answer a question in real time.

He argued that European copyright law may already offer a way to address part of the problem. Under existing EU law, publishers and journalists may be able to claim payment collectively, without waiting for a new legal framework.

"What are we waiting for? Germany is a large member state. This should be introduced in Germany," he told the forum.

One option, Senftleben suggested, is a legally required payment system in which every AI response that draws on journalism triggers a payment. A collecting organization would gather the money and distribute it among publishers and journalists, in the same way that music royalties are collected and distributed.

Once such a system exists, publishers and authors could use its rates as a starting point when negotiating individual licensing deals with AI companies.

Lutz Mache, senior manager of government affairs and public policy at Google, told the GMF panel that Google is willing to negotiate agreements with German media companies and to discuss new AI products with them.

Google has also started testing other ways to pay publishers for their contributions to AI-generated answers. Its "AI Contribution" pilot, which is being tested with selected publishers, aims to reward content that plays a significant role in answers produced by products such as Gemini and AI Overviews. But the program is still an early experiment, not a general payment system open to all publishers.

Microsoft, Anthropic, and OpenAI have recently said they support clearer, standardized signals that let website owners state whether their content may be used to train AI models.

However, not everyone thinks more regulation is the answer.

Jörg Heidrich, a lawyer who specializes in technology law and serves as AI commissioner at the German media company Heise, warned against adding new rules without considering their effects on the wider tech sector.

Europe has already fallen behind in the global AI race, he argued. More regulation, he warned, could make it harder for European companies to compete with major providers based elsewhere.

Heidrich also pointed to smaller players, including startups, independent developers, and research institutions. They depend on access to data to build and train AI systems. He argued that the debate over copyright and payment risks overlooking these groups, and that new restrictions could hurt their work.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

items.title: The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready?
items.summary: Countries like the U.S., U.K. and China are pouring billions into AI-integrated military software and hardware, despite legal and ethical concerns. Canadian defence technology companies, military experts and defence officials all say keeping humans in the loop will be key.

scraped.title: The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready? | CBC News
scraped.description: Countries like the U.S., U.K. and China are pouring billions into AI-integrated military software and hardware, despite legal and ethical concerns. Canadian defence technology companies, military experts and defence officials all say keeping humans in the loop will be key.
scraped.h1: The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready?
scraped.body_text:
The drone looks like a small fighter jet. Artificial Intelligence is flying it, and it's firing a missile. A human approved the shot, but AI carried it out.

That's not science fiction. It may be the future of modern warfare.

In July, American defence company Anduril's YFQ-44A drone, known as Fury, fired an air-to-air tactical missile at a simulated target in California's Mojave Desert. In October, a pilot in an F-22 fighter jet was able to get the drone to carry out simulated combat tasks.

It's the latest step in the global race for autonomous weapons as armies try to gain a tactical edge.

With governments increasingly integrating AI into military software and hardware, Canada faces a question: should it join the autonomous arms race and start investing more in AI-enhanced weapons despite legal and ethical concerns?

AI drone warfare is here. Should Canada buy in?

YFQ-44A is a collaborative combat aircraft (CCA), designed to fly alongside manned fighter jets. It's meant to extend the jet's reach, while reducing risk to the pilot. The drone would use AI to carry out many fighter jet tasks, including firing weapons on command and eventually engaging in close aerial combat.

"You're getting artificial intelligence in a platform that is deadly," said Yvan Blondin, who commanded the Royal Canadian Air Force from 2012 to 2015.

Ottawa drone makers tool up for increased defence budget

As Canadian defence spending ramps up, London firms excited about opportunities

Blondin believes these drones will become integral to modern militaries by the 2030s.

The U.S. has two prototypes , including Fury. Australia has a Boeing-built CCA — and they're working on an underwater version built by Anduril. The U.K. is spending five billion pounds to boost drones and autonomous systems in their military.

Western armies say humans will stay in control and responsible for weapons using lethal force: it's part of NATO's policy on responsible use of AI.

Canadian officials told CBC that warfare must stay a fundamentally human endeavour, and said that no machine, weapons systems or algorithmic code can be held responsible for complying with International Humanitarian Law. But Blondin says other adversaries may not wait.

If one country uses autonomous AI in a conflict, Blondin wonders how other countries would respond — would they raise their ethical standards, or drop them entirely?

"In times of war, would China bother with the step of having a human in the loop?" he asked.

In a statement sent to CBC News, the Department of National Defence said the Royal Canadian Air Force is examining how these systems could be useful for Canada, but that no decision has been made about plans to procure CCAs.

The Canadian Armed Forces supports the development of autonomous functionality, the statement said, on the condition that it would be "operated within a responsible chain of human command and control and commits to uphold the reliable and lawful use of such weapon systems."

Military commander vows fast action on AI and robots, sees 'untapped potential' for Canada

In Canada's drone-killing 'Sandbox,' companies compete for a $1M prize

Canada has no collaborative combat aircraft, but Dominion Dynamics CEO Eliot Pence wants to change that.

His defence technology company is building Scout, a CCA that would fly ahead of a crewed fighter, three or four drones per jet, beyond the radar's edge — and be able to strike by firing a weapon, like a missile.

Dominion Dynamics CEO Eliot Pence stands in front of a subscale model of Scout, a collaborative combat aircraft that the Canadian defence technology company is building. Scout would fly ahead of a crewed fighter beyond the edge of its radar and be able to strike by firing a weapon, like a missile. (Nicolas Legault/CBC)

Pence, who previously worked at Anduril, says the need for CCA is about sovereignty, especially over the Arctic, which makes up about 40 per cent of Canada. The country doesn't have the fighter jets to cover all that territory, Pence argues, noting that leaves a gap in Canada's ability to carry out intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance — a gap Dominion is trying to fill.

"The best, most efficient and technologically advanced way of doing that is by pairing those jets with autonomous systems."

Dominion stands to benefit if Ottawa buys in.

Pence says he's raised about a third of the $500 million needed to build the prototype, and though Ottawa has bought into Dominion's simulation platform, there's no government contract for a prototype.

"We don't care. We're going to build it anyway."

Pence says Dominion wants a human to remain the last decision maker for the drone, and is building that boundary into the decision-making of its AI models.

But they have yet to figure out what, specifically, all those safeguards would be, says Benoit Breault, senior vice-president for aerospace engineering at Dominion.

Some boundaries are straightforward, Breault says — for example, any use of force will require human approval.

Benoit Breault, senior vice-president for aerospace engineering at Dominion, is working on safeguards to make sure a human is the last decision maker for the drone they want to build. (Nicolas Legault/CBC)

Other boundaries may seem less critical at first blush, but can become unexpectedly dangerous. For instance, if engineers want the drone to return home, can AI decide what route to take?

"You don't want to return to base straight into dangerous environments or contested airspace," Breault said.

He's also thinking about how to avoid overwhelming the pilot. Too much information from three or four drones could make it difficult for the pilot to maintain control of CCAs.

Drones and AI are rewriting the rulebook on naval warfare — with uncertain consequences

But right now, Breault acknowledges development of the human-machine interface is still "embryonic."

He says they're still trying to determine answers to important questions like, "How exactly are we going to provide information to the fighter jet pilots? How exactly are the decision recommendations going to be displayed."

These details are central to ethical concerns about autonomous weapons systems, says Craig Martin, a former Canadian navy officer and an expert in armed conflict laws who teaches at Washburn University in Topeka, Kan.

"This is the million dollar question," he said. "What is the extent and the nature of the human control that's being exercised over that weapon system?"

Martin is worried about automation bias — where humans put too much trust in the machine, especially if, for instance, they have just seconds to respond. Martin says AI systems can also fail if they're used in environments where they weren't trained. For instance, a system trained for use in Afghanistan could make mistakes if it's used in Ukraine.

Such errors, he says, "can actually compound in sort of exponential feedback loops that result in biases that can possibly lead to the killing of civilians."

This month, diplomats will meet in Geneva to see if countries want to enter into negotiations about rules governing the use of autonomous weapons. Craig Martin, a former Canadian navy officer and an expert in armed conflict laws, wants Canada to lead that conversation. (Andrew Lee/CBC)

UN Secretary-General António Guterres wants a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons by the end of 2026.

Guterres renewed that call in August, a month after a Russian drone, acting with no human operator, killed three civilians in Ukraine , the New York Times reported. The drone was reportedly a cheap, expendable weapon that picked its own target. It was in a different category from CCAs, but both that type of drone and CCAs are autonomous enough that they are able to make some of their own decisions.

Martin is calling for changes to international law that would ban fully autonomous weapons and restrict semi-autonomous weapons. This month, diplomats will meet in Geneva to see if countries want to enter into negotiations about rules governing the use of these weapons — and Martin wants Canada to lead that conversation.

Canada voted yes to a 2025 UN resolution calling on countries to lay the groundwork for possible negotiations on a treaty governing the use of lethal autonomous weapons systems.

DND officials say Canada will continue to participate in international talks about these weapons. It's also ramping up defence spending, having committed to NATO's target of spending five per cent of GDP on defence by 2035.

Whether or not Canada buys in to autonomous weapons, Blondin, the former RCAF commander, says they're coming.

"This is a discussion we need to have as a society."

Senior Reporter

Jennifer Yoon covers the latest national and international news for CBC News on television, radio and digital. You can reach her at jennifer.yoon@cbc.ca.

items.summary: Six people were killed and 15 wounded after a gunman opened fire on Saturday afternoon in a busy market square in Krakow, Poland, authorities said.

scraped.title: Shooting in Polish city of Krakow leaves 6 people dead and more than a dozen injured | CBC News
scraped.description: Six people were killed and 15 wounded after a gunman opened fire on Saturday afternoon in a busy market square in Krakow, Poland, authorities said.
scraped.h1: Shooting in Polish city of Krakow leaves 6 people dead and more than a dozen injured
scraped.body_text:
Six people were killed and 15 wounded after a gunman opened fire on Saturday afternoon in a busy market square in Krakow, Poland, authorities said.

The gunman, a Polish citizen, aimed at random people as he drove into the Main Market Square, a major tourist destination in the centre of the city, Krakow police said. Police officers are among the wounded.

The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a gunfight with officers a short distance away from the initial violence, police said. The death toll earlier stood at five, but the Malopolska regional government updated it to six in a post on social media platform X.

Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, told TVN24 that the perpetrator was wearing military-style fatigues and used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police said they found many other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car.

Cisło said the gunman acted alone and that the public is safe. Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland.

Emergency personnel speak to a person at the site of the shooting near Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday. (Jakub Porzycki/Reuters)

Images from the scene showed police officers and ambulances covering the area, and a Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter also landed in the square.

A tram driver reported at about 3 p.m. local time that his vehicle was shot at by a man in a moving car while passing nearby the main square, the Krakow municipal transport company said. The window to the tram driver's cabin was shattered.

An estimated 15 million tourists visit Krakow annually, the majority passing through the Main Market Square.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in a post on X, said police are investigating the attack. And Polish President Karol Nawrocki said his thoughts were with the victims, the wounded and their families.

A member of the Municipal Guard police force runs at the site of the shooting in Krakow on Saturday. (Jakub Porzycki/Reuters)

Other details were not immediately available.

"We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that's shattered the peace of Poland," Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X.

"America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow."

Krakow, the second-largest city in Poland, is about 250 kilometres from the capital, Warsaw.

items.title: Canada's military is using Palantir software. What are the risks?
items.summary: Canada has multimillion-dollar contracts with U.S. tech firm Palantir. Experts warn the deals could expose military data to U.S. authorities and deepen Canada's reliance on foreign technology, while DND says its systems keep government data secure in Canada.

scraped.title: Canada is relying on a controversial U.S. tech company for military software | CBC News
scraped.description: Canada has multimillion-dollar contracts with U.S. tech firm Palantir. Experts warn the deals could expose military data to U.S. authorities and deepen Canada's reliance on foreign technology, while DND says its systems keep government data secure in Canada.
scraped.h1: Canada's military is using Palantir software. What are the risks?
scraped.body_text:
Why Canada’s military deal with Palantir sparks sovereignty fears

Canada has multimillion-dollar contracts with Palantir, a controversial U.S. software company. Experts warn the deals could expose Canadian military data to U.S. authorities and leave Canada reliant on critical technology supplied by a foreign company.

Documents obtained by the Investigative Journalism Foundation revealed that the Department of National Defence (DND) has had a contract for Palantir's Gotham software since 2020 that was internally flagged as "not for public disclosure." Initially valued at $14 million, it could be worth up to $63 million.

DND told CBC News that Gotham brings together information from military databases and operates on closed, classified networks inside secure facilities in Canada. The department declined to say exactly what information Gotham processes, citing national-security concerns.

DND says its security assessment determined that no government data, prompts, outputs or metadata handled under the contracts could be stored, accessed or processed outside Canada.

But experts argue U.S. law could still provide American authorities with a means to acquire information within an American company's possession, custody or control. Others warn Canada could become dependent on military technology that would be difficult to replace.

A view of the Palantir building is seen during the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting 2026 in Davos, Switzerland, in January. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

Palantir Technologies was co-founded in 2003 by five people, including CEO Alex Karp and board chair Peter Thiel. It has since become a major technology contractor for governments and militaries.

Its software integrates information from multiple datasets so users can identify connections and patterns across large amounts of information.

Michael Steinberger, a journalist and author of The Philosopher in the Valley: Alex Karp, Palantir, and the Rise of the Surveillance State , said the company has drawn criticism over its involvement in military operations and immigration enforcement in the United States.

Some of its most important work, he said, involves Project Maven, the U.S. military's artificial-intelligence program used to analyze military data and support targeting operations.

"This is being used extensively now in U.S. military actions," Steinberger said.

When asked about Project Maven, a Palantir spokesperson told CBC News: "We do not conduct surveillance. The Maven platform provides the U.S. warfighter a live, synchronized view of the battlespace to help them make better-informed decisions and reduce errors … all of this is conducted with strong safeguards and accountability logs."

Palantir's work with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also drawn criticism.

"Its technology seems to be a critical node in the immigration crackdown that's happening here in the United States right now," Steinberger said.

Palantir CEO Alex Karp is shown at the 48th Annual Meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos in 2018. (Peter Klaunzer/EPA-EFE/Shutterstock)

The company has also increasingly identified itself with U.S. national interests.

U.S. President Donald Trump praised Palantir earlier this year for having "great war-fighting capabilities and equipment."

In June, Palantir posted on X a list of 22 principles drawn from The Technological Republic , a book co-written by Karp. They include the assertion that Silicon Valley has an "obligation to participate in the defense of the nation" and describe some cultures as "dysfunctional and regressive."

Karp has also appeared in company advertising saying "the West is superior, and we have to fight for these values."

Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, an independent public policy think tank, said the concern extends beyond Palantir's politics to Canada's reliance on an outside supplier for critical digital infrastructure.

"We're potentially growing a digital dependency, enriching what is fundamentally a U.S. company at the expense of our sovereignty," she said.

A protester opposed to data analytics firm Palantir Technologies' role in the National Health Service (NHS) holds a sign in a demonstration outside St Thomas' Hospital during a global day of action against the company's healthcare contracts, in London, in October. (Toby Shepheard/Reuters)

The debate over Palantir comes amid a broader push in Europe for "digital sovereignty" — greater domestic control over technology and data.

In July, France and Germany pledged to reduce reliance on foreign providers by examining domestic alternatives after ending Palantir's contracts with their intelligence services.

In the U.K., MPs have called on the government to end Palantir's 330-million-pound ($619 million Cdn) National Health Service contract, citing "serious mistrust" of the company after a Financial Times report that a small number of company employees had access to identifiable patient data in the Palantir-built platform. The National Data Guardian, an independent adviser on the use of health and social-care data in England, said the incident breached data-governance principles.

A Palantir spokesperson at the time told the Financial Times that "Palantir software can only be used to process data precisely in line with the instruction of the customer. Using the data for anything else would not only be illegal but technically impossible due to granular access controls overseen by the NHS."

Barry Appleton, an international lawyer who practises both Canadian and American law, says the U.S. CLOUD Act could compel U.S. companies to produce data stored outside the United States. (CBC)

One potential concern is whether U.S. authorities could compel access to Canadian information.

Barry Appleton, an international lawyer who practises both Canadian and American law, pointed to the U.S. CLOUD Act, which allows authorities, with appropriate legal process, to compel covered U.S. companies to produce data within their possession, custody or control, regardless of whether it is stored inside or outside the United States.

"I'm talking to you today while we're having massive trade wars," Appleton said. "Do I want Canada's trade strategy to be able to be surveilled and read by the United States today? No, I don't."

DND says its Palantir systems have been assessed for this kind of exposure. It says government data, prompts, outputs or metadata could not be stored, accessed or processed outside Canada and that Gotham information is protected on closed, classified networks in secure Canadian facilities.

"The United States CLOUD Act does not have any authority over servers located in Canada," DND said.

Appleton disputes that interpretation.

"The CLOUD Act is not about where the server is located," he said.

"Any data at any time that Palantir has, if it was subject to an order under the CLOUD Act would have to be produced," Appleton said because "it's decided by American courts under American law, not under Canadian law."

Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp listens as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a reception with business leaders, at the 56th annual World Economic Forum (WEF), in Davos, in January 2026. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

Jennifer Evans, a policy researcher and founder of PatternPulse AI, said DND's statement that data is stored on closed, classified networks in Canada doesn't make clear what level of security is being used.

She agreed with Appleton that the CLOUD Act "means that there is potential data visibility to some of the highest levels in the U.S. government."

Evans said DND should disclose more about its contract with Palantir, including whether it uses air-gapping, which isolates computers or networks from unsecured networks and the internet.

A Palantir spokesperson told CBC News in an email that it is "a software company" and rejected suggestions that the company takes ownership of or uses its customers' information.

"Our customers own and control their own data. Palantir never uses or retains customer data for its own purposes or shares data with other customers," the spokesperson told CBC News.

A second potential risk is Canada's dependence on a foreign supplier for military technology.

A Ukrainian artilleryman sets up a Starlink satellite internet system near the front line in the Donetsk region in October 2026. Ukrainian officials said Starlink speeds had been throttled earlier that month, disrupting military operations. (Stringer/File Photo/Reuters)

Bednar points to Space X's Starlink internet technology, owned by Elon Musk. Beginning Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of throttling Starlink's speeds, disrupting military activity. The accusations came after Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply the world with millions of tonnes of Russian diesel.

While it's unclear who was responsible for the slowdown, Bednar says the episode shows how reliance on a company with ties to the U.S. government can leave militaries vulnerable.

"These are not neutral technologies. So let's stop treating them as if they're neutral," Bednar said.

Evans said few companies compete with the breadth of Palantir's software but pointed to Canadian alternatives, including Vancouver-based Caseway and Ottawa-based Anvil.

"They don't come anywhere close to the breadth and depth that Palantir offers," she said. She added that it will take time for them to develop comparable technology.

Bednar said Canada should nevertheless invest in developing that technology domestically.

"Building and owning this kind of necessary digital infrastructure for defence should be a primary goal for Canada," she said.

Journalist

Ashley Fraser is the TikTok producer for CBC News and is currently a senior reporter for CBC's The National. Previously she worked as a field producer and audio producer at CBC Radio and CBC News. Her videos were part of the team that won a silver Digital Publishing Award in best news coverage for covering the 2024 U.S. election. Email her ashley.fraser@cbc.ca

items.title: Has the curtain come down on the age of Trump?
items.summary: Americans exposed the limits of Donald Trump's electoral power and weakened his grip on the Republican Party. But the Democratic landslide in the midterm elections does not spell the end of MAGA nor guarantee a lasting political realignment.

Long Read

Topic: US Elections

( ABC News: Lindsay Dunbar )

The Trump political juggernaut has hit a wall. But while Democrats are celebrating, the battle for America's political future is only just beginning.

In the year America celebrated its 250th birthday, voters delivered a once-in-a-century election result signalling a break from a president who has dominated US politics for the past 10 years.

Donald Trump, to mark both the US semi-quincentennial and his own 80th birthday in June, put on a cage fight on the South Lawn of the White House. At these midterm elections, he was repeatedly body-slammed by voters. This was a very personal repudiation of a pharaoh-like figure who had tried, implausibly, to convince Americans they were enjoying a "golden age".

It represented the rebuke of a leader with authoritarian leanings who has sought to turn the White House into something akin to a palace, and Washington into a monument to himself.

Needless to say, exit polls showed voters were angry about the spike in fuel, food and, in rural states, fertiliser prices caused by a trade war that Trump framed as a "Liberation Day". The conflict with Iran had turned every gas station in America into a billboard for the Democrats. But alleged government corruption was also prominent in voters' minds, even higher in some exit polls than cost-of-living concerns.

Ahead of the election, a poll by Fox News showed alleged government corruption was actually the number one issue.

The billionaire president and his family have been getting ostentatiously richer while many Americans are suffering personal recessions.

Hard-pressed voters eyed decadence in the gold-bedecked walls of the Oval Office when their own quality of life was deteriorating. When Trump flew into the heartland to campaign, he did so aboard a $400 million Boeing 747-8 luxury airliner gifted by the Qatari royal family.

This wasn't simply an "it's the economy, stupid" election. It was also about the self-enrichment of Trump, his family members and acolytes such as Elon Musk, the world's first trillionaire. American voters were rejecting the excesses of an increasingly imperial presidency. Ending his campaign in front of the renovated Reflecting Pool in Washington seemed to many voters the perfect expression of his narcissism and tone-deafness.

More so than winning this election through the attractiveness of their policies, Democrats became the beneficiaries of the anti-Trump backlash. And theirs was a landslide win. The stuff of fantasy politics.

In regaining control of the US Senate, they took deep red Republican bastions: Texas, Kansas, even South Carolina.

In the House of Representatives, Democrats will enjoy at least a 50-seat advantage. It is the kind of lopsided congressional majority not seen since Barack Obama's victory in 2008 which took a couple of successive waves to achieve. The cumulative vote in all the House seats, which gives the national picture, showed the Democrats had close to a 13-point lead over the Republicans.

To put that in historical perspective, in the famed " Republican revolution" of 1994 the GOP beat the Democrats by 6.8 points.

For the first time in 16 years, the Democrats will control a majority of governorships. These include noteworthy racial firsts. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman ever elected governor of an American state. Texas will now have a Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa. Disquiet and fear amongst Hispanic voters over ICE raids helped her triumph.

Not only the landscape but the face of US politics changed. For the first time in the country's history, the House of Representatives will have a Black speaker, New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries.

Small wonder, the term "bluenami" is being used. But it is also a red meltdown.

This is the first time in the Trump era his Republican Party has been severely punished. This result recalls the post-Watergate midterms in 1974 when Republicans were punished for the transgressions of Richard Nixon. Nixon had been forced to resign the presidency less than three months before Election Day.

That 1974 election brought about a generational shift. The Class of '74 included the so-called "Watergate babies". Remarkably, 87 members of the new Congress were aged under 40.

This election hasn't produced quite such an infusion of young blood. Still, at a time when Capitol Hill has often looked like a gerontocracy, the average age of lawmakers will be significantly lower. James Talarico, the Presbyterian seminarian with choir boy looks who won in Texas, is 37. Incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff, who comfortably regained his seat in the Republican target state of Georgia, is 39. Abdul El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim US Senator, is 42. Annie Andrews, who took South Carolina, is 46. Melat Kiros, who was endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America in Colorado's first district, became the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress. She is just 29 years old.

What this election does not necessarily signify is a long-lasting political shift, or permanent realignment.

While the Republican Revolution of 1994 seemed to herald a period of conservative domination, just two years later Democrat Bill Clinton won his second term as president.

The 1974 midterm elections foretold that Republicans were set for a prolonged spell in the political wilderness. Yet Ronald Reagan won the presidency in 1980, and Republicans dominated the presidency for the next 12 years.

Democrats, understandably, are joyous about the outcome of the 2026 midterms. Yet their celebrations should come with circumspection.

A poll conducted in the run-up to this election suggested 52 per cent of voters had an unfavourable view of the Democratic Party; only 29 per cent had a favourable view. For months beforehand, the Real Clear Politicspolling average showed the American public looked on the Democrats only marginally more favourably than the Republicans.

Nevertheless, this is a mighty political achievement, which raises an important question: has the curtain come down on the age of Donald Trump?

As always, it is dangerous to write off or underestimate Donald Trump.

Just seven weeks after the storming of the US Capitol on January 6, 2021 as Congress met to certify the 2020 presidential election results, I watched as Trump was greeted like a conquering hero at a conservative conference in Orlando, Florida. The event had the feel of a cargo cult.

Likewise, after Trump-backed Republican candidates failed to make expected breakthroughs in the 2022 congressional midterms, pundits composed obituaries for the MAGA movement which proved wildly premature.

Yet this week's results are certainly a game-changer.

Any ambitions Trump might harbour of illegally defying the 22nd Amendment, which limits presidents to two terms in office, have surely been snuffed out. The notion of Trump 3.0 is even more outlandish now. A Trump dynasty also seems more unlikely. The thought of President Donald Trump Jr taking the oath of office in 2029 or 2033 requires a giant leap of imagination.

Instead, Trump has been badly weakened. His fear factor, within a Republican Party that over the past decade has come to resemble a Trump Party, has been diminished. Signs of his waning power have come already from his Vice President JD Vance who, in a 600-word screed on social media, broke spectacularly with the president.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

But the president had not said so last night, and the ambitious vice president, who is eyeing a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, is already trying to distance himself from a damaged brand.

In anointing his political heir, Trump might not be the all-powerful kingmaker after all. Maybe Republican presidential aspirants will not even crave his endorsement. When Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz published his own 1700-word election post-mortem on X — he described the midterms as "an ass kicking" — it did not include a single word of praise for a president who is used to sycophantic encomiums from his party.

Trump, however, still commands fierce loyalty from millions in his MAGA base. His approval rating among self-described "MAGA Republicans" is 96 per cent. Again, it is worth remembering what happened in the aftermath of January 6. Republicans could have banished Trump into the political wilderness. Instead, his grip on the party tightened. He successfully managed to purge the party of Trump critics, such as former Congresswoman Liz Cheney, and easily saw off the challenge from rivals such as Florida Governor Ron DeSantis in the 2024 Republican primaries.

This election was not only a rejection of Trump but a repudiation of his hyper-aggressive style of politics.

In Michigan, he slandered Democrat Abdul El-Sayed as a "jihadist" and "terrorist", repeatedly called him "Mohammed". But in this bellwether of bellwethers, El-Sayed won comfortably.

The defeat of Trump acolyte, Vivek Ramaswamy, was also emblematic. Ramaswamy aired one of the most vile political attacks in US campaign history, which featured the mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Aston, castigating her daughter as a liar for accusing her ex-husband, who had been criminally charged of rape and then fled from police, of sexually molesting her as a child. Senior Republicans, including the state's outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, called for Ramaswamy to take down the ad. Trump described it as "very powerful".

Voters overwhelmingly rejected that kind of hateful politics.

James Talarico, who Trump labelled "Talafreako", made this yearning for a gentler kind of politics the centrepiece of his victory speech in Texas.

"We are tired of being told to hate each other," said Talarico. "It has been 10 years of this kind of politics, politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning, politics as professional wrestling."

Much of the MAGA agenda, however, will survive. Strong borders. Economic nationalism. A rejection of globalisation and frictionless free trade. The insistence that US allies must cough up more money for their own defence.

Democrats will be more wary of pushing what might be called "woke" issues. Even New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez remarked in August that " Woke 1.0 was crazy ".

Democrats have already made concessions to Trumpism.

This election they focused on economic issues rather than identity politics. Crucially, however, in the 11 years since Trump came down that golden escalator he has not managed to create a pre-eminent new political order.

For much of the past century, as the historian Gary Gerstle noted in his 2022 landmark study, The Rise and Fall of the Neoliberal Order , US politics was dominated by two political orders.

First, the New Deal created in the 1930s by Franklin Delano Roosevelt, marked by broad consensus between Democrats and Republicans on the role of the state in regulating capitalism and providing a basic welfare safety net for the economically disadvantaged.

Next, from the 1970s to the 2010s, came the neoliberal order, based on a reduced role of government and greater emphasis on the market, which was championed by Reagan and acquiesced in by Clinton, who presented himself as a market-friendly "New Democrat".

Since the Great Recession of 2008, however, no party has managed to impose its ideas on the other, or accrued enough power for long enough in Washington to do so. Instead, we have entered what Gerstle describes as an "interregnum characterised by disorder and instability".

This election offers further proof that we remain in this liminal phase, with neither side establishing lasting dominance.

Trump believed there had been a conservative vibe shift in 2024 after he regained the presidency by winning all seven battleground states. Republicans also controlled both houses of Congress. Two years later, Trump and his party have been hammered.

In a chronically polarised nation, we are witnessing a period of unusual political volatility.

At the presidential level, three consecutive two-term presidencies (Democrat Bill Clinton, Republican George W Bush and Democrat Barack Obama) have been followed three consecutive one-term presidencies (Republican Trump, Democrat Joe Biden, Republican Trump).

Not since the late 19th century, when Grover Cleveland lost the presidency only to win it back four years later, have we seen the presidency switch quadrennially between the parties. Likewise, no party has managed to command Capitol Hill for an extended period. Already this century the House has changed hands five times.

In the entire second half the 21st century, during which Democrats dominated the House of Representatives, that scenario has only occurred three times. In the final 25 years of the 20th century, the Senate changed majority control just three times. In the first 25 years of the 21st century, it has flipped eight times.

Now we will see divisions not only between the parties but within them. Progressive Democrats will point to the success of El-Sayed in Michigan, and the energising effect of Zohran Mamdani's 2025 mayoral victory in New York, as proof that a left-wing version of economic populism can succeed at the national level.

Among the Democratic victors on Tuesday were a record number of candidates backed by, or affiliated with, the Democratic Socialists of America. Centrists will cite the breakthrough in Texas of Talarico, a moderate Christian Democrat, and the mega-church pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas as evidence that the party should occupy the middle ground.

All the party's winning presidential candidates since World War II — Harry Truman, John F Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson, Jimmy Carter, Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — have been pragmatic centrists.

The orthodoxy that only a moderate can win the White House will now be challenged, and contested, ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

On the right of politics, what remains of the more traditionalist wing of the Republican Party might argue the party has to move away from its Trump branding and become more recognisably Reaganesque. Reagan was a free-trade internationalist who backed traditional conservative governance, compared with Trump's populist nationalism that embraces economic protectionism and rejects global alliances and institutional norms.

MAGA diehards will remain faithful to Trump, though some will argue he has not been MAGA enough, especially by launching an unpopular war with Iran. Think-tanks, such as the Heritage Foundation which produced the controversial policy blueprint Project 2025, have lurched a long way to the right. So, too, have media channels such as Fox News and NewsMax, whose "angertainment" business models are based on stoking culture war outrage.

So, it is by no means inevitable that the party will move back towards what is sometimes called the sensible centre.

How could the Republicans remain viable if MAGA voters withdrew their support? Some are now likening the Trump Republican Party to the Trump casino empire. That did not end well.

If, moreover, Texas becomes the new California — the Golden State voted Republican in every presidential election between 1968 and 1988 but Democrat ever since — then it could face a prolonged shut-out from the White House. Try gaining an Electoral College majority without at least one of the country's two most populous states.

Looking to the future, the youth vote does not augur well for the Republicans. Nationally, in House elections, exit polling suggest 66 per cent of voters aged 18-29 voted for a Democrat candidate.

Always, though, we must be wary of over-extrapolating in the aftermath of what look like transformative elections. I have seen too many victorious parties over-reach and then face push-back from voters. Remember the heady talk after Barack Obama's election in 2008 that suggested he would usher in a phase of post-partisanship, and even post-racialism.

As a correspondent in the US at the time, I witnessed how the country's first African-American president was followed into the White House by the untitled leader of the Birther Movement, who placed himself at the head of the anti-Obama white backlash. As Obama himself described the shift after Trump's victory in 2016: "History doesn't move in a straight line. It zigs and zags."

For the past decade, anti-incumbency has so often been the driver of American politics. That, and the negative partisanship that comes with it. Voters often cast their ballots against a party rather than for a party. In these midterms we saw it again. In a 50/50 nation, where for much of this century the results of elections have been far narrower than on Tuesday night, politics has been marked by deadlock not dominance.

What we do know for sure is that the Democrats have just won the authority to scrutinise and investigate. When the new Congress meets on January 3, expect Democratic lawmakers to use those subpoena powers to the full.

Robert Garcia, the top ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, which tends to spearhead congressional investigations, has said already that allegations of Trump family corruption will be his main priority, with the president's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, coming under closer scrutiny. On election night, he posted two words on social media: "LAWYER UP!"

Garcia also released a statement pledging to take on "the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS [Department of Homeland Security] and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files". Hakeem Jeffries has accused the "Trump Cartel" of "massive corruption" and warned: "We are going to hold the crooks accountable."

With a majority in the House, the Democrats could for a third time impeach Donald Trump (previously, only two presidents — Andrew Johnson and Bill Clinton — have faced the charge of committing high crimes and misdemeanours). But winning a conviction in the Senate trial that would ensue requires 67 votes, the kind of super-majority the Democrats are not close to achieving. Besides, attempts to punish Trump have often worked in his favour, by allowing him to claim a political form of martyrdom.

The Democrats could also try to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth for waging military hostilities without congressional authorisation, which is a violation of the 1973 War Powers Resolution. Moves are already afoot in what is now a lame duck Congress, spearheaded by the anti-Trump Republican Thomas Massie, to trigger an impeachment vote against Hegseth as soon as this week.

The newly-elected 120th Congress, whose members will take their seats in the new year, could become known as the Accountability Congress. But House Democrats will also want to make it an Action Congress, by passing bills, on healthcare especially, that meet the concerns of struggling American voters — even though they could be blocked by Republican filibusters in the Senate, which require 60 votes to break, or vetoed by the president.

Ethics reform is an area the Democrats could highlight, such as beefing up financial conflict-of-interest rules in the executive branch and placing limits on presidential pardons. The post-Watergate Congress placed a heavy emphasis on ethics reform, with the creation of the Office of Government Ethics and independent Inspectors General within federal departments.

Among the challenges for the Democrats will be to restore the power of Capitol Hill, which has been the home for the past two years of an incredible shrinking Congress.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has sought to expand the power of the presidency and to govern almost by decree through signing so many executive orders with the flourish of his Sharpie felt tip pen. Already, he has signed 292 executive orders during his second term, well over 100 more than Joe Biden issued during his entire four-year term.

The conservative-dominated Supreme Court, while sometimes checking his power, has helped him create a more maximal presidency. In Trump v Slaughter, the court ruled in June that the president can fire the heads of independent regulatory agencies at his behest, without being required to show "cause".

In its landmark Trump v United States ruling in 2024, brought in connection with the criminal charges he faced over his attempt to overturn the presidential election, it decided presidents possess substantial immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts taken while in office. Among the three branches of government, Congress has felt like the third wheel.

The founding fathers, however, had a very different power ranking in mind. The legislature was supposed to be the most powerful branch of government, which is why Congress was vested with the power of the purse. The presidency was meant to be second. The Supreme Court a distant third.

Democrats on Capitol Hill will attempt to restore parity with the executive branch, especially over trade policy, and to overtake the Supreme Court. Supreme Court Justice John Roberts has been a more influential figure than the departing Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson. Incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will attempt to restore the sway of a role traditionally regarded as the second most powerful government position in the country.

After the Republicans' shellacking at the polls, it will be tempting to describe Trump as a "lame duck" president, the usual descriptor for an incumbent whose party loses control of Congress and cannot seek re-election. With Trump, that would be an act of folly. Normal nomenclature does not apply to such an abnormal president.

Trump will not be a lame duck until the final second of the final minute of his presidency. In his last supposed lame-duck phase, from his defeat at the 2020 election to inauguration day in 2021, he propagated the "Big Lie" about Joe Biden stealing the election, amassed his supporters in Washington and did little to restrain them when they first started storming the US Capitol.

Trump still has enormous executive powers at his disposal. He remains the commander-in-chief of the world's most powerful military. He still has control of the FBI and Justice Department, and could use both in an attempt to take vengeance on political opponents. Overcoming a presidential veto requires a two-thirds super-majority in both houses of Congress, which alone the Democrats cannot muster. Trump has issued 12 vetoes over the course of his two terms; congress has only overridden one of them.

By appointing as his new White House chief of staff arch loyalist Stephen Miller, the hardline architect of the ICE immigration crackdown, Trump is signally there will be no retreat from MAGA. Heading the West Wing is a figure who Trump will regard as a wartime consigliere, an aggressively combative figure in upcoming battles with Congress.

Often, if presidents are thwarted on the home front by an obstructionist Congress, they look to make their mark in the foreign realm. Trump could press for a peace deal in the Ukraine war, on terms that would likely be highly favourable towards Vladimir Putin. He could renew the kind of summitry with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, which became such a feature of his first term diplomacy.

He might agree to carve up the world into spheres of influence as part of a grand bargain with Putin and President Xi Jinping of China, which would require concerns in Taiwan. Trump has made no secret of his desire for regime change in Cuba.

As the dust settles after such an extraordinary electoral event, it is worth noting what did not happen in the 2026 congressional midterms.

For sure, Donald Trump tried to disrupt the polls beforehand, by attempting to limit postal voting and demanding, unsuccessfully, that states surrender their voter registration lists to the Justice Department in Washington.

Yet worries that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, or even federal troops, would be deployed at, or in the close vicinity of, polling stations on Election Day did not eventuate. Nor has Trump tried to interfere with the count. The Republican defeat, of course, was too big to rig. In a closer election, disputed contests could easily have become flashpoints. But it is worth pointing out that, although he has distanced himself from the results, he had not disputed them.

In the year America marked its 250th birthday, the country faced a democratic test, and passed.

Nobody was assassinated during the campaign. Election Day passed without violence. On January 3, when the new Congress is seated we will not see a repeat of the American insurrection that unfolded on January 6, 2021.

That alone, in a country as divided and fractious as America, is cause for celebration.

scraped.h1: Ella Thompson on the Melbourne music scene and new album Triumph & Sadness
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Al Newstead

Double J

Topic: Music

Ella Thompson begins touring this month behind her new album, Triumph & Sadness, a showcase of masterful soul music. ( Supplied: Nick McKinlay )

Writing her new album, Ella Thompson fell in love with a quote from French philosopher Simone Weil.

"Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity," Thompson says.

"I'm really interested in how artists and writers have responded to that idea over the centuries. How we give attention to others and ourselves; what we pay attention to and how it can also distort our view of the world."

Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

When art and attention have become increasingly "commodified and distorted, exploited and manipulated" in our current AI-and-algorithm-saturated world, Thompson's new record is its own form of generosity.

Its title, Triumph & Sadness, conveys the bittersweet.

"I'm always drawn to that sweet spot in music, art and writing," Thompson explains, "where you find that balance in between the extremes.

"For this record, every triumph, there is something sad behind it, of seeing the state of the world."

A masterful set of warm, cinematic soul music that would fit snugly into any self-respecting vinyl enthusiast's collection, the album again proves Thompson as one of Australia's underrated masters of the genre's sound and spirit.

Boasting tasteful, timeless arrangements — slinky guitars, keys and airtight rhythm section adorned with lush brass, flutes and harp — the music offers the soulful sweetness while Thompson's thoughtful lyrics provide the bitter.

She interrogates tricky realities with effortless vocal performances ranging from smouldering to show-stopping.

She scales impressive heights on the jubilant Make You Believe and My Weakness, a song inspired by a Caravaggio painting based on the myth of Narcissus and being "absorbed by things that don't really matter much,"

However, Thompson approaches the subject — losing meaningful attention and connection with others to self-obsession — with humour as much as critique.

"I think tragedy can be funny as well. We beat ourselves up about our phone addictions and all these sorts of thing, but it is kind of funny," she says.

"I like dramatic soul music. I don't necessarily like drama in my real life."

Thompson has been embedded in the Melbourne/Naarm music scene for years.

She fronted electronic duo GL, genre-shifting pop group Dorsal Fins, and has lent her imperious pipes to Paul Kelly, The Bamboos and even Mark Ronson .

But Triumph & Sadness, like her previous solo records Ripple On The Wing (2024) and Domino (2023), reaches back full circle to the jazz and soul of Thompson's childhood.

She grew up absorbing the personal and political stories, sounds and studio craft of greats like Billie Holiday, Nina Simone and Curtis Mayfield.

She was later mentored by her idol , trailblazing Australian jazz, blues and soul artist Renée Geyer , who took Thompson on her first tour at age 16.

That advice shaped Thompson's entire approach, acutely aware that the tradition she's working in, soul music, has deep social and spiritual roots.

"I try to be respectful of where this music is from and not just the aesthetic of it."

For Ella Thompson, soul music is about the connection between people, the environment and the world we live in. ( Supplied: Nick McKinlay )

Marvin Gaye and Sam Cooke's progressive protest records; Aretha Franklin and Curtis Mayfield's searing emotional deliveries — Thompson recognises that many "of those great records have a brilliant message and they're made from a particular social context".

"One that isn't too dissimilar from the one that we're living in now… There's definitely parallels. We've come a long way but in a lot of ways, we haven't."

Lesser contemporaries and countless algorithmic playlists get caught up in reproducing the genre's sound, forgetting that soul is essential, not optional.

It's a conversation between artist and listener about what it means to be human, Thompson observes.

Music that emerges from a specific community is something Thompson admires in the records she loves, and an authenticity she commits to.

"I love hearing that sense of place in music. I'm making music here in Naarm, with creatives here."

Like its predecessors, Triumph & Sadness was made alongside Thompson's regular crew: Liam McGorry, trumpet-toting alumni of Dorsal Fins and Saskwatch, and Henry Jenkins, formerly of The Cactus Channel.

Together, with a crack studio band comprising members from instrumental labelmates Surprise Chef and Karate Boogaloo, Thompson shares an intuition forged through years of collaboration.

"There's definitely a shared language [and] shorthand."

Cooking on the same wavelength, they dish up tasty grooves on Parable, the sizzling Dandelion and swooning, harp-assisted Lover's Game.

Everything was recorded in four days at an all-analogue studio in Castlemaine.

"There's no computers in the building and we cut all the band tracks direct to tape," says Thompson.

"Usually the third or fourth take… that's the one [and] there's no editing.

"All of the records from the '60s and '70s that we love so much and have studied were recorded in that way."

The pressure of getting it right is outweighed by the benefit of capturing "that raw feeling in the room. And going back to that bittersweet thing, it's falling in love with those imperfections as well."

Starting a solo career, after years of experience in the local scene, still felt in some ways like "beginning again", says Thompson.

"That can be really humbling.

"Confidence is something that's taken me a long time to build in my artistic direction. But I feel lucky to have arrived at [this] point now.

"There's nothing else I'd rather be doing than making records with my friends," she adds.

"I'm really grateful for the opportunities to be able to do that."

Thompson has just headlined her first international shows in London and Paris, where she undertook an artist residency at Cité internationale des arts, writing "songs for a month thanks to APRA … Always just gathering acorns and see how they grow."

The sense of development and community she finds in the Melbourne music scene is "really inspiring," she says.

"Our music might not reach everybody, but that's OK. It's a craft that people are really dedicated to and have a lot of respect for each other… show up for each other."

The soul of Triumph & Sadness isn't just in its sumptuous sound but its spirit of resilience.

"Where we go through these difficult parts of our lives, we still need music, art, community, friendships to uplift us out of that and feel triumph and to overcome adversity."

Ella Thompson's tour for Triumph & Sadness kicks off on November 13 at The Vanguard in Sydney.

She then plays Melbourne, Adelaide, Healesville and Meredith Music Festival in December .

What started as a test to understand how sun exposure was aging my skin took a turn that I wasn’t expecting.

What started as a test to understand how sun exposure was aging my skin took a turn that I wasn’t expecting.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Sheena Vasani

With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.

Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem , from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both.

This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside.

I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others.

The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck.

The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight.

There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score.

The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score.

The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking.

My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too.

The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun.

That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade.

I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary.

At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.

Photography by Sheena Vasani / The Verge

While some retailers were offering preorder discounts on the remastered Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time , it’s not too late to save if you missed out. Costco members can currently get $5 off the digital version online, bringing the price down to $54.99. Considering an annual Costco membership runs $65 , that discount almost offsets one month of your plan — a prime example of “gamer math.”

My colleague Andrew Webster recently shared his thoughts on Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive, noting how impressed he was with how much impact a few modern quality-of-life changes had on what is otherwise a classic experience. The updated graphics are as thoughtful as they are beautiful, pairing realistic scenery with puppet-like characters. Perhaps, more importantly, Link can now jump anytime he likes, rather than being limited to specific ledges.

Twenty-five years ago, Kevin Lewandowski founded Discogs , arguably the destination online for obsessive vinyl collectors and music nerds of all stripes. It is a marketplace for buying and selling records, obviously, but it’s also become so much more. It’s a shockingly comprehensive database that covers not just albums and singles, but all the various versions and pressings. It’s a really fun rabbit hole to disappear down when you’re trying to figure out what obscure pressing of Ministry’s The Mind is a Terrible Thing to Taste or Psalm 69 you had in high school, because you definitely blasted the cover of “Lay Lady Lay” all the time and 100 percent never owned Filth Pig .

In the years since it debuted, Discogs has grown to be much more than just a site where audiophiles go to trade rare first pressings of Beach Boys records. There are forums, groups, user-created lists, and more. It’s part eBay, part Reddit, and IMDB — just specifically for music.

With more and more people turning their back on the algorithm and rediscovering physical media , now seemed like a perfect time to check in with Lewandowski.

What is your most indispensable tool?

My AeroPress. I use it multiple times a day. In fact, I just made a coffee with it [sips coffee].

How many tabs do you have open right now?

Probably around 30 on my work computer. My personal computer is worse — probably 40 or 50.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I look at X and Instagram occasionally, but I don’t really post.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

It’s not really a gadget, but I like to tinker. Lately I’ve been playing around with Home Assistant software and built my own setup to control things like the garage door and outdoor lights. So I guess my favorite gadget is one I made myself.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

Probably a game like Rez , which came out around 2000. It’s a rhythm game where you’re almost controlling the music as you play, about as close to DJing as a video game can get. I’ve actually had an idea for my own version with a similar concept. It’s still just an idea, though.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I’ll either clear everything off my desk or change locations completely. Go to a coffee shop or sit outside. Sometimes I just need a different environment.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

Records. I was at Mint Gallery in Portland last week and picked up four. I still really like going into a record store and finding something to bring home. And I also recently picked up three reissues from the Moodsville / Acoustic Sounds series.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

The Secret Weapon.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

I don’t use memes very often, but one I was kind of proud of was putting a Discogs screen into a North Korean war room photo. I was advised that maybe it wasn’t one for the company chat.
