The public option sounds like a step toward universal health care, but it’s really a delay tactic. The latest versions would force public plans to mimic private insurers, while the fight over the arcane details buys the industry another decade or two.

The concept of the public option is designed as a distraction. Wasting years on policy rabbit holes is the point. It’s a perfect nonsolution to our three-headed crisis of health care cost, access, and quality. (Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

T he difference between a vampire and a bad health care policy idea is that vampires jump out of their coffins and drink blood at sunset. Undead health care proposals emerge from think tank closets and suck the life out of useful ideas when the sun rises on a national health care debate. As public fury at exploding costs and deadly corporate claims denials boils over into historic Democratic election gains, can someone please find a wooden stake for the public option?

Improved and expanded Medicare for All would give everyone full coverage at much lower cost than the combined private premiums, taxes, and out-of-pocket payments that are eating up family income today. But it violates a cardinal rule of federal politics: never do anything that causes corporations or the ultrawealthy any pain.

Instead, corporate Democrats wanting to be seen “doing something” about the imploding US health care system have long peddled a vague public option notion because it sounds like the marriage of a big noncorporate vision (it’s public!) with competition and freedom of choice (it’s an option!). Liberal nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and pundits revived its rotting corpse in response to pro–Medicare for All candidates’ primary victories and Tuesday night’s stunning results.

It’s a perfect nonsolution to our three-headed crisis of health care cost, access, and quality. Nobody knows what a “public option” is because there’s no common definition and nothing like it has ever been seen in the wild, so it can be anything weaselly politicians want it to be. It needs to be put out of our misery.

T here’s danger in chasing the content of various “public options.” The concept is designed as a distraction. Wasting years on policy rabbit holes is the point. But killing it requires some analysis, so it’s worth pointing out that every one of its shape-shifting forms withers under cursory scrutiny.

Rising Democratic Senate star Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) says she “wouldn’t say no forever” to a White House run if “there’s not anyone else who’s on the right path.” Slotkin’s favored path leads to one of the sillier public option proposals. In January, Slotkin, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-IL) introduced the Affordable Consumer Health Options and Insurance Competition Enhancement (CHOICE) Act, or the Affordable CHOICE Act (“ACA” — get it?). The CHOICE Act would get the federal government into the business of selling crummy insurance to almost nobody by allowing the feds to market their own versions of “bronze,” “silver,” and “gold” plans on the Obamacare exchanges.

Even at record enrollment, the Affordable Care Act exchanges covered less than 7 percent of Americans. Nearly everyone with insurance has Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurance through a job. Three-quarters of US working-age adults are eligible for job-based coverage, nearly all of which is considered legally “affordable” by ACA rules. That means almost all workers are barred from receiving ACA premium subsidies. Presumably they could buy a Slotkinized plan by paying the full premium cost if they really wanted one. Nice option.

Subsidized or not, Slotkinized plans would cover only between 58 and 82 percent of the actual cost of health care after premiums, depending on the “metal” label attached to the plan.

CHOICE Act public option plans would have to play the same failed “cost control” game as private insurers, building their own private provider networks and trading privileged access to their patients for discounts off market price from providers who join those networks. So, Senator Slotkin’s options will come loaded with the copays, coinsurance, and deductibles that private insurance corporations use to coerce patients into accepting in-network doctors and hospitals. It’s a mockery of “affordability” for patients and would offer neither better nor worse provider payments than UnitedHealth, Aetna, or Cigna.

The contrast between Senator Slotkin and the winner of Michigan’s other Senate seat couldn’t be clearer. At his victory celebration, Abdul El-Sayed turned his three-line slogan into a roaring call and response, with Medicare for All as the closer: “Money out of . . . POLITICS! Money in your . . . POCKET! Medicare for . . . ALL!” Corporate Democrats are still trying to paint Medicare for All as too radical and urge progressive winners toward “moderation,” torturing voting data into arguments about electability. The facts: In 2024, Elissa Slotkin defeated Mike Rogers by a 0.3 percent margin. With unlimited American Israel Public Affairs Committee and corporate cash arrayed against him and in the face of nakedly racist opposition, El-Sayed beat Rogers by a full 7 percent.

C riticize one slippery idea and the optionites will just say, “Hey, I didn’t mean that public option.” In two recent posts , economist Paul Krugman hyped a Medicare “buy-in” version to “allow individuals, and possibly more important, employers, to sign up for Medicare benefits, paying actuarially fair premiums to Medicare reflecting the health status of their workers” (emphasis added). Krugman insists that “many people and many employers would surely take it.”

Surely many who need it the most wouldn’t. The US health care system is so broken in part because we’ve asked six million separate employers who don’t know and shouldn’t be expected to know much about health care to buy it for most of us. But even they know that premiums reflecting the health status of workers would immediately price employers who most need an affordable option — those with high-cost employees — out of any “buy-in.”

The Krugmanite option violates a core Medicare precept. Of course, individual Medicare premiums shouldn’t exist at all. Paying taxes should buy your health care. Even so, except for a few high-income people, everyone pays the same Medicare premiums right now. “Actuarially fair premiums” tailored to health risks contradict the basic notions of solidarity at the heart of public benefits and the very idea of insurance, which is supposed to pool risk across groups of people, not segregate it.

Offering existing original Medicare as a standalone option for employers and nondisabled individuals younger than sixty-five to “buy” is an idea only a Nobel-winning trade economist dabbling in health care could love. Original Medicare’s cost-sharing has already driven most eligible people into Medicare Advantage plans run by the very companies that Krugman dismissed as “parasites.”

So, to fully cover their workers, employers would have to — you guessed it — buy supplemental insurance from the private insurance industry. Never underestimate the power of Nancy Pelosi’s Iron Law of Democratic Health Policy: Congress shall make no law respecting expansion of health care access that does not subsidize the private health insurance industry, and all gestures to the contrary shall be performance art.

S ome people may actually take these ideas seriously, but the essence of public optionism is a bully’s taunt.

Virtually every economic analysis of the issue has concluded that a single-payer system would generate large savings to fund both expanding coverage to everyone and dramatically improving existing coverage. Two key sources of those savings are huge, useless administrative costs: the insurance industry’s skim, and the massive bureaucracies that providers have to build just to get paid by thousands of private insurance plans whose terms and members constantly change.

Original Medicare is far more efficient than private insurance, spending 97 to 98 percent of revenue on actual health care, while private plans capture more than 10 percent of our premiums as overhead and profit.

If public insurance is so darned efficient, the argument goes, a public option should outcompete private insurance. That would have the dual benefit of giving people cheaper, better coverage, and proving to a socialism-averse public that something like Medicare for All could work. So prove it, lefties!

The problem, of course, is that operating in existing markets under rules that will force public options to behave like private insurers strips these plans of the permanence and power that make Medicare and truly “public” insurance relatively efficient.

Medicare controls prices because it permanently covers everyone in the largest group of people who use a lot of health care. When you turn sixty-five and enroll, you’re in for life. If hospitals want to treat the group of people most likely to need their services, they have to take Medicare prices.

The CHOICE Act makes a head fake in that direction. The bill instructs the Health and Human Services secretary to create a provider network and set hospital and physician prices “through a negotiated agreement with health care providers,” without naming which providers or how they’ll negotiate. In the absence of successful negotiations, CHOICE Act plans can just pay any claim at existing Medicare prices. That may sound like a little public muscle flexing to hold prices down, but the CHOICE Act also allows hospitals and doctors to opt out of the public options’ networks, turning Medicare prices into a backstop that applies only to out-of-network claims.

Having a guaranteed right to impose low prices on out-of-network care would give public option plans a little pricing leverage. But in the end, the Slotkinized plans would likely wind up creating networks and setting prices in a manner similar to private plans, whose tussles with hospitals are based entirely on market power. Having surrendered the power that allows Medicare to set its own prices and competing as start-ups with private insurance to entice “covered lives” to enroll, the public options would soon find themselves face-to-face with massively powerful regional health systems affiliated with Ivy League schools or the Catholic Church. Have fun.

To persuade the necessary “covered lives” to enroll, CHOICE Act plans will have to ape private plans by constantly marketing themselves and enrolling and disenrolling clients. Alongside the headache of managing networks, that work requires skimming billions in premium dollars off the top, just like private insurers.

Slotkin, Krugman, and their optional pals have also managed the remarkable feat of finding an idea that would add a little more bureaucracy to the already bloated administrative expenses that choke US hospitals. The CHOICE Act doesn’t create an option. It envisions hundreds of local public option plans with premiums set geographically — ACA plans are offered on a county-by-county basis. Viewed from a hospital’s business office, that means at least three separate local plans, one per “metal,” with each becoming just another payer with its own unique prices, networks, utilization review, and patient cost-sharing to follow, track, bill, and sue when payments don’t show up.

Finally, should policymakers and regulators fool themselves into thinking that these options will be efficient because, you know, they’re “public” and offer below-market premiums, the plans face a potential flood of high-risk sign-ups (the “adverse selection” problem). As Jim Kahn and Hank Abrons point out in Health Justice Monitor , even the more-expansive-than-Krugman version offered by The American Prospect is particularly vulnerable on this question. Being stuck with disproportionately high-cost patients wouldn’t be good for plans trying to prove the efficiency of public insurance, but it would be great for politicians seeking to prove that the government really can’t do health care.

We could go on forever about the details, but the content doesn’t really matter. These ideas are little more than lumps of lead over which political alchemists like Slotkin and Krugman chant their two magic words to dazzle us into believing they’re creating gold. Public options aren’t incremental reforms toward universal coverage. They’re increments of nothing that enable the status quo.

This fantasy nonidea endures because fighting for it achieves a critical bipartisan goal: buying time for corporate control of the rest of the health care system. A legislative timeline would likely look like this: two years until the Democrats have a shot at the White House, followed by a year or two of GOP panic about “communism.” Throw in two to three years to write the regulationss, then five or ten years to roll out the plans and watch them fail. Presto! A decade or two of corporate looting passes, with trillions of dollars squandered and another million or two preventable deaths.

There are plenty of meaningful steps on the way to a publicly financed universal health care system that ensures everyone gets the care they need without facing personal bankruptcy or fighting off bloodthirsty private bureaucrats. Politicians who want to improve access or cost control could jump on a few of these sample bandwagons. Don’t expect a rush, though. Most of these ideas take a bite out of the industry’s hide, and letting poor people who make an extra penny keep their health care will give alleged conservatives apoplexy. But here they are:

Set fair hospital prices by regulation for all payers, to stop the gouging of employers and patients and end the episodic waves of terror that engulf communities when big insurance companies and hospitals threaten patients with loss of access during local rate negotiations.

Lower the age at which everyone becomes eligible for Medicare to fifty or fifty-five.

Eliminate the extreme cost-sharing in the original Medicare program.

Abolish the Medicare Advantage privatization scheme that lets private insurance companies overcharge the federal government tens of billions of dollars a year, and use the savings to fund said elimination of original Medicare cost-sharing.

Buck Washington, DC’s current antitrust fad by lifting restrictions on employers who want to join together to bargain for health care and administer benefits. Look, employer control of health care makes no sense. But if corporate politicians fantasize that it’s a route to better benefits and lower costs, let bosses gather the power to control prices and administrative costs, as long as they do it themselves without the insurance industry, and as long as they’re willing to pay the price of offering uniform plans across their cartel — no more tiny tweaks to networks or boutique cost-sharing provisions for each employer.

Dramatically expand the time people can stay on Medicaid. Medicaid’s constant means-testing makes it an unreliable source of coverage. California applied for a waiver to keep kids enrolled through the first five years of their lives instead of making their parents reapply every year. Do more of that and for longer.

The worst thing about public optionism is enduring smug lectures that Medicare for All is a political fantasy that could never happen from people promoting a vague, unworkable idea now enjoying its twenty-third year of politically viable nonexistence. Yet The American Prospect casually assumes that a series of essential Medicare for All elements against which the industry will fight like rabid dogs can easily be grafted onto a public option.

Health care is a public good. Pretending that having government act like a health insurance corporation will do anything useful is absurd. Let’s kill this putrefying political monster right now.

John Canham-Clyne is an independent health care journalist and publisher of the online investigative newsletter Healing and Stealing .

scraped.description: Skepticism toward moral absolutes has made the modern mind leery of the very idea of evil. Philosopher Susan Neiman makes the case that explaining wrongdoing is not the same as reckoning with its moral significance.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:

Skepticism toward moral absolutes has made the modern mind leery of the very idea of evil. Philosopher Susan Neiman makes the case that explaining wrongdoing is not the same as reckoning with its moral significance.

Susan Neiman argues that understanding Donald Trump requires that we take evil seriously. Her latest book asks what happens when we allow cynicism to displace moral judgment. (Nelson Almeida / AFP via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

Review of Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era by Susan Neiman (W. W. Norton & Company, 2026)

L eftists have an unusual relationship to the language of good and evil. On the one hand, we have a reputation for being righteous. . . . at times even self-righteous. Our publications are saturated with enough morally strident language to make a preacher blush. Even the most “scientific” of scientific socialists aren’t entirely immune, from tireless invocations of Rev Martin Luther King Jr and constant demands for justice and freedom for all to calls to end subordination and marginalization around the globe . On the other hand, leftists tend to be averse to describing structures, let alone people, as evil. Exploitative? Yes. Domineering? Of course. But evil? At best, that’s language reserved for your Hannah Arendt reading group.

Philosopher Susan Neiman takes umbrage at this reticence. Author of the acclaimed Evil in Modern Thought and the controversial Left is Not Woke , Neiman thinks we ought to call a spade and spade and describe the Trump administration as what it is: evil. The disturbing question that follows is: If what Donald Trump stands for is evil, why have millions of people chosen to get behind him not once but three times? As Neiman herself notes:

Knowing as much as can be known about a public figure whose cruelty and corruption have been on display for a decade, how was it possible that Americans elected him twice? One New York friend pointed out that no one who ever dealt with the man wanted to see him again — except for the American people.

But Neiman is less interested in explaining why Americans voted for Trump than in the larger philosophical question of what constitutes evil. As she writes, “My concern is with the moral ideas that Donald Trump embodies and reinforces, ideas that are destructive enough to warrant the word evil .”

N eiman’s understanding of modern evil is deeply indebted to Hannah Arendt’s pioneering description of it as “banal.” She acknowledges that Arendt’s description of Adolf Eichmann himself as a thoughtless man devoid of hateful antisemitic feelings is untrue. But Arendt’s broader point about modern evil lacking any “Satanic majesty” remains true. Neiman reminds us that the “Holocaust could never have happened without the willing participation of millions of people who were not particularly committed fascists or fascists of any kind. They were simply willing to accept whatever demands made their lives easier.”

This all-too-human tendency to fall not through active malice but selfishness and indifference is one Neiman thinks is very characteristic of modern American history. Neiman notes how since 1945, “it’s hard to find an example of US foreign policy that isn’t principally Schmittian, though they are usually accompanied by the sort of liberal hypocrisy that Schmitt despised.” Carl Schmitt , the German jurist who joined the Nazi party in 1933, understood politics fundamentally as a struggle between friends and enemies and rejected liberal appeals to universal principles as an ideological fiction that masked power. Schmitt would likely be pleased that the second Trump administration has largely dropped even the veneer of liberal hypocrisy. If hypocrisy is the tribute vice pays to virtue, even the Bush administration at least had the decency to labor for months to convince the American people that the Iraq War was justified. When attacking Venezuela and Iran, not to mention saber-rattling at arrogant Greenlanders and Canadians, the Trump administration is typically much more transparent about the unbridled self-interest at play. After deposing Nicolás Maduro, Trump relished America’s access to Venezuelan oil, proclaiming “to the victor belong the spoils.”

Neiman’s core worry is that the transparently evil cynicism on display will become so normalized that we ignore its vulgarity. As the “Schmitt-Trump consensus grows, it’s easy to conclude that no other outlook is possible, and cynicism becomes inevitable.” While I sympathize with this outlook, it does seem to run counter to the longer history of American atrocities Neiman chronicles. If it is true that most American foreign policy since World War II has been basically Schmittian, it would seem that Trump simply constitutes a further moral step downward rather than a new kind of wicked hegemony. Sometimes Neiman gestures in this direction as when she insists this is “not a book about Donald Trump” but about “. . . . the conditions that allowed him rise.” These include the “imperialism the US has practiced for over a century,” which she insists can only be called “evil.” If that’s the case, then what is at stake is really more a general American malaise than some transformative and deepening “‘Schmitt-Trump consensus.”

Neiman often seems to want to pull back from such a pessimistic thesis. For instance, while she disagrees with the thrust of US foreign policy, she nonetheless expresses deep respect for “individual members of the military.” Neiman admires how their training prizes duty, fellowship, service, and sacrifice — all ideals someone like Trump simply doesn’t understand. It was exactly these principles that led Neiman to hope that “soldiers sworn to defend the Constitution would never follow the worst of his orders after seeing how thoroughly their commander in chief disdained the values they upheld.” Those hopes were dashed when Trump 2.0 strode to power and replaced the military administration with his coterie of brownnoses and appointed Pete Hegseth secretary of war. Neiman insists that we relearn the watchwords of Trump 1.0: “Don’t normalize this.” Doing so helps make the evil deeds of administration seem typical, and consequently over time, not morally objectionable.

I think this ambiguity over whether Trumpism constitutes a continuation of, or break with, the past flows from a few sources. As a leftist, Neiman is keen to acknowledge the harm wrought by American foreign and domestic policy. However, I suspect Neiman is reluctant to suggest to her largely American readers that the country has always had a predilection toward Trumpy behavior. More strategically, she may worry that doing so would further legitimate Trumpism by making it seem normal. It would also blunt the force of the immanent critiques often used to mobilize Americans against their government’s abuses: holding up the country’s shining principles as a mirror to its often-brutal practices and saying, “We don’t look like we ought to.”

Whatever the case, I think Neiman would be better off following Arendt herself by situating the emergence of Trumpism in a much more concrete historical narrative. There was tendency, until recently, for many — especially conservative anti-Trumpers — to describe the Trump administration as an aberration in the American right’s history. Contemporary historians are increasingly pushing back on this view. In Taking America Back , David Austin Walsh stresses how the American right has always had plenty of overt racists, conspiracy theorists, Augusto Pinochet apologists, and outright fascists. William F. Buckley, the alleged poster boy for a more intellectual and less extreme conservatism, was happy to recommend segregation and defend Francisco Franco to own the libs.

Under Trumpism, the more extreme factions of the Right have simply moved from the back seat to the driver’s seat. But they have always been a part of American life. Taking a dialectical approach to American history, however, means recognizing that, just because many Americans have done evil things, the country as a whole is not evil. If anything, the inspiring story of America is of progressive movements successfully mobilizing against wicked practices to bring about a more just society. The arc of the moral universe may be long . . .

M uch of Neiman’s book ranges beyond its central concern, taking on topics from the hegemony of neoliberal ideology to war crimes in Gaza to her long-standing critique of wokism. At their best, these chapters read more like essays that collectively present a panoramic view of the world.

The chapter on wokism was especially interesting. Neiman is very critical of wokism for both principled and strategic reasons. She insists that the Left ought to reclaim its defining principle of inclusive universalism. As she puts it, the “idea of universalism once defined the Left; international solidarity was its watchword. This was just what distinguished it from the right, which recognized no deep connections, and few real obligations, to anyone outside its own circle. The Left demanded that the circle encompass the globe.” Neiman is very critical of identity politics, which eschews universalism in order to insist that “you have deep connections and real obligations only to those who belong to your tribe, though others may have limited use as allies.”

I have considerable sympathy for this view. Neiman is no doubt historically correct that trading Enlightenment reason and universalism for postmodern skepticism and what the Marxist David Harvey calls “militant particularism” constituted a shift from the Left’s historical stance. Marxist literary theorist Terry Eagleton made a similar observation in The Illusions of Postmodernism , noting the irony that some leftists had come to endorse philosophical positions typically associated with the Right. While motivated by different political concerns, this skepticism shares the conservative privileging of cultural particularity over reason and universalism.

A Left that embraced universalism would, of course, be more comfortable with the language of “moral idealism” Neiman affirms, and that would, by and large, be beneficial. That said, I think the question of how to recommit to universalism without falling back into exclusionary modes of thinking that imagine a single perspective ought to speak for everyone remains unresolved. Here, I think the best work has been done by philosophers working at the intersection of liberalism, Marxism, and black radical thought, notably Tommie Shelby and the late Charles Mills.

Both Shelby and Mills are comfortable couching demands for racial justice in the universalistic terms of Rawlsian political theory. But they recognize that universalism risks becoming what Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel criticized as an “abstract universalism” if it is insensitive to the particular forms of subordination experienced around the globe. In the United States, securing the basic rights and liberties to which everyone ought to be entitled means renouncing the legacy of systemic racism.

I was slightly more frustrated with the Chapter on “Socialism Reconsidered.” Despite the title, much of it reads like a microcosm of the book itself, weighing in on any number of different issues in quick succession. The most interesting sections of the chapter reintroduce readers to the socialism of Albert Einstein.

Einstein was, of course, a self-described socialist who was outspoken about his desire for humankind to evolve past the predatory capitalist phase of existence. But, as Neiman points out, these political convictions are rarely addressed by American biographers and commentators, who are usually content to footnote Einstein’s nonprofessional interest in “social justice.” Reacquainting readers with Einstein’s convictions is worthwhile, but the chapter would have been far more interesting if it had remained focused on reconstructing and developing his political ideas more systematically.

It’s perhaps inevitable that Neiman’s book sometimes ranges too broadly, given the complexity of the era it attempts to understand and critique. Anyone who wades into American politics these days can feel immediately overwhelmed by the sheer volume of issues demanding attention: wokeness, neoliberalism, identity politics, Trumpism, the rise of fascism, oligarchs’ control of social media, war in the Middle East, and so much more. There is a risk that the crushing weight of all this might lead many to lapse into the apathetic withdrawal Neiman worries about. Or perhaps worse, to reach for simplifying ideologies that offer a retreat from the complexity of the world. It’s to Neiman’s Socratic credit that she offers moral clarity without resorting to the comfort of cheaply bought moral certainties.

Matt McManus is an assistant professor at Spelman College. He is the author of The Political Right and Equality and The Political Theory of Liberal Socialism among other books.

scraped.description: Comedian Deniz Göktaş spent 88 days in a high-security prison for insulting Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. He turned his sentence into a punch line, but the chilling consequences of the case extend far beyond one comedian.

scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Comedian Deniz Göktaş spent 88 days in a high-security prison for insulting Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. He turned his sentence into a punch line, but the chilling consequences of the case extend far beyond one comedian.

Comedian Deniz Göktaş’s imprisonment over a performance is of a piece with Turkey’s longer history of conflict between political satire and state power. (YouTube)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

H ave you ever made a joke that offended someone? Maybe they took it personally or stopped speaking to you. A joke can put strain on a relationship or leave someone feeling isolated. But what if the consequences for a joke go far beyond social fallout? What if a comedy performance lands you in a high-security prison cell? For Deniz Göktaş, this question is no longer hypothetical.

Until recently, Göktaş performed for relatively small audiences, playing bars in Kadıköy, an Istanbul district known for political satire, and occasionally in university halls elsewhere in Turkey. He was part of a niche comedy scene.

Things changed when he took his show to one of Istanbul’s most prominent stages and uploaded the performance to YouTube, opening it to a much wider audience. He knew the show might attract attention. Not just because of the words he spoke onstage, but also because the title and stage image played on a grisly visual gag. Ölü Deniz (“Dead Sea”) was a dark play on his first name, Deniz (“Sea”), while an enormous, sculpted image of his face lay on its side as if decapitated.

What began as a night of laughter would end with Göktaş spending eighty-eight days behind bars in a high-security prison. His case exposed not only the limits of free expression in Turkey but also the fraught relationship between political satire and political power.

T he thirty-two-year-old comedian was detained at Istanbul airport on July 2, after his ninety-minute special was released on YouTube. Prosecutors cited passages from the performance in bringing charges: insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, inciting public hatred and hostility, and praising crime or criminals.

At his first hearing, on September 28, 2026, Göktaş addressed the court:

“As a comedian, seeing that sentences can have such a powerful impact makes me proud. But as a citizen, I am saddened by my country’s record on freedom of expression.”

He said he worried the case would discourage others from performing and lead them to censor themselves.

The court ordered his release after sentencing. By then, he had spent eighty-eight days in pretrial detention. He told the court he had been held in a cell without sunlight or contact with other prisoners at Çorlu Karatepe High Security Prison, a facility known in Turkey as a well-type prison.

The court acquitted him of praising crime or criminals. It convicted him of insulting the president and, because public hatred and hostility were not established, reclassified the incitement charge as insulting religious values. The sentences were eleven months and twenty days and seven months and fifteen days, respectively.

The case raised a question beyond the sentences themselves: How had a comedy performance been transformed into a criminal prosecution? Göktaş’s defense argued that prosecutors had removed the alleged offenses from their original context onstage, but the heart of the matter was a dispute over how a comedian’s words should be interpreted.

W hile Göktaş was still in prison, I spoke with his friend and fellow stand-up comedian Emre Günsal.

Günsal distinguishes Göktaş’s comedy from much of what passes for “political humor” in Turkey. A comedian can get an easy laugh simply by mentioning a politician, referring to a current scandal, or repeating a political cliché the audience already agrees with. In Turkey, Günsal says, that is the least risky kind of political comedy.

Göktaş’s work is more deliberate. He combines political satire with social observation, using comedy to say something about the political climate, social tensions, and the shrinking space for free expression. The result can be both funny and cathartic for those who feel alienated or frustrated by the society in which they live. Günsal considers Göktaş one of the leading figures of this tradition in Turkey today.

This may help explain Göktaş’s appeal among young people and audiences opposed to the government. Günsal describes Göktaş’s work as a form of emotional release, then trails off: “Seeing someone stand onstage, knowing millions of people will watch, and say the things that others are afraid to say openly because of what might happen to them. . . . ”

Göktaş made a similar point in an interview with The New York Times after his release. He recalled a viewer writing beneath his performance that watching it made them feel as though they lived in a free country. The comment, he said, captured exactly what he had hoped to achieve.

But he was modest about comedy’s political power. Humor, he suggested, can help people feel understood, given them motivation and the courage to speak, and offer psychological support.

P olitical satire and state power has a long and vexed history in Turkey.

In 1946, two of the country’s best-known writers, Sabahattin Ali and Aziz Nesin, founded Markopaşa , a socialist-leaning satirical newspaper that sharply criticized class inequality and the government of the day. The paper faced distribution restrictions, pressure on printing houses, confiscations, closures, and criminal prosecutions. Its writers and cartoonists were arrested or forced into exile. Markopaşa remains one of the most important examples of socialist and oppositional humor in Turkey.

In later decades, political satire found new forms in cabaret theater and humor magazines, including the work of Ferhan Şensoy and the satirical magazines of the 1990s and 2000s. By the time of the 2013 Gezi Park protests, irony and satire had become prominent forms of political expression.

The protests began with opposition to plans to redevelop Gezi Park near Istanbul’s Taksim Square. The government framed the unrest in terms of hooliganism and terrorism. Many protesters, meanwhile, used humor and irony to defy the government’s account of the movement. Researchers have documented how humor and satire became a form of dissent in an environment where traditional media were subject to tight control.

In his courtroom defense, Göktaş placed himself in this tradition, invoking Aziz Nesin, Rıfat Ilgaz , Ferhan Şensoy, and Turkey’s major satirical magazines. Then he reached back to Nasreddin Hodja , the legendary Anatolian folk figure whose stories have circulated for centuries. Traditionally dated to 1208–1284, Hodja occupies a place in Anatolian culture somewhat comparable to the traditions of folk wisdom and social satire in American humor.

Göktaş distilled the connection between that tradition and contemporary Turkey into a single sentence: “If Nasreddin Hodja were doing stand-up today, half his show would be about President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.”

Göktaş argued that calling Erdoğan, who has governed Turkey for more than two decades, a “dictator” was political characterization, not an insult. As the country’s most powerful political figure, Erdoğan should be expected to face satire and harsh criticism, he said. He argued that politicians must be open to ridicule as well as praise.

The language of this debate is not new in Turkey.

A few days ago, I came across a street bookseller on the narrow Kadıköy street where Deniz Göktaş had performed stand-up for years. Among the books on the shelves was Görülmüştür , a collection by journalist and writer İlhan Selçuk, published in the 1980s.

Leafing through it, I found an essay titled “Freedom of Thought and Tolerance.” One sentence stood out: “Where freedom of thought does not exist, tolerance is nothing more than an empty word.”

Selçuk’s point resonates in the Göktaş case. If political or religious satire is tolerated only as long as it offends no one, can that be called freedom of expression?

O ne of the clearest examples of this problem was Göktaş’s joke about “divers.”

Prosecutors treated it as an insult to women who wear modest swimwear because of their religious beliefs. In court, Göktaş said he used the audience’s expectations to set up the joke. He described people emerging from the sea with their hair concealed and their bodies covered in black clothing. The audience, he said, assumed that he was describing women wearing modest Islamic swimwear. Then came the punch line : “f–king divers.”

The case raised a basic question: Can a stand-up performance be judged solely by a written transcript, stripped of its context onstage?

Göktaş invoked American comedian Lenny Bruce, who had faced similar problems. Bruce satirized the courts with the line, “In the Halls of Justice the only justice is in the halls.” He was repeatedly arrested and prosecuted on obscenity charges during the 1960s. In 1964, a New York court sentenced him to four months in a workhouse. He remained free while his appeal was pending and died in 1966 without serving the sentence. Thirty-seven years after his death, in 2003, New York governor George Pataki granted him a posthumous pardon.

Bruce’s trials showed how words spoken by a comedian onstage should not be evaluated independently of their delivery, facial expressions, timing, and relationship with the audience.

Göktaş argued that tone of voice, pauses, physical performance, audience reactions, and the surprise of the punch line all help make up a joke’s meaning. He compared evaluating a stand-up performance by its transcript to understanding a film by listening only to its soundtrack.

T o better understand how Turkish law treats the line between satire and incitement, I spoke with Professor Tolga Şirin. Göktaş was still being held in a high-security prison.

For Şirin, any legal assessment had to begin with context.

“What does it mean within a stand-up performance?” he asked. A legal assessment, he said, must account for irony, exaggeration, satire, and the possibility that a comedian will deliberately lead an audience in one direction before reversing its expectations. Evaluating a few sentences only according to their literal meaning can exclude other reasonable interpretations and privilege the harshest possible criminal reading.

Şirin stressed that this was not merely an aesthetic question: “The fact that a statement offends or disturbs some people is not sufficient in itself.” Context matters particularly to the charge of inciting public hatred and hostility. Under the Turkish Penal Code, the offense requires more than a statement that people find offensive. It also requires the emergence of a clear and imminent danger to public safety.

Prosecutors cited complaints submitted through CİMER, Turkey’s online public petition and complaints system operating under Turkey’s presidency.

In his defense, Göktaş addressed the 185 complaints submitted against him. He argued that the overwhelming majority of complainants had never watched his full performance but had instead reacted to selectively edited clips circulated on social media. He described the backlash as an artificially orchestrated campaign.

For Şirin, the complaint count alone could not establish a legally significant danger. Otherwise, organized groups could make speech they disliked into a punishable offense simply by launching petition campaigns.

“Public peace is not measured by the number of people who are offended,” he said.

Göktaş said he performed Ölü Deniz 198 times over approximately three years, before more than a hundred thousand people in cities across Turkey, without receiving complaints about the statements in question. According to him, the controversy began only after the performance was uploaded to YouTube and short clips started circulating on social media.

“What development has caused a statement made and made accessible months ago to suddenly create a clear and imminent danger today?” Şirin asked.

When I asked whether the prosecution could affect other comedians and artists, Şirin’s answer was unequivocal: “This is absolutely an act of intimidation.”

According to Şirin, Göktaş had pushed against the fear surrounding political figures and sensitive subjects that many people hesitate to joke about. In Şirin’s view, the proceedings could deter other comedians and artists from crossing the same boundaries.

G ünsal’s account shows how the chilling effect described by Şirin can manifest itself on the stand-up stage.

Small comedy venues in Istanbul have long provided spaces where comedians can speak relatively freely. The risk changes when a performance circulates on the internet. Jokes lose their original context and reach a much larger audience.

After Göktaş’s arrest, Günsal saw comedians grow more reluctant to post political sets.

He believes the greater problem is not simply censorship but the inability to tell where the line lies. “There is no clear line telling you, ‘Say this and you go to prison, but you can say that,’” he explained. Even careful comedians cannot know how their words will later be interpreted. The uncertainty can result in performers ruling out jokes before they have even written them.

Günsal knows that risk firsthand. In April 2020, he was arrested after a clip from one of his performances circulated on social media. The case involved comments about Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder of the Turkish Republic, and the historical religious figures Rumi and Shams of Tabriz.

He spent eleven days in prison. In 2021, he was sentenced to three years and five months; the sentence was suspended. Six years later, while Deniz Göktaş was behind bars, Günsal tells me that political comedy had become both more difficult and more necessary.

After his release, Göktaş told The New York Times that he never regretted releasing the performance during his time in prison, not even for a second. As his popularity grew, he said, he had more to lose and began censoring his own material even before his arrest.

Asked about American comedians’ complaints about cancel culture and online backlash, he replied: “I don’t want to brag, but we have cancel culture — and jail.”

T here is another revealing detail in the Göktaş case.

When the investigation began, he was abroad. According to his courtroom defense, he cut his vacation short and returned to Turkey rather than fleeing.

He said that most of his close friends had moved abroad because they no longer saw a future in the country. He had been trying to persuade them to come back.

Günsal described this decision as one of the qualities he most admired in his friend. Günsal believes Göktaş could perform stand-up in English and appear regularly on stages abroad. But Göktaş does not want to build a new home somewhere else. That determination to keep calling Turkey home is something Günsal admires.

Deniz Göktaş is no longer in prison. But the impact of his case cannot be measured solely by his release on September 28. Perhaps the more telling measure will be the jokes not written, the performances never uploaded to the internet, and the comedians who censor themselves before finishing a sentence because they cannot predict where the legal boundaries lie.

The Göktaş case is not merely about whether one comedian crossed the limits of free expression. It is also a struggle over who gets to draw those limits in Turkey.

Dora Mengüç is a journalist who previously served as news manager at Sözcü TV and has worked across major newsrooms for more than two decades. He is currently a correspondent for Deutsche Welle and writes internationally for outlets including Le Parisien Matin .

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Due Process

"It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here ... to warrant the unusual step of ... find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."

Eugene Volokh | 11.7.2026 12:25 PM

From U.S. v. SGO Corp. Ltd. , decided Tuesday by Judge Kathleen Williams (S.D. Fla.):

For a six-year period, the Government investigated SGO executives for their role in a money laundering and bribery scheme related to the May, 2016 Philippine elections. The investigation culminated in a six-count indictment (" First Indictment "), returned on August 8, 2024, which charged [executives of] SGO and Smartmatic … [with] conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (" FCPA ") (Count I); violations of the FCPA (Count II); conspiracy to commit money laundering (Count III); and international laundering of monetary instruments (Counts IV, V, and VI). The FCPA "prohibits officers of a domestic concern from making corrupt payments to a 'foreign official.'"

SGO was not charged. In fact, SGO had been cooperating with the Government since 2021, years before the First Indictment was returned. {Although the Parties may dispute the breadth and quality of SGO's efforts to cooperate, there is no question that SGO and the Government were engaged in discussions and the exchange of documents related to this matter.}

The original trial date was set for October 7, 2024 … [but was eventually reset for 2026]….

As the court notes, the Trump Administration was skeptical of FCPA prosecutions, deprioritized FCPA enforcement generally, and "elected to close FCPA investigations into multiple companies." But despite that, in October 2025, the government added SGO as a defendant in the case. SGO then moved to dismiss the superseding indictment, alleging vindictive and selective prosecution, and sought discovery in support of that motion, "premised on political events that have embroiled Smartmatic in the wake of the 2020 election":

Since that election, multiple high-profile individuals and organizations connected to then-Former President Donald Trump have alleged that Smartmatic, a subsidiary of SGO, interfered in the election…. President Trump has also reposted content blaming Smartmatic for interfering in United States and Venezuelan elections, calling Smartmatic "disgraceful" and expressing that those who "rigged" the 2020 election must pay. In response to the statements by President Trump's confederates, Smartmatic brought various defamation suits, which are largely ongoing. SGO contends that President Trump's personal animus against SGO and assertion of its rights against President Trump's confederates precipitated the filing of the Superseding Indictment….

The court lays out the demanding standard for defendants' attempts to get discovery related to allegations of vindictive or selective prosecution, but concludes that in this case the standard was met. A brief excerpt (for more, including citations to precedents to which the court analogizes this case, see the full opinion ):

First, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by evidence that the Government bucked a trend in enforcement activity in prosecuting the defendant…. [W]hile the Blanche and Bondi Memos and Executive Order 14209 explicitly announced an intention to rein in and limit FCPA enforcement, particularly against corporations, SGO was charged, nonetheless.

Second, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the timing between a defendant's assertion of a right and the allegedly vindictive prosecutorial act…. [Here,] it is telling that the Government chose not to indict SGO originally, that SGO was charged only after President Trump reassumed office and after SGO had been cooperating with the Government for years, and that the Government has presented no evidence adduced between the First and Superseding Indictments warranting SGO's addition as a defendant.

Third, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the Executive, prosecutor, or law enforcement's stated positions, even when they do not explicitly admit that the case was brought against the defendant for an improper purpose…. The Court finds probative not just that President Trump signed an executive order regarding FCPA enforcement but also that President Trump has personally expressed animus towards SGO regarding election interference. Indeed, President Trump's confederates were sued by SGO for making false claims regarding SGO's role in interfering with the 2020 presidential election that President Trump lost….

After evaluating the totality of the circumstances in this case, the Court has concluded that limited discovery regarding SGO's Motion to Dismiss is warranted…. [T]ere is "some evidence" tending to support SGO's Motion to Dismiss: the individual Defendants were charged over a year prior to when the Superseding Indictment against SGO was returned; for years prior to the initiation of this case and up until the Superseding Indictment was returned, SGO was cooperating with the Government; the Government charged SGO amidst a public shift away from charging defendants for similar FCPA violations; SGO brought suit against the President's confederates prior to being charged; and the President has expressed at least some degree of animus towards SGO. "It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here … to warrant the unusual step of … find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."

[T]he Government shall provide the Court with the following for ex parte and in camera review under seal:

scraped.description: From U.S. v. Spitzer (N.D. Ga.), filed by Magistrate Judge John Larkins on Oct. 9, and just affirmed Wednesday by...
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Free Speech

Eugene Volokh | 11.7.2026 12:00 PM

From U.S. v. Spitzer (N.D. Ga.), filed by Magistrate Judge John Larkins on Oct. 9, and just affirmed Wednesday by Judge Eleanor Ross:

The indictment alleges that on July 23, 2024, Mr. Spitzer posted the following message on the website for the American Federation of Teachers, a labor union, regarding its president ("Individual #1"):

[Individual #1] is an ignorant incompetent cunt that should be worried for her safety. Fact that she is still alive. Liberal nazi deserves the bullet to head. Resign before she ends like what happened to trump at his speech. They won't miss fat bitch.

The indictment alleges that the post violated 18 U.S.C. § 875(c), which makes it a federal crime to transmit in interstate commerce any communication containing a threat to injure another person.

Mr. Spitzer argues that assuming the allegations in the indictment were true, it fails to state an offense because the posting was not a "true threat," or even a threat at all, and thus is protected by the First Amendment. As he sees it, the posting was simply political speech about a public figure and did not advocate the use of force or violence against Individual #1.

{In an effort to contextualize the posting, Mr. Spitzer points to an internet article in which Mike Pompeo, the former U.S. Secretary of State, described Individual #1 as "the most dangerous person in the world"; examples of "conservative politicians and commentators" criticizing her approach to school closures during the pandemic; and examples of Individual #1's own political statements. But these are not facts that the Court can consider at this juncture because they fall outside the four corners of the indictment.}

The government responds that whether Mr. Spitzer's posting qualified as a true threat is a question for the jury and that a pretrial determination of the sufficiency of the evidence is procedurally improper. The government further asserts that Mr. Spitzer improperly relies on facts not alleged in the indictment to contextualize the posting. The government has the better argument….

Considering the allegations on the face of the indictment—as this Court must—the Court finds that a jury could conclude that Mr. Spitzer's alleged posting constituted a "true threat." There are at least four separate references to harming or killing Individual #1, including: that she should be "worried for her safety"; that she "deserves a bullet to [the] head"; that unless she resigns she risks being shot similar to the attempted assassination of President Donald J. Trump; and that she will not be missed. In addition, the posting makes an oblique reference to her still being alive, which when combined with the other statements, can reasonably be interpreted as evidencing a present intent to intimidate and place Individual #1 in fear of bodily harm or death. The screed's liberal use of epithets further tends to show that the posting was not simply on a matter of public concern, but rather a threat against Individual #1 personally….

In his reply, Mr. Spitzer relies on the Supreme Court's decision in Watts v. United States , to argue that "political hyperbole" is not a "true threat." True enough, but Watts is distinguishable. In that case, the Supreme Court overturned the conviction of Watts, an 18-year-old Black protester who was charged with threatening President Lyndon B. Johnson during a political rally at the Washington Monument during the 1960's. During the protest, Watts said:

They always holler at us to get an education. And now I have already received my draft classification as 1-A and I have got to report for my physical this Monday coming. I am not going. If they ever make me carry a rifle the first man I want to get in my sights is L.B.J. They are not going to make me kill my black brothers.

The Supreme Court held that considering the full context of the statement—including that it was conditional upon Watt's joining the military (which he said he would not do) and that the listeners laughed at his statement—it was "political hyperbole," not a true threat. In contrast, Mr. Spitzer's alleged statement is much more threatening for the reasons explained above. Also, significantly, Watts was decided after trial, based on a developed evidentiary record, which underscores why dismissal at this juncture is not appropriate.

Accordingly, dismissal of the indictment is not warranted. But, of course, Mr. Spitzer is free to renew his challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence at trial….

Brent A. Gray and Eric John White represent the government.

scraped.title: Arkansas Bar Official Allegedly Transferred Points from Some Bar Examinees to Others
scraped.description: From the Arkansas Supreme Court Thursday: Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then...
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Bar Exam

Eugene Volokh | 11.7.2026 11:33 AM

From the Arkansas Supreme Court Thursday :

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

The full statement from the court:

An internal review by Robert Brech, Executive Director of the Supreme Court of Arkansas's Office of Professional Conduct and Programs, has uncovered extensive irregularities involving the Court's Office of Professional Programs and the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination. The matter was turned over to state and federal authorities.

As of today, the Prosecuting Attorney's Office for the Sixth Judicial District filed formal criminal charges against Nancie Givens for 65 counts of tampering with a public record under Arkansas Code Annotated section 5-54-121 in connection with the alleged altering of numerous Arkansas Bar Examination scores and the deletion of files purportedly intended to conceal that misconduct. The charges followed a criminal investigation initiated in April 2026 by the Arkansas State Police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. As always, all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

Moving forward, we are committed to holding those involved accountable, taking continued corrective oversight of the Arkansas Bar Examination, and determining the appropriate course of action.

* * * * *

In February 2026, Givens, the former Executive Director of this Court's Office of Professional Programs, resigned. At that time, Robert Brech was serving as Executive Director of the Court's Office of Professional Conduct. Following Givens's resignation, the Court directed Brech to supervise the Office of Professional Programs, which oversees the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination.

Upon his review of the Office of Professional Programs' records and administrative operations, Brech discovered that a large number of files and electronic communications were modified or deleted in early January 2026. Approximately 11,400 files were deleted or rendered unavailable. Most of those files included Arkansas Bar examinee applications, profiles, and examination score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by this Court's rules to retain for twenty-five years.

Brech immediately notified a member of this Court, who directed him to determine the extent of the missing records and identify any other irregularities. On the basis of his review of the remaining files, Brech identified numerous discrepancies involving Arkansas Bar Examination scores across at least eight test administrations between July 2020 and July 2025. At that time, the matter was referred to the appropriate state and federal authorities.

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

The vast majority of examinees who were previously informed that they had passed the Arkansas Bar Examination by the Office of Professional Programs did, in fact, pass the exam. Those examinees affected will be notified by the Office of Professional Conduct as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status.

The Court is working with state and federal authorities to recover deleted and missing data, analyze all test administrations within that time frame, and determine the full scope of this grave and potentially criminal abuse of power. The people of Arkansas deserve, and the Court is committed to providing, total transparency in this matter. However, further disclosure will be forthcoming in a manner so as to not compromise the ongoing state and federal criminal investigations. Accordingly, additional disclosures will be limited as those efforts remain underway.

As an immediate step, independent of any state or federal criminal investigation or prosecution, Nancie Givens has been referred to the Office of Professional Conduct for investigation of extensive violations of the Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct. See Ark. R. Prof. Conduct 8.1(a) & 8.4(a)-(e). Furthermore, new testing procedures and security measures were implemented with the February 2026 administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination to ensure systemic accountability and safeguard the integrity of the examination.

* * * * *

We recognize the profound consequences for affected examinees, the Bar, and the public at large. Our paramount concern is safeguarding litigants, the integrity of the legal profession, and public confidence in the administration of justice. While these matters remain under criminal and administrative investigation, we commit to pursue continued corrective measures in an effort to reestablish confidence in our institution.

scraped.title: Iran War Day 253: U.S. Conducts ‘Minor’ Strikes
scraped.description: State of the Union: CENTCOM offered a $20 million reward for information on Iran’s nuclear program.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
President Trump appeared to confirm Friday that the U.S. military had carried out limited strikes on targets in Iran. Following reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, Hengam Island, and the mainland area of Bandar Abbas, the president told reporters, “We do minor strikes, but they knock out. [Iran] built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five.” These are the first U.S. strikes since the midterm elections.

Also on Friday, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced it would offer a reward of up to $20 million for “information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel.”

Attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have continued, with the UK Maritime Trade Operations organization reporting at least eleven ships hit during the week ending November 6.

AAA reports that the average price of regular gasoline is $4.04 per gallon, and the average price of diesel is $6.21 per gallon.

Luke Nicastro is a senior editor at The American Conservative. Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

items.summary: Just because it wasn’t only the war doesn’t mean it wasn’t mainly the war. The post Republicans’ Post-Midterms War Denialism Is an Exercise in Special Pleading appeared first on The American Conservative. Politics Republicans’ Post-Midterms War Denialism Is an Exercise in Special Pleading Just because it wasn’t only the war doesn’t mean it wasn’t mainly the war. Republicans took a pounding on Tuesday that made past wave elections look like a mild drizzle by comparison. Just whatever you do, d...

scraped.title: Republicans’ Post-Midterms War Denialism Is an Exercise in Special Pleading
scraped.description: Just because it wasn’t only the war doesn’t mean it wasn’t mainly the war.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
Just because it wasn’t only the war doesn’t mean it wasn’t mainly the war.

Republicans took a pounding on Tuesday that made past wave elections look like a mild drizzle by comparison. Just whatever you do, don’t blame the Iran war.

In a bizarre crashout in the early morning hours after the GOP’s midterm debacle, the radio commentator Erick Erickson likened blaming the war for the result to pretending the 2020 election was stolen.

That bold truth-teller Sen. Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican who slithered away rather than defend his Senate seat in a supposed act of defiance against President Donald Trump, also poured cold water on the idea.

“Do you honestly believe, for example, respectfully, Mr. Vice President, that we saw the departure of Hispanics over the war?” he asked on CNN the day after the seat he declined to defend fell to the Democrats by 20 points. “Give me a break. It’s more complicated than that."

Among the reasons it has taken so long for “standing up to Trump” to go anywhere in the GOP is that until relatively recently, most of the Republicans who do so are worse than he is. But I digress.

Vice President J.D. Vance has taken a lot of heat for stating the obvious about the war. Some like to imagine his Trump-ordered Iran diplomacy is somehow a form of insubordination. They should instead ruminate on the number of Republican congressional seats that could have been salvaged if the memorandum of understanding had held and the war had ended in June. The New York Times has confirmed Vance’s account that the White House received polling to that effect.

The Wall Street Journal ’s Kim Strassel thinks it’s a “hoot” that Vance recognizes the war’s downsides rather than blaming the tariffs exclusively.

“Trump’s first-term success came from largely following that Reagan playbook,” she writes. “The second-term leaned into me-too progressive populism—at the veep’s urging—and it ain’t working.”

Or, hear me out, Trump’s first-term success—which still resulted in a 40-seat loss in the 2018 midterm elections—was because he followed the Reagan playbook of limited military interventions, no new foreign wars, and his more limited tariffs regime was compatible with inflation running consistently below the Federal Reserve’s preferred target of 2 percent.

The second term leaned into me-too progressive neoconservatism dressed up in “How do you do, fellow MAGA?” populist garb against the veep’s advice, and it ain’t working.

That’s not to say the tariffs have helped, especially in the farm states where Republicans took a beating. Anything that cut against affordability was always going to be politically damaging, even if the goal was to reshore jobs. Voters continued to be angry about the economy despite relatively low unemployment under both Trump and former President Joe Biden because of the high cost of living.

Beyond the fact of the tariffs, their implementation has been capricious and haphazard. On this, there is much in common with how Trump has conducted the Iran war: purely unilateral moves, no working with Congress or recognizing its constitutional powers, no clear explanation to the public of what is going on or what the point is, and no empathy for families straining under several years of elevated inflation.

Even many Buchananite economic nationalists have long favored free trade with Canada and comparable economies, the target of Trump’s current trade war. Perhaps we have been at war with Canada , like Iran, for decades.

But the Iran War is the single biggest driver of inflation and the reason it hasn’t continued to come down. The war is the primary reason inflation remains stubbornly above where it would need to be for the Fed to consider lowering interest rates. The spike in gasoline and diesel prices is felt more broadly than the tariffs, and it also makes the tariffs’ bite worse. And for better or worse, Trump never implied he wouldn’t impose tariffs during the 2024 campaign.

There is never just one cause of something like the GOP’s midterms flop. Trump’s foibles are what they are at this point, and they aren’t likely to improve at the age of 80. He has never worn well with his more timorous supporters, and he has now been around for a decade.

Even in 2006, Republicans had other problems besides the Iraq War. But this furious denial of the war’s impact is reminiscent of those who wanted to blame GOP congressional losses 20 years ago on earmarks. Yes, earmarks often were used for wasteful projects. They were part of the culture of corruption and neatly illustrated Republicans’ abandonment of any pretense of fiscal discipline.

But the attempt to pretend they were a bigger driver of the 2006 blue wave than Iraq was always absurd. Hawks are upset today because two decades ago, they would have had a Republican vice president who went along with their ridiculous spin.

The persistence of inflation has also elevated other issues like corruption as Republican problems. This cost the GOP seats. This is downstream of the war, which itself alienated some people who voted for Trump and Republicans just two years ago, and left the party limited to voters and media voices who were always going to go down with the ship when the blue wave came.

Strassel allows that voters are “unhappy about the war, though the numbers might be different if the president had been clear about an exit strategy.” But hawks and Vance-bashers have made clear they don’t want to hear about exit strategies beyond “Just win, baby!”

“I don’t think the war itself was per se a mistake,” Erickson says. “I think half-assing the war was a mistake.” But it is the war itself that led to the Strait of Hormuz quagmire and it is the “half-assing” that is keeping this a more limited, less deadly (to Americans) operation than Iraq.

How many times will Republicans in Congress listen to the same people with the same result? Will the last one let us know before they turn out the lights?

W. James Antle III is executive editor of the Washington Examiner magazine and a contributing editor of The American Conservative .

items.title: The ‘Invade the World, Invite the World’ Election
items.summary: You can’t transform a nation’s demographics without upending its politics. The post The ‘Invade the World, Invite the World’ Election appeared first on The American Conservative. Politics The ‘Invade the World, Invite the World’ Election You can’t transform a nation’s demographics without upending its politics. The Republican Party got smacked in the midterm elections because of voter frustration over the Iran War and its economic consequences, as even many Republicans, including Vice Preside...

scraped.title: The ‘Invade the World, Invite the World’ Election
scraped.description: You can’t transform a nation’s demographics without upending its politics.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
You can’t transform a nation’s demographics without upending its politics.

The Republican Party got smacked in the midterm elections because of voter frustration over the Iran War and its economic consequences, as even many Republicans, including Vice President J.D. Vance, have acknowledged.

But the scale of the Democrats’ sweeping victory was enabled by another factor: America’s racial-demographic transformation over the past several decades, driven largely by mass migration. If only whites had voted, the Republican Party would have strengthened its hold on the Senate, the House of Representatives, and state-level offices. If only nonwhites had voted, well, even the Chinese Communists would envy the Democratic Party its utter dominance.

“Invade the world, invite the world,” as the right-wing social commentator Steve Sailer famously put it, summarizing our inept leadership’s military and immigration policies. That’s the story of this election.

Georgia, once a ruby-red state, has gone from being supermajority white in 1990 to minority white today. So even though white Georgians favored the Republican candidates by wide margins, the Peach State sent Jon Ossoff back to the Senate and elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as governor, both Democrats.

The results in Texas—the most populous state traditionally held by the GOP—were even more shocking. But the data tell the same basic story. Only 37 percent of Texans are white, which is a big reason why Democrats dominated in the Lone Star State. Texas Hispanics, who tend to be fairly conservative, not only shifted blue but turned out in large numbers.

Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, the list goes on and on, but you get the idea.

To be sure, if the Trump administration had governed more competently during the past two years—and especially if it hadn’t launched the disastrous Iran War—then whites and nonwhites alike wouldn’t have swung as sharply as they did toward the Democrats, and Republicans might have held onto the Senate. But that’s not the whole story. America’s racial diversity sets the context for its elections, and that context is an increasingly difficult one for Republicans to navigate.

I’ve argued in print and online (and online again) that the Democrats are heading toward a permanent majority because of America’s changing demographics. Few people agree with my analysis—and even the authors of the classic text The Emerging Democratic Majority (2002) have disavowed their book’s thesis—but I harbor little doubt.

If you remain skeptical, reflect on these two facts for a while: 1) No Republican presidential candidate since Herbert Hoover has won a majority of votes from any nonwhite racial group, and 2) America will be majority nonwhite by around 2045.

Done reflecting? Here’s another fact: Whites remain more divided than other racial groups between the two parties. A Democratic coalition of white liberals and nonwhites, if it holds, will achieve stable domination years before America’s electorate turns majority-minority.

Several factors have slowed the emergence of a permanent Democratic majority. The voting electorate is whiter than the general population. The Red Team can occasionally win more than 40 percent of Hispanics, America’s largest minority group. Many non-college-educated whites have fled to the GOP, partly in reaction to the Democrats’ boutique cultural fixations like transgenderism. And countermajoritarian institutions—gerrymandering in the House, malapportionment in the Senate, and the electoral college—mostly benefit the Republicans.

Some analysts, after Donald Trump’s dramatic victory in 2024, posited a new “multiracial coalition” that would keep the GOP in the game. It was wishful thinking. Trump made inroads with nonwhites, but he merely brought the GOP back to its George W. Bush numbers, more or less.

The margin of error for Republican presidential candidates is apparently slim. In 2024, Trump mobilized blue-collar whites and did reasonably well among minorities. And yet, facing a disastrous candidate installed at the 11th hour, Trump won the popular vote by a smaller margin than Hillary Clinton in 2016.

What transpired this week was a different matter altogether—an electoral backlash that some thought impossible in our age of polarization—and it will have long-lasting political consequences. The Dems will probably maintain their Senate majority over several election cycles, and if Texas just became solidly blue, Republicans won’t stand a chance at winning the White House in 2028.

Of course, a permanent Democratic majority doesn’t mean an eternal one. Perhaps the Democratic Party will splinter between its moderate and progressive factions, or maybe a viable third party will emerge that, over time, replaces the GOP. On the other hand, in cities and states that long ago became majority nonwhite, the Democrats enjoy one-party rule, and governance generally suffers.

A nation is its people, as right-wingers often say. And you can’t transform a nation without upending its politics.

Andrew Day is the senior editor of The American Conservative . He has a PhD in political science from Northwestern University. You can follow him on X @AKDay89 .
