scraped.title: Europeans got blue blinders in wake of midterm sweep
scraped.description: Western elites are tying the elections to Ukraine while ignoring the anti-Iran war sentiment that sent the GOP packing
scraped.h1: Europeans got blue blinders in wake of midterm sweep
scraped.body_text:
Western elites are tying the elections to Ukraine while ignoring the anti-Iran war sentiment that sent the GOP packing

The Democratic sweep of the midterm elections has been greeted with a wary relief across Europe . After two years of President Donald Trump's tariffs, threats to annex Greenland and scolding of European NATO allies on defense spending, many European politicians see the Republican defeat as a welcome course correction.

Yet the reactions also expose the contradictions of the European Union’s own foreign policy, particularly toward the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Rather than examining the causes of Trump’s defeat, EU leaders have chosen to interpret it as a vindication of their own ideological beliefs.

The EU high representative for foreign policy, Kaja Kallas, unsurprisingly, saw in the election a hope that the new Congress will strengthen transatlantic unity and support for Ukraine, presumably reversing Trump’s insufficient devotion to the Ukrainian cause, which she criticized earlier.

In a similar vein, Christel Schaldemose, a vice president of the European Parliament, voiced “cautious optimism” that the results could “benefit Ukraine and the green transition.” Spain’s center-left prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, meanwhile, interpreted the vote as a “rejection of inequality, hatred, sexism and climate denial.”

Yet there is no evidence that the GOP debacle was caused primarily by Trump’s perceived lack of support for Ukraine or that it was a vindication of a progressive social agenda.

Rather, the polls, including Associated Press-NORC , New York Times/Siena , Fox News , and Gallup , consistently showed that, on average, around 75% to 80% said the “cost of living” (gas prices) and Iran war played an important role in how they planned to vote. In exit polls, 74% of voters said the war was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their decision Tuesday. Vice President JD Vance himself rated the Iran war as the top reason for the Republican wipeout.

Those in Europe who quickly seized on the anti-war sentiment were, revealingly, not the centrists opposed to Trump for ideological reasons, but his erstwhile admirers on the nationalist right.

Jordan Bardella, leader of France's National Rally, and Alice Weidel, the leader of Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD), both parties leading the polls in their respective countries, blamed Trump’s defeat on the economic consequences of his war in Iran.

This was an astute political move by the nationalists. They opposed the Iran war from the start, while some of the European leaders who initially welcomed the war are now complaining about its consequences.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a particularly revealing example. When Israel attacked Iran in June 2025, he praised it for doing the West's "dirty work." He defended the much larger American-Israeli bombing campaign launched in February 2026, declaring that this was “no time to lecture our allies on international law.”

Now Merz laments that the war has cost Europe more than €100 billion through higher energy prices. The “dirty work” has come with a hefty bill.

The European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who spoke of a “democratic transition” in Tehran as the U.S. and Israeli bombs began falling, now places the war’s price tag at €127 billion ($143 billion) in additional fossil fuels. Neither Merz nor von der Leyen are on the record of connecting publicly the outcome of the elections to the war on Iran, however.

Merz and von der Leyen epitomize a broader European failure. EU governments had little meaningful influence over Washington's decision to go to war. Nevertheless, some, like Germany, supported it. Others, like France, acknowledged that the war violated international law, but put emphasis on Iran’s “destabilizing behaviour” in the region. Still others, like Italy, Portugal, Bulgaria, and Cyprus cooperated by allowing the U.S. to use military bases on their territories to attack Iran. Spain's Pedro Sánchez was a notable exception, fully opposing the war from the outset.

Now, EU leaders find themselves in a bind of their own making, being blamed by the opposition for enabling a war that impoverishes their own citizens. And the cost of that support is no longer measured in inflation and prices alone, but also security. Iran made it clear that, should the U.S. and Israel attack again, it will retaliate against any country that facilitates those attacks. The NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte foolishly boasted that “5000 sorties” of U.S. aircraft were launched from Europe. European countries that cooperated in these actions are becoming legitimate targets, from Tehran’s perspective .

The only way out of this predicament is for EU leaders to follow Sanchez’s lead and refuse to play any role in supporting, in any way, any further U.S. or Israeli attacks against Iran. Instead, they should work to recover their own diplomatic role in the Middle East , including engagement with Iran and working with regional countries , like Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia , Qatar and Oman, to de-escalate tensions.

Yet Europe’s inability to distance itself from Washington’s war on Iran wasn’t simply a matter of bad judgement. It reflected EU leaders’ belief that submission to Trump was a necessary price to keep him on the side of Europe and Ukraine against Russia .

That was an obvious miscalculation; Trump has consistently shown his preference for cutting a deal with Moscow. European leaders must now understand that hoping Democratic control of Congress will simply mean a restoration of hawkish trans-atlanticism would be no less delusional than appeasing Trump has proved to be.

It is possible that a Democratic Congress could seek to increase military assistance to Kyiv and impose tougher sanctions on Moscow. But there is another possibility: Democrats may well choose to concentrate on domestic affairs and the economic consequences of the Iran war, leaving Trump considerable room to pursue negotiations with Moscow. The elections, after all, had little to do with Trump’s Ukraine policy.

The inherent uncertainty about the U.S. approach is part of the problem. EU elites must finally recognize that their security cannot remain hostage to the shifting fortunes of American domestic politics.

Fortunately, two European countries have recently demonstrated a way forward. On October 27, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke directly with the Russian President Vladimir Putin about the war in Ukraine and prospects for renewed negotiations.

Both Finland and Norway are NATO members, share borders with Russia, and strongly support Ukraine. Yet their leaders recognized that deterrence and diplomacy are not mutually exclusive. Although their initiative did not produce an immediate breakthrough, it showed that Europeans can engage Moscow without abandoning Kyiv or waiting for Washington to act.

The wars in Iran and Ukraine expose two sides of the same European predicament. In the Middle East, Europe has paid an enormous economic price for military decisions it did not control – and failed to oppose. In Ukraine, it has committed substantial resources while hoping for Washington to take the lead in confronting Russia.

Both gambits failed. A Democratic Congress cannot rescue Europe from the need to pursue its own strategic autonomy. That means more than higher defense spending or buying fewer American weapons. It also requires rejecting unnecessary wars, engaging adversaries, and pursuing diplomatic initiatives independently.

Contrary to the claims of many EU elites, the vote in the U.S. appears to be less a sign of a global rollback of national populism than a reflection of a growing backlash in the West against endless wars. The governments in Europe can only ignore that sentiment at their own peril.

scraped.title: Stephen Miller To Take Over As White House Chief Of Staff
scraped.description: Stephen Miller, perhaps the Trump administration's foremost immigration and deportation hawk, will take over as chief of staff.
scraped.author: Breccan F. Thies
scraped.h1: Stephen Miller To Take Over As White House Chief Of Staff
scraped.body_text:
Miller has demonstrated laser focus on mass deportations and how government policy needs to benefit the American people.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, perhaps the Trump administration’s foremost immigration and deportation hawk, will take over as chief of staff after Susie Wiles resigned her position Thursday night.

President Donald Trump announced Miller’s promotion on social media, stating Miller is one of his “most trusted advisors,” adding, “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

The shake-up at the top comes after devastating midterms for Republicans, where many voters were angry with the protracted war in Iran and its resultant high gas prices and a lack of focus on domestic issues like affordability.

Staffing changes after election defeats are fairly common, and more could come. Officials in top positions at the Department of Justice have also started turning in their resignations, including Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon and Assistant Attorney General for the National Security Division John Eisenberg .

Some on the right, like Steve Bannon, who served as the White House chief strategist in Trump’s first term, called for Wiles to be removed , stating, “I think that you have to look to people like Susie Wiles, the chief of staff, and the political consultants that are there … because of the results, they should be removed and removed immediately.”

Matthew Peterson, a Claremont Institute fellow and founder of FORUM, a debate platform for the new right, added that Wiles’ ouster “needed to be done a good long while ago, but was necessary this week,” calling Miller’s succession a “game changer.”

“Wiles is obviously an extremely capable operator, good at managing Trump, and deserves credit for the win,” he stated. “But after the first heady 6-9 months of the admin, as time went on, her lack of internalized understanding of the actual MAGA agenda became damning. The amount of stuff that has been blocked, from MAHA to immigration, and the fools who have been suffered — long after proving they can’t do the job — is, well A LOT.”

Miller is well-liked on the right as someone who has demonstrated laser focus on mass deportations and how government policy needs to benefit the American people, economically and culturally.

When speaking of mass deportations, Miller said , “At every turn illegal aliens have always been treated better than Americans.”

“Do you have any idea how many resources will be opened up for Americans when the illegals are gone? No more waiting in line at an emergency room, no more massive traffic in Los Angeles,” he continued. “Your health insurance premiums go down, your public school classroom size will shrink dramatically. They have more time to educate every student. You won’t have to compete for public benefits.”

Miller’s message on why drug traffickers from South and Central America needed to be “treated just as brutally and just as ruthlessly” as ISIS or al-Qaida is because successful domestic family formation is dependent on securing the homeland, adding , “A country cannot pursue economic growth, cultural enrichment, art, architecture, education, science, if it doesn’t have fundamental security first.”

Fraud is another area in which Miller has spoken about an issue fully in terms of Americans’ birthright and how it is being stolen by foreigners who do not belong in the country, stating, “The main thing I want the American people to know is that if you’re a middle-class taxpayer in this country, before President Trump came along, you spent half your working life paying for fraudsters and scammers, many of whom are refugees, illegal aliens, and foreigners who came to this country to loot and plunder us.”

scraped.title: Disability Is Bad. Plus…
scraped.description: In today’s Weekend Press: Suzy Weiss sits down with Dustin Hoffman’s right-hand woman. Spencer Klavan on the Greek comedy that explains Trump’s ruin. Kat Rosenfield on a masterful new movie. And more!
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
Welcome back to The Weekend Press ! Today, Kat Rosenfield reviews “Fjord,” a new movie that examines whether liberal democracies actually tolerate conservative Christian immigrants. Suzy Weiss drinks with the woman inside Dustin Hoffman’s head. Spencer Klavan on the ancient Greek tragedy that Republicans need right now. And more!

But first: Disability isn’t “magic.”

Good intentions can become ugly realities. And nowhere is that clearer than in how we treat the mentally unwell.

America closed an overwhelming number of its psychiatric hospitals, because surely its schizophrenics didn’t deserve to be locked up like they were in prison? And so, many of them ended up on the street.

An anxious mother hears her teenage daughter say she has developed multiple personality disorder, like the other girls on TikTok, and takes her to see a therapist. And so, pediatricians report, they’re overwhelmed with patients more likely to be suffering from social contagion than genuine illness.

Disability activists encourage us to see autism as a “superpower,” to help erode stigma. And so, those with a profoundly life-inhibiting form of the disorder are erased from the awareness-raising conversation.

“The rhetorical alchemy of recasting disability as something not bad, or even as a positive good, might serve the needs of relatively high-functioning people with relatively high-status disabilities,” writes Freddie deBoer in our lead essay. “But this way of thinking utterly abandons those for whom disability is a daily assault on their ability to function.”

His piece is an excerpt from his remarkable new book, All in Your Head : Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to Be Disordered . It’s not a memoir, but it is personal; Freddie has spent a lifetime suffering from bipolar disorder, and, he writes, “stigma has never been one of my hundred biggest problems.”

The same is true of most disabled people. “Talk to someone struggling to live with cystic fibrosis. Talk privately to the caretakers of severely autistic adolescents who are prone to violent outbursts,” writes Freddie. “They don’t need euphemisms. They don’t want saccharine narratives.”

They want society to recognize the painful realities of their lives—and offer material support.

And therein lies a lesson for the newly empowered Democratic Party: A true politics of the left is not about shouting at people on social media, even if that’s more fun. It is about doing the hard, and not very sexy, work of legislating to make life in America fairer for the most vulnerable.

Read his full piece below:

If you want to watch a movie that will make you think, go see “Fjord.” It follows a devoutly Christian family that migrates from conservative Romania to very liberal Norway—only to have the state take their kids away from them because it doesn’t approve of their parenting. “This is the so-called paradox of tolerance,” writes Kat Rosenfield, in her latest essay. “In an age where welcoming immigrants has become a fundamental tenet” on the left, the fact is that “new arrivals often come armed with values, beliefs, and practices that make progressives profoundly uncomfortable.”

Ariel Levy co-wrote Dustin Hoffman’s new memoir, "Look At Me," which is out this week—but before that, she first met the leading man at a museum in the ’80s. “We followed him around and around the Met because I was so into him,” Levy said. Now, 40 years later, he’s grown so famous that Time called him “the fifth Beatle”—and he has hated every second of it. “He was like ‘It was unbearable. I wanted to climb out of my skin,’ ” she said. Over two Manhattans with Suzy, Levy explains how she got inside the mind of Hollywood’s most reluctant star—and what he makes of his legacy.

Where does American politics go from here? While we all debate the future, Spencer Klavan thinks the best answer lies in an ancient Greek comedy, Aristophanes’s “Clouds,” about a clash between a moral relativist and a traditionalist. The latter’s “solid ideals are fatally undermined, because he turns out to be a venal fraud,” Klavan writes in today’s Things Worth Remembering. The play offers the Trump administration an enduring lesson: “When the Right Argument destroys its own case through mismanagement and corruption, the Wrong Argument wins.”

Is foie gras the new paper straw? This week, among all the election headlines, you may have seen that the French delicacy has been banned in Denver and D.C.—but is this anything more than a feel-good nod to animal rights in a nation full of pigs in cages? In the latest episode of Second Thought , Suzy and Dan Ahdoot get into it—as well as last weekend’s most cancel-worthy Halloween costumes, and the Englishman who just got home after spending nearly 30 years walking around the world. “This is such a British celebrity,” says Suzy. “Just someone who plods along in pain for half of their life.” He didn’t even enjoy it!

Click the link below to watch the episode, or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

This week, we published a full slate of election coverage—which you can catch up on here . Also, Larissa Phillips reflected on the ideological whiplash of being a MAHA mom; Arthur Brooks gave advice on how to raise your kid to be a reader; and Evan Gardner reported on bona fide data centers in space!

A new batch of ads from single Free Press ers is live on the site. Click here to meet a fabulous octogenarian in Los Angeles; a Canadian conservative; or a touring musician in Oz. Your special someone could be just one email away! If you’d like to take a chance at Free Press love, write a paragraph that defines you, including your age, where you live, and what you’re looking for, and send it over to Cupid@TheFP.com .

How should you spend the rest of your weekend? We asked our columnist Kat Rosenfield for her recommendations . . .

🚶 Walk . . . the Hudson Highlands for a scenic stroll in the woods at Harriman State Park—or channel your inner mountain goat and scramble up the Butter Hill loop for spectacular vistas at Storm King (where I spent a very enjoyable Tuesday this week not-thinking about politics or elections). The October crowds are gone, but thanks to an exceptionally mild fall, the foliage is still near peak.

🎵 Listen . . . To the best late autumn mood music, by English folk musician Vashti Bunyan, whose 1970 album Just Another Diamond Day was critically underrated in its time but has since acquired a cult following; the songs are the ideal soundtrack for skipping through a golden wood at twilight or chopping root vegetables for a stew.

🎃 Eat . . . As a wise man once said,“ It’s decorative gourd season, motherfuckers ”— but also, more importantly, decorative gourds are also edible gourds. My husband and I love this recipe for acorn squash roasted and stuffed with Moroccan-spiced lamb sausage, rice, and mint, which is beautiful enough for a Thanksgiving side dish but easy enough for anytime. Pair it with a cute salad and a big, fat glass of red wine.

That’s all, folks! Have a great weekend.

“the ideal soundtrack for skipping through a golden wood at twilight or chopping root vegetables for a stew”

Now that is funny, intentionally or not. The gourd season line, too. She is the best writer of the bunch. Maybe the best mass media culture writer anywhere.

I may even actually try the music and the recipe.

"... rhetorical alchemy...."

Almost exclusively the province of the Left.

scraped.title: Two Drinks with Ariel Levy
scraped.description: Ariel Levy co-wrote Dustin Hoffman’s book and has profiled everyone else. What does it take to get a famous person to open up?
scraped.author: Suzy Weiss
scraped.body_text:
Ariel Levy first met Dustin Hoffman in 1984. It was a couple of years after Tootsie came out, in which Hoffman plays a difficult actor who reinvents himself as an actress named Dorothy Michaels. Levy, who was 10 years old and with her parents, spotted the actor at the museum. “We followed him around and around the Met because I was so into him,” Levy tells me.

Fortysome years later, Levy feels more or less the same. She co-wrote his memoir, Look at Me , which is out this week, and tells me, “He’s the Dustin Hoffman you hope Dustin Hoffman will be.” The first time they met as adults, at his home in Los Angeles, Hoffman, now 89, played piano and they looked at pictures together. Disappointingly, he didn’t remember the time at the museum. Everyone who has spotted Hoffman over the past 60 or so years would have a story like that.

“After The Graduate , he was so famous. Time magazine called him the fifth Beatle,” says Levy. We’re at the Chelsea Hotel. Levy sips a Manhattan, while I take down a Negroni and french fries. Apparently, Hoffman hated the attention. “He was like ‘It was unbearable. I wanted to climb out of my skin,’ ” says Levy. Hoffman was no one’s idea of a leading man: short, with a “screechingly Semitic” face, she says. His friend, actor Robert Duvall, said he looked like “Barbra Streisand in drag.” Duvall, plus his friends Gene Hackman and Robert Redford, died while he was writing the book. Did that have Hoffman thinking about his legacy?

“I think he thinks that’s too much to hope for,” says Levy, recalling the Arthur Miller quote that “immortality is like trying to carve your initials in a block of ice in the middle of July.”

scraped.title: A 2,400-Year-Old Explanation for the Republican Midterm Disaster
scraped.description: Trump promised to restore the principles that built America. But his execution has veered so far into depravity as to put many young people off the project altogether. So too in Aristophanes’s ‘Clouds,' writes Spencer Klavan.
scraped.author: Spencer Klavan
scraped.body_text:
Depending on your perspective, the Republicans’ recent belly flop in the midterm elections might seem like a tragedy, a farce, or a bit of both. Hysteria and ecstasy have been easy to come by. Wisdom, it must be said, has not.

At moments like this, when panic and fanaticism reign in the present, I find it helpful to take a break from the fracas of the news feed and look for enduring insights from the past. Right now, in particular, I’m getting a lot out of an ancient Greek comedy: Aristophanes’s Clouds .

When Clouds was first produced in the late 5th century BCE, Athens was just beginning to lose its grip on the sprawling naval empire it gained in the wake of a stunning victory against Persia a generation before. A little like America after the World Wars, Athens emerged from the Persian Wars as a freshly minted world leader, flush with cultural and political confidence. Just as America’s postwar energies largely dissipated into partisan infighting and foolhardy military expeditions, Athens found its golden-age glow quickly fading away as chronic overreach brought it into conflict with its rival Sparta in the disastrous Peloponnesian War.

All of this sets up Clouds to be remarkably informative about the question of how the MAGA movement, in just a few short years, ceded its extraordinary momentum to the young Turks of the Democratic Party.

Let’s back up to set the scene. Clouds ’ playwright, Aristophanes, had a long-standing feud with various Athenian political leaders—especially Cleon, a general in the ongoing Peloponnesian War and a blustering populist hawk (not entirely unlike Donald Trump in his later years). But Aristophanes was no revolutionary itching to tear down the system and bring on anarchy. Rather, his plays bitterly savage Athens’s leaders not because they represent law and order, but because, in his view, they mis represent it by thundering about virtue while indulging their own vices.

scraped.title: The world after Trump
scraped.author: John Gray
scraped.h1: The world after Trump He oversaw the end of the American age
scraped.body_text:
“Trump’s rise was a by-product of the neo-liberal cult of globalization.” (Finn Gomez/Getty)

For future historians, Donald Trump’s awkward curtsey when greeting Xi Jinping’s wife, Peng Liyuan, when they arrived at the White House for tea in September of this year may serve as a turning point. In a genuflection not accorded to his allies, the President saluted the epoch he has brought into being. Impelled by a degenerate capitalism in which everything is for sale, and a singularly manipulable demagogue, America is aligning itself with the adversaries of what used to be called the Western world. As in the Yalta conference in February 1945, when a triumvirate of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union carved up Europe into spheres of influence, a new global order is taking shape. Unlike the Yalta settlement, which ended with the Soviet collapse, the international system projected by America, China and Russia today implies a precipitous retreat of Western power.

Trump’s presidency has now entered its most dangerous phase. With little left to lose after an earth-shaking midterm wipeout, he is released from political restraint. He has accepted the result with apparent grace, dismissing the fact that the elections were a referendum on his presidency with the assertion that he was not on the ballot — an amusing claim, since he spent the campaign saying the opposite. The mood in the party is sombre. The Florida governor Ron de Santis, mooted as a presidential candidate, has described the results as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans”. No doubt rightly, given its impact on prices at the pump, the vice-president JD Vance — also looking to his future — has averred “the reason we lost is the war”. They and many others are pointing the finger at Trump, but he may not care.

In control of the House and Senate, the triumphant Democrats can launch as many legal challenges as they like. They can block legislation, launch investigations into his crimes and impeach him, but he retains the presidential veto, and the supreme master of the attention economy will not be out of the limelight for long. An adventure in Cuba would be a welcome distraction, and he may yet trigger a greater cataclysm in the Gulf. Trump’s second administration is the experimental refutation of liberal legalism. Post-Trump America is not a constitutional republic but an illiberal democracy, the triumph of politics and executive power over law and procedure.

By John Gray

Those who believe Trump shares a mindset with the world’s leading tyrants are mistaken. Neither the Russian nor the Chinese leader displays his all-consuming narcissism. Putin is an archetypal creature of the Soviet system , a cold-eyed killer schooled in the art of survival. Xi is a suspicious autocrat possessed by the insecurity of his position. Putin’s aggression combines self-preservation — his own survival inseparable from that of his regime — with a neo-tsarist vision of a mystical “Russian realm” targeted for destruction by the West. Xi’s “Chinese dream” is the project of making China into the global hegemon and an unapologetic affirmation of Chinese civilization.

Embodying nothing except his own emptiness and venality, Trump is the ideal dupe for these flinty tyrants. Possibly he fears Putin as the possessor of kompromat of some sort — there must be many possibilities — and he has certainly done business with the regime. But if Trump is behaving like a Russian asset, it is not because he was recruited as a Manchurian candidate in Moscow 40 years ago. Putin never expected Trump to become president (any more than Trump did himself) and seems to view him with bemused contempt. Trump sees the Russian dictator through the lens of his ideal self-image as strongman and admires him as a model of how to use state power to accumulate personal wealth.

Those who speak of the Putinisation of America can point to undeniable parallels. Putin is a master of vranyo , the Bolshevik practice of telling lies that both speaker and audience know perfectly well are falsehoods — as when he denied that the “little green men” invading Crimea in 2014 were Russian troops. The goal is not persuasion but domination: by imposing a narrative that is transparently false, the very idea of a domain of facts independent of power is undermined. With his incoherent boasting — claiming to have “ completely and totally obliterated ” Iran’s nuclear capability, then justifying a resumption of the war to destroy it — Trump also asserts power over facts. The difference is that Putin knows he is lying, whereas in Trump’s moment-by-moment solipsism, truth has no meaning.

For his critics, Trump is the kingpin of a Putin-style kleptocracy. It is true that his second administration has seen the presidency monetized to an unprecedented degree . Diplomacy has become a rent-seeking family business. Insider trading has been normalized. In August of this year, the Trump Media and Technology Group (TMTG) launched a premier data feed allowing Wall Street banks and high-frequency trading firms access to his market-moving Truth Social posts milliseconds before they become available to the public, with subscribers paying a hundred thousand dollars a month for the service.

By the time they leave office, Trump, his family and acolytes will have amassed immense riches. Likewise, Putin’s extraction of capital from Russia’s economy has, by some estimates , made him richer than Elon Musk. Yet wealth and government interact differently in Putin’s Russia and Trump’s America. Under Trump, the US is ruled by a variant of capitalism in which the state is used as a means of corporate enrichment at the expense of America’s strategic interests. In Russia’s version of state capitalism, corporate influence is curbed when it threatens the state itself. The same is true in China.

When Russia’s richest oligarch, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, became involved in opposition politics and negotiations to sell part of his oil company, Yukos, to American firms, he was arrested at gunpoint on his private jet, sentenced to 10 years in a Siberian penal colony and Yukos bankrupted. When the CEO of the Alibaba Group, Jack Ma, criticized China’s financial regulators, he was taken out of circulation and his business empire dismantled. In contrast, the Trump administration authorized the export of high-end computer chips of Jensen Huang’s Nvidia for export to China. During Xi’s visit to Washington, Trump bent the knee in more than one sense. He reportedly pitched the Chinese leader regarding purchases of American military technology, violating decades-long commitments to Taiwan and other allies. He prioritized corporate gain over national security and America’s standing in the world.

Trump’s “transactional” diplomacy consists of the exchange of American power for promises of private gain. The settlement of the Ukraine war being brokered by Trump’s special envoys, his son in law, Jared Kushner, and the real estate investor Steve Witfkoff, follows this playbook. A multibillion-dollar deal to acquire the international holdings of Lukoil, Russia’s largest remaining private oil company, has apparently been discussed, along with reopening the Nord Stream pipeline, blown up in September 2022. Elon Musk’s Space X — on Trump’s instructions, according to Musk — imposed speed limits on Starshield, which allowed Ukraine to intercept Russian drone and missile attacks. Sanctions have been paused, and Trump has called more than once for Zelensky’s removal.

Trump’s aim is full-scale economic détente with Russia, which he believes will realize large profits for him and his coterie. Very likely he and they will benefit, but there is something spectral about the fabulous wealth envisioned in these sordid machinations. Why should Putin respect the terms of any deal? The “energy ceasefire” Trump believed he had agreed with him was flouted within hours. Much of Trump’s chicanery is based on fantasies — the reverse of realpolitik . If Ukraine is being sold out, it may be for next to nothing.

Lured by dreams of financial gain, Trump has torn up whatever remained of an American-led “rules-based” order. This is more than the much-discussed passing of a unipolar order. American power is imploding, with the post-Cold-War leviathan now a floundering, flailing behemoth. Rather than an “unreliable friend”, the US seems closer to the enemies of the countries that depended on it for their security. Yet there can be no assurance that America’s new strategic partners will keep their end of the deal. When they met in St Petersburg in October, Witkoff praised Putin as a “humanitarian” for releasing an American prisoner captured in eastern Ukraine in April 2022. Such a toadying eulogy may be understandable. For the US, Yalta 2.0 may yield little more than the prisoner’s release. The presumed exchange is that Russia ends its support for Iran while the US forces Ukraine to surrender; but America has no way of ensuring Russia’s compliance, let alone that of China or Iran.

The Iran debacle itself began with a whim that set in motion a fateful escalation. The illusory prospect of another Venezuela-style coup, semi-magical in its flawless operational execution, was irresistible. What Trump described in March as “a little excursion” has been a forced march to strategic defeat. The result of decapitating the Iranian leadership has been to install a military dictatorship more repressive than the decaying theocracy it replaced. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has become a permanent threat to the Strait of Hormuz. The pre-war status quo, in which it was an open international waterway, is irrecoverable.

This was not unforeseen. Similar bombing campaigns have been war-gamed many times, with similar results. As Barbara Tuchman showed in The March of Folly: From Troy to Vietnam (1984), history is not so much a catalog of error as a succession of follies whose consequences can be known in advance.

However the war develops, America has forfeited its position in the Middle East. Over the past months, its bases in the Gulf and Iraq have been disabled and its armories depleted. Tens of billions of dollars have been expended using costly missiles against cheaper and more quickly replaceable drones. Iran’s partner in the “Axis of Resistance”, the Houthis have turned another vital waterway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, into a high-risk corridor, while launching a deadly wave of strikes on Saudi airports and refineries.The Gulf monarchies are constructs of European colonialism propped up by American security guarantees that have proved effectively worthless. It cannot be long before regime change comes to the Kingdom, weakened by festering rivalries within the House of Saud since Mohammed bin Salman’s Ritz Carlton coup in November 2017. How could the debt-laden US withstand the collapse of the petrodollar, which channeled Saudi oil revenues into an AI-led stock market bubble already showing signs of bursting?

Another “short, intensive” bombing campaign against Iranian nuclear and energy facilities, which seemed to be prefigured in the “limited” American strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz early this week, would only postpone a further American retreat. Trump’s curtailing aid to Israel has been seen as reducing the likelihood of a resumption of the war. But Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump may still think they can “finish the job”.

Iran’s economy is being slowly strangled by the American naval embargo that is blocking its seaborne oil exports. Yet the regime retains the capacity to devastate the Gulf’s energy production, causing acute shortages of diesel — the fuel on which the global economy runs — and irreplaceable agricultural chemicals. Undersea cables and data centers could also be attacked. The true Iranian nuclear option is disabling water and desalination plants. Weaponizing its geography, with its mountainous streams, inland rivers and lakes, Iran could wreak an enormous civilian catastrophe in the desert kingdoms of its Gulf enemies.

At a global level, a species of total war is already underway. In the delirium of the Western mind, Gaza has been singled out as a unique catastrophe, but the reach of the battlefield into civilian life is practically universal. In Ukraine, Putin’s relentless bombardment destroys schools and scientific academies and cuts off electricity and water, aiming to render Kyiv uninhabitable and drive out millions of desperate refugees. Across Europe, Russia is orchestrating assassination, arson and cyber-strikes, together with drone strikes that could easily spiral into mass casualty events.

The Baltic and Nordic states have fortified their defenses, but most European countries seem paralyzed. Poland — the most militarily prepared — is in the throes of constitutional crisis. Emmanuel Macron’s technocratic centrism has reached its endgame. Teetering on the edge of default, the Fifth Republic is rehearsing the upheaval that will come when Marine Le Pen enters the Élysée Palace — as must now be likely — and Jean-Luc Mélenchon mobilizes an insurrection against her. “Cost-of living” rioting and looting has spread to Belgium, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Germany, Switzerland and Albania, among other countries. It is hard to envision the French banlieues and AfD strongholds in former East Germany accepting the cost of deploying European troops indefinitely in Ukraine. Nor is it clear that Europe could afford to forgo the billions of euros’ worth of oil and gas it buys from Russia (which help Putin fund the war). A European solution is a mirage, and for all the heroic resourcefulness of its struggle, Ukraine cannot go it alone. Unless Zelensky’s supporters in Washington can somehow tie Trump’s hands, the logic of the situation is a brutal partition.

In America, Trump’s rise was a by-product of the neo-liberal cult of globalization. It was not simply an increase in inequality that stoked “populist” revolt. Whole sections of society were denied any productive role. Capital was exported and manufacturing offshored, labor imported and communities abandoned. With their workless families, drug habits and short lives, the human detritus of American industry could be safely left to molder on their reservations. Yet post-industrial decline has now affected much of the middle class. Occupations and career structures have melted into air. Neoliberal economics was the enterprise of re-engineering capitalism without a bourgeoisie, and the hollowing out of middle-class life has continued under Trump’s corporate kleptocracy. There was bound to be a countermovement from the Left. New York mayor Zohran Mandami’s “democratic socialism” is not a movement of organized labor. Like Jeremy Corbyn’s and Zack Polanski’s movements, it is a bourgeois populism, varnishing the status anxieties of heavily-indebted graduates and downwardly-mobile professionals with high-rent progressive causes. Incubated in campus seminaries of anti-Western orthodoxy, Mamdani’s leftism is set to be a deciding force in Democratic politics.

A sea change is underway in the Republicans as well. As he limbers up for a presidential campaign in 2028, JD Vance is cultivating the same nativist constituency that is the audience of Tucker Carlson — aside from Trump, America’s most accomplished demagogue. A devil’s brew of anti-Semitism, historical revisionism and conspiracy theory is shaping up as the ruling ideology of the MAGA Right. As in Europe, the old center ground no longer exists.

By B. Duncan Moench

The midterm clean sweep was a repudiation of Trump more than an endorsement of the Democrats. The winners included Dr Abdul El-Sayed (Michigan, US Senate) and Dr Abdul Hamawy (New Jersey, US House), Egyptian-born Muslims closely aligned with the progressive wing of the Democrats who campaigned strongly against the war. Foreign policy positions that used to be bipartisan are being questioned and rejected in both parties. Europeans who are still invested in the notion that the Trump era is an unfortunate anomaly would be wise to think again. Nothing is further from reality than a reversion to Nikki Haley-style interventionism. It is not fantastical to see the US becoming the first advanced post-Western state and joining Russia in a China-led Eurasian bloc.

That does not mean such a concert of powers would be stable. If a trilateral summit between Xi, Putin and Trump is held at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in Shenzhen scheduled for later this month, their exchanges may well come to nothing. In some ways this looks less like February 1945 and more like the run-up to August 1914. Now as then, great powers are engaged in wars for control of natural resources against a background of tangled and shifting alliances. With multiple players and no one in charge, miscalculation by any of them could bring disaster on all.

Another future is possible, however. Rather than drifting towards another Great War, we may be entering an era of peace. A curious kind of peace, to be sure, accompanied by unending bloodshed. Proxy wars and urban terrorism will rage unabated. War and peace will, in effect, be one and the same. The West will cease to exist as a geopolitical or civilizational bloc. But joining forces with its adversaries will fuel another stock market boom, and what neo-Marxian theorists fondly call “late capitalism” will enjoy a new lease of life. Having used the neoliberal interlude to build a mercantilist juggernaut, China will re-establish globalization in a dirigiste form that entrenches its economic primacy, with Russia exploited as a vassal state. A certain equilibrium will prevail, underpinned by the shared interests of transnational ruling classes.

Then again, none of this may come to pass. The future may not be advancing authoritarianism but accelerating disintegration. If Taiwan is not easily absorbed, Xi’s autocracy may be overthrown, and China could revert to disunity of a kind recurrent in its history. Putin might be toppled by war-weary oligarchs, only to be replaced by a more extreme anti-Western despot ruling a nuclear-armed Muscovy surrounded by breakaway fiefdoms. The United States may fragment, with enclaves of anarchic high-tech vitality booming alongside wastelands of poverty and desolation, presided over by an enfeebled federal government.

But of one thing we can be certain. Donald Trump has brought Western hegemony to a close. A world-historical figure as much as Napoleon or Mao, the founder of MAGA has ushered in a post-American age.

John Gray is a political philosopher and author. His books include The New Leviathans: Thoughts After Liberalism, Feline Philosophy: Cats and the Meaning of Life, Straw Dogs: Thoughts on Humans and Other Animals, Gray’s Anatomy: Selected Writings , and Seven Types of Atheism.

scraped.title: Inside the Chinese manosphere
scraped.author: Tianle Zhang
scraped.h1: Inside the Chinese manosphere Surplus men face lives without women
scraped.body_text:
“Frustration is boiling over in the nascent Chinese manosphere.” (Wang Zhao/AFP/Getty)

“Frustration is boiling over in the nascent Chinese manosphere.” (Wang Zhao/AFP/Getty)

Chinese middle schoolers have had to get their heads around some new reading material this year. Following a once-a-decade reshuffle of the literature syllabus, China’s ninth graders are going back to school with new books. In addition to Three Hundred Tang Poems (a canonical anthology of medieval verse), Red Crag (a realist novel set during China’s civil war), and Jean-Henri Fabre’s Souvenirs entomologiques (a 19th-century treatise on bugs authored by an anti-Darwinian Frenchman), the most striking addition to the curriculum is that landmark of Gothic romance, Jane Eyre .

It’s not immediately clear why Beijing has given Charlotte Brontë’s classic such prominence in the classroom. Thankfully, the West’s top China watchers are on the case. If you’ve read the spate of recent articles from Western media outlets concerning Jane Eyre in China — articles in which there’s been much white-knuckled pearl clutching over China’s “compulsory curriculum” ( The Times ) , “mandatory reading list” ( CNN ), and other histrionic synonyms for, well, a middle-school syllabus — you’ll find one explanation repeated ad nauseaum . The Ministry for Education has, so we’re told, assigned the didactic, pro-family Jane Eyre as a last-ditch effort to reverse China’s precipitous population decline. As the Economist puts it: “The independent-minded heroine, Ms Eyre, who rejects two proposals before ultimately marrying and bearing a son, has a thing or two to teach young Chinese, the Communist Party thinks.”

To be sure, Chinese officials are wary of the looming demographic crisis. As of this year, marriages have hit a decade-long low ; birth rates an all-time low ; and China expects a population decline of 250 million by 2050. But even if the nomenklatura did imagine that a 19th-century English novel was the way to win young Chinese hearts and minds to baby-making, Jane Eyre would be a strange choice. For one, the novel just doesn’t really seem to care about Jane’s maternity; Jane’s son, whom Brontë never bothers to name, exists by virtue of a single subordinate clause tossed off in the middle of the book. Our author devotes twice as many words to describing the embroidered chaises of Thornfield Hall as she does to Rochester Junior. Second, Middlemarch and Pride and Prejudice enjoy similarly storied literary reputations in China; and the orphaned children, Christian ascetics, and wife in the attic that make Brontë’s novel such an unlikely candidate for the transmission of stolid family values are conspicuously absent in the other two novels. If the Ministry for Education really wanted to assign a conservative-minded English classic, why wouldn’t they have gone with Jane’s more presentable cousins?

By Tianle Zhang

When one turns from CNN to the Chinese sources, however, a much clearer picture emerges of Jane Eyre ’s actual purpose in the classroom. Anyone expecting Brontë to be filtered through dense layers of Marxist-Leninist propaganda and Xi Jinping Thought, however, will be sorely disappointed. According to the Beijing Daily article which announced the updated curriculum , the novel will be taught in a course module on “Maturity”, which takes a fairly orthodox view on Jane Eyre ’s key themes: “[Jane Eyre] recognized that love ought to be founded upon the basis of spiritual equality, rather than wealth, social status, or outward appearance.”

For the Chinese government, then, the point of teaching Jane Eyre isn’t to promote biological reproduction, but true love. I realize that, at first pass, the notion of faceless Communist Party bureaucrats spreading romantic ideals among the youth sounds absurd. However, Beijing’s pedagogical intervention makes perfect sense when seen against the backdrop of the gender wars raging everywhere in contemporary Chinese society.

Like pretty much everywhere else in the world, gender relations in China are in complete free-fall. We’re all too familiar in the West with developments like the manosphere, tradwives, looksmaxxing, incels, cucks, chads, etc; recent Chinese history has seen the emergence of similar controversies, coded dogwhistles, and ultra-extremist ideological factions along gendered fault lines. One key moment was the April 2024 suicide of Fat Cat (胖猫), the online alias of Liu Jie, who jumped off a bridge following a breakup. In the aftermath, his girlfriend became the target of a concerted nationwide witch hunt led by Chinese incels on the assumption she was a 捞女 / lāo nǚ , or gold digger. Meanwhile, a terminally online subset of “ feminist eugenicists ” have developed what they term “uterine morality”, or a refusal to settle for “ugly, poor, sick, and abusive men” in an effort to secure the best possible genetic material for their offspring. This January, China’s Ministry of State Security even issued a communiqué framing 性别对立 / xìngbié duìlì or “gender antagonism” as a threat to national security. It’s this toxic mire of gender politics that Chinese teenagers will have to negotiate in order to date, marry, and have children; a plight that makes even the wildest of Rochester’s indiscretions seem tame by comparison.

Contemporary China has left behind what was arguably the central achievement of the Mao era: economic parity between men and women. Following socialist collectivization, Chinese society became highly egalitarian, with the percentage of women working outside the home hitting roughly 90% in urban areas by the Seventies . With women entering the workforce en masse , the state took on the role of performing domestic labor, investing heavily in free childcare centers, collective kitchens, and other welfare programs. The state meanwhile suppressed the development of feminism outside of the proscribed boundaries; as China scholars Angela Xiao Wu and Yige Dong argue , the state’s firm control of “women’s work” reduced femininity to economic categories. Popular representations of women were accordingly non-sexualized, and to some extent androgynous, emphasizing their class identities as proletarians and farmers.

China’s socialist era ended with Deng Xiaoping’s capitalist reforms, whereupon the state abandoned its commitment to egalitarianism for the full-throated pursuit of economic development. As privatization shuttered the state-funded public daycares and kitchens, domestic labor was relegated back to the domain of the family — in practice, back to women. These developments were part of a broader retrenchment of traditional gender norms in the Deng era. The Puritanism of Mao’s China was submerged under a tidal wave of (at the time) risqué advertisements, television shows, and eventually, digital media, as an emerging consumer culture found a natural ally in sex appeal.

While Deng’s reforms generated rapid economic growth, they also intensified class stratification. By the Eighties, socialist egalitarianism was fading; as Wu and Dong write: “against the spectacular rise of wealthy elites and a massive middle-class were forty million laid-off state workers and more than 200 million migrant laborers”. Chinese citizens could stomach the decidedly unsocialist existence of an ultra-rich class so long as everybody else’s living standards went up, too. But this is no longer the case. Youth unemployment in 2026 hit a record high, while precarious gig work is rapidly replacing full-time employment . And with China’s broader economic slowdown showing no signs of abating , there seem to be few options available to check a rising tide of class resentment . This neoliberal precarity is one of the structural problems behind today’s gender crisis.

While most Western readers can easily relate to issues like youth unemployment and class resentment, there’s another problem at work that’s unique to the Chinese situation: a “ marriage squeeze ” resulting from a dangerously lopsided gender ratio. This is one of the unintended consequences of the government’s laws on family planning. When the one-child policy was implemented in the Eighties, many couples practiced sex-selective abortions to ensure they had sons, given the traditional preference for a male heir. As a result, there are 24.7 million more Chinese men than women, a surplus greater than the population of Florida.

To combine years of neoliberal precarity with a radical gender imbalance would destabilize marriage rates in any country. However, in China’s specific cultural context, the confluence of these two structural factors have created a marriage market that’s nothing short of apocalyptic. These two factors come to a head in the widespread custom of bride price, or 彩礼 / cǎilǐ , a prerequisite step to marriage where the groom’s side of the family must make a payment to the bride’s. From a traditional Chinese perspective, because the bride was considered exclusively a member of her husband’s family, cǎilǐ was paid as ritual compensation to the bride’s family for having “given away” their daughter. Historically, this took the form of tea, jewelry, or deer hides and for most of modern China, bride price was seen as a quaint formality. However, escalated competition over marriageable women has now resulted in a textbook case of supply and demand. Twenty years ago, the average bride price hovered around 10,000 to 20,000 RMB (~$1,500 – $3,000). It has since skyrocketed to around 140,000 RMB (~$21,000) in 2021, a crippling economic burden, especially for rural, low-income households.

Even under ideal economic circumstances, the surge in bride price would have presented a serious financial barrier to would-be grooms. China’s fiscal downturn has made scrounging together the funds more difficult — and the situation is made even worse by the particular cultural dynamics at work when two families come together to negotiate cǎilǐ . In a perverse twist , the poorer the groom, the higher the expected bride price, and vice versa. The logic here is that if the bride’s family feels uncertain about the groom’s financial prospects, they’ll hedge their bets by setting a higher cǎilǐ, which then acts as a kind of surety for the bride’s future.

In a culture where remaining single and childless carries a heavy stigma, the romantic prospects for the less fortunate among China’s 25 million surplus men are, to put it mildly, bleak. Frustration is boiling over in the nascent Chinese manosphere . Echoing a widespread view, one popular post on WeChat ties the rise in bride price to feminism: “I was born in the 1980s. When I got married, there was no bride price […] Now feminism has even brainwashed some women born in the 1970s into thinking they’re ‘goddesses.’ Policies to boost childbirth are useless. Why not crack down on feminism instead?”

The language of anti-feminist reaction merges with pre-existing chauvinistic rhetoric. “Feminists are anti-family, anti-Han race and anti-state,” imputes one aggrieved commentator. Thus, parallel to the red-pill rhetoric of Western incels, a vocal minority of Chinese men are framing themselves as victims of an international feminist conspiracy. Some of these anti-feminists have even taken to attacking married men; by paying cǎilǐ , so the argument goes, successful grooms undermine “the collective male effort to lower the ‘cost’ of marriage”, making them traitors to their gender.

Meanwhile, Chinese feminism has also developed in response to the destabilized marriage market. Recall that the defunding of socialist institutions for childcare and housekeeping pushed these obligations back onto the family unit, increasing the pressure on women to re-adopt traditional roles as homemakers. In response to these institutionalized values, one strand of Chinese feminism advocates malicious compliance: “ entrepreneurial ” feminists attempt to leverage their attractiveness to maximize bride price returns on the marriage market. One such entrepreneurial feminist known online as Ayawawa became infamous for her “PU-MV” equation; according to this heuristic, Chinese women ought to balance a high MV, or “mating value” (sexual attractiveness) with a low PU, or “paternity uncertainty” (alleviating masculine concerns of infidelity by appearing chaste, innocent, virtuous, etc.).

Then there’s the other branch of contemporary Chinese feminism: the “non-cooperative” feminists, who join the chorus of victimized men in their outright rejection of the marriage market: “No kids, no ring, keep living serene” is their go-to slogan . Instead of relying on well-matched grooms to provide economic security, these feminists take the path of Western girlbosses in striving to secure financial independence via their own careers. Mirroring their counterparts in the manosphere, the extremely online “zero-compromise” feminists decry married women as “love-brained”, “precious wives”, and “marriage donkeys”.

Any hope of reconciliation under present circumstances seems well nigh impossible. For a generation of red-pilled men whose ideals of masculinity are still based on “economic success and possession of female sexuality”, confronting the sexually unavailable, financially independent grouping of non-cooperative feminists would amount to a double emasculation. Meanwhile, the utilitarian mindset of entrepreneurial feminism would appear to confirm the manosphere’s most paranoid fantasies about gold-digging wives. As for the few Chinese couples who do end up tying the knot, marriage nowadays is no longer seen as the fulfillment of romantic love, but as a byproduct of rational economic calculation . As things stand, further rounds of acrimony and radicalization are inevitable.

If only due to its destabilizing knock-on effects on marriage, childbirth, and general political stability, the gender wars have come under increasing scrutiny from Chinese officials. At first glance, though, the recent government actions taken on this issue seem haphazard. The CCP has led a (spectacularly unsuccessful) effort to crack down on bride prices even while it enshrines cǎilǐ into law as the bride’s premarital property. And keywords such as “extreme feminism” are censored online even while the Supreme People’s Court rules in favor of the female plaintiff in a landmark case on engagement rape, enraging the manosphere.

By David Lloyd Dusenbury

Yet from a wider perspective, a consistent pattern does emerge. For the manosphere, soaring bride prices are due to unchecked greed of gold-digging feminists — not the result of family planning policies or China’s neoliberal turn. Similarly, for many contemporary feminists, women’s aspirations for economic independence can only be achieved through individual action: either by gaming the marriage market (if you’re an entrepreneurial feminist), or by focusing solely on one’s own career (if you’re the non-cooperative sort). The exclusive focus on the individual action of economic agents, on the grindset , ignores the conscious dismantling of Mao-era collective institutions which forced women back into performing domestic labor in the first place.

How does Jane Eyre fit into all this? What may have seemed like the height of idealism is, properly understood, a fairly cynical ploy. In treating Brontë’s novel as a sermon on the transcendent value of love (“only when two people truly love one another can they achieve true happiness,” quoth Beijing Daily ), it becomes another avenue to direct frustration about social ills away from the decisions of policymakers, and into the safely apolitical domain of interpersonal relationships. Schoolboys otherwise in danger of becoming “red-pilled” may learn from the lesson of Rochester, who finds his beloved in Jane regardless of his looks or finances. And as China’s schoolgirls follow Jane’s repeated repudiations of earthly wealth for the higher affairs of heart and mind, they’ll be less inclined to countenance the economic focus of non-cooperative feminism. The story of Jane and Rochester, then, will act as a gentle corrective to the radicalizing tendencies of both the manosphere and Chinese feminism — a balm which nonetheless serves the very same ends of occluding a structural critique. Because so long as netizens are busy talking about gold diggers and gender traitors — or, indeed, waxing poetic about true love — they won’t be talking about high-level policy decisions that led to the broken marriage market, or the changes that would need to happen to fix it.

scraped.title: Martin McDonagh’s American paranoia
scraped.author: Tom Shone
scraped.h1: Martin McDonagh’s American paranoia In “Wild Horse Nine”, the truth is worthless
scraped.body_text:
“Do you ever get paranoid that you’re not being paranoid enough?” (Wild Horse Nine/IMBD)

“Do you ever get paranoid that you’re not being paranoid enough?” (Wild Horse Nine/IMBD)

“Do you ever get paranoid that you’re not being paranoid enough?” asks John Malkovich in Martin McDonagh’s new black comedy, Wild Horse Nine . It is 1973 and Malkovich’s character Chris, an aging, morphine-addicted CIA agent, is fresh from plotting a coup in Chile along with his colleague Lee (Sam Rockwell). The pair have decamped to Easter Island where Chris, high on opiates, starts blabbing the agency’s secrets to whoever will listen: his part in the Kennedy assassination, and his more recent work plotting to topple President Allende. “Enjoy him while you can, ladies,” he tells two Chilean students he comes across at the airport. “Your country is gonna get fucked.”

Some early viewers have been offended by the movie’s “cool, jokey complacency”. The jokes come mostly “at the expense of the myriad political victims of America’s relentless interventionist politics”. Certainly, for those used to the paranoid thrillers from the Seventies like The Parallax View (1974) or The Domino Principle (1977), which sought to lay bare America’s secret history, McDonagh’s flip, caustic tone seems a deliberate affront. In place of Deep Throat’s gravelly sotto voce in an underground garage, we have a spook laughing about messing up other people’s countries while on a mini-break.

McDonagh, in having Chris spill secrets from his bar stool, deliberately upends the conventions of the great conspiracy thrillers of the Seventies, which depended on the scarcity of disclosure. Their climaxes usually came with a congressional inquiry or a newspaper scoop: Sydney Pollack’s Three Days of the Condor (1975) ends with Robert Redford’s CIA bookworm on the pavement outside the New York Times, having handed over the story. All the President’s Men (1974) ends with a fusillade of teletyping. To adapt the old Watergate maxim, crimes require a cover-up to register as crimes — and a heroic press to unmask them.

Fifty years on, the secrets are out. Or rather, the secrets are content. Conspiracy theories are the raw material of some of the most popular podcasts and YouTube channels in the world, and they are regularly spouted from the presidential podium. Meanwhile the actual record has never been more available: WikiLeaks cables, Edward Snowden’s slides, and tens of thousands of pages of JFK files declassified by presidential order. There is, if anything, too much of it. Revelation no longer registers, in the same way that Trump’s malfeasance barely registers, because he is so open about it. Asked in January why he was allowing so much conflict of interest, he said plainly: “because I found out that nobody cared.” Why bother with the cover-up?

By Thomas Peermohamed Lambert

The flourishing of American paranoia in the Seventies took its cue from Richard Hofstadter’s seminal essay The Paranoid Style in American Politics , first published in November 1964. For Hofstadter, this political approach was used by everyone from John Robison to Joe McCarthy, waving his lists around frantically in hearings. It was pedantic, mock-scholarly, piling up documents and footnotes, then leaping from real facts to a fantastic conclusion: usually the unmasking of the hidden enemy set on destroying American civilization. For all the implausibility of, say, Hollywood being a hotbed of Soviet sleeper agents, the paranoid worldview ends up more coherent than reality, because it leaves no room for accident or ambiguity. Everything can, ultimately, be explained. The paranoiac is therefore a dramatist who has forgotten they are making it up.

If the style of Seventies paranoia cinema owes a lot to Hofstadter, it is Dick Cheney we must thank for much of the content. At a lunch with editors of the New York Times on 16 January 1975, President Ford was pressed on why anyone should trust the commission he had appointed 12 days earlier to investigate the CIA. The agency’s own internal record of its past operations — the so-called “Family Jewels” — held material, Ford said, that would “blacken the reputation of every President back to Harry Truman”.

“Like what?” asked one of the editors.

“Like assassination.”

When Ford’s commission duly reported that June, the assassinations weren’t in it. Cheney, the president’s 34-year-old deputy assistant, had gone through the draft with a pen, paying particular attention to the 86-page chapter on plots against foreign leaders. He inserted recommendations the commission had never voted on, deleted ones it had, and, where the commission had found CIA activities unlawful, recast them as merely exceeding statutory authority or as “improper”.

Cheney’s pen marked a bad day for American democracy but a great one for the country’s thriller writers. The reality of the CIA’s plots, even in the redacted form that appeared in the report of the Senate’s Church Committee that November, was a catalog of bungled kidnaps and assassination attempts, subcontracted to Mafia hoods, Cuban exiles and Corsican gunmen, and, cigars poisoned with botulinum.

It was enough, in the words of the report, to “strain the imagination” — and the gap between the redacted public record and the reality fed thriller writers and Hollywood screenwriters with the myth of CIA invincibility for 50 years, in everything from Sam Peckinpah’s The Killer Elite (1975) to Oliver Stone’s JFK (1991), which gave the CIA a starring role in Dallas, right up to the Bourne films, which have the CIA tracking a man across Europe in real time from a bank of screens in Langley.

When the agency’s darkest skeletons were finally declassified in June 2007, director Paul Greengrass printed out all 693 pages and gave them to the cast of The Bourne Ultimatum (2007) — in retrospect, maybe the last gasp of the paranoid style in American filmmaking. The movie’s Operation ‘Blackbriar’ was directly based on the illegal surveillance operations of CIA counter-intelligence chief James Jesus Angleton which over two decades had secretly opened more than 200,000 letters passing between the United States and the Soviet Union as well as indexing some 300,000 Americans for being in the anti-war movement.

Today, believers don’t need official documents. Online, they can find thousands of fellow fantasists to back up their ideas and algorithms to amplify their most outlandish theories. The Covid pandemic proved a ferocious accelerant. Uncertainty about whether everyone else would follow the rules fed a more generalized distrust not of the “enemy above”, as Jesse Walker puts it in The United States of Paranoia (2013), but the “Enemy Within”: paranoia directed not at shadowy government agents, but at neighbors behind their picket fences and lawn sprinklers. As a Twilight Zone episode once had it, the monsters are on Maple street.

The circle of distrust narrows, but it never quite reaches the mirror. What the paranoiac fears most is not persecution but irrelevance. Better to be the object of a thousand plots than to discover that no one is thinking about you at all. That is Chris’s predicament in Wild Horse Nine . Malkovich plays him as an Angleton gone to seed, monologuing into a Dictaphone for a memoir to be published after his death, and blabbing state secrets to strangers to watch them react. He isn’t a whistleblower; he’s a man testing whether disclosure still has any voltage, and finding that it doesn’t.

This is the condition Hofstadter didn’t foresee: not that the paranoid style would turn apocalyptic, but that its apocalypses would become so commonplace as to be banal. The hero’s discovery is everyone else’s Tuesday. What’s left, when revelation is worthless, is loose-lipped farce. In HBO’s White House Plumbers (2023), the Watergate burglars, as played by Woody Harrelson and Justin Theroux, are bunglers straight out of Veep : they can barely get through a door. Chaos or conspiracy? How about both?

Tom Shone is an American film critic and writer. The updated version of his book The Nolan Variations is out now.

scraped.title: "Mercy For The Wolves": California DAs Revolt After Newsom Wipes Out Death Row
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: "Mercy For The Wolves": California DAs Revolt After Newsom Wipes Out Death Row
scraped.body_text:
California's district attorneys are vowing to keep seeking the death penalty in new cases , and some are looking for a way to block Gov. Gavin Newsom's commutation of all 548 death sentences in the state before it takes effect. As we reported , Newsom announced Thursday that he would commute every death sentence in California to life without parole, writing in a letter that "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values."

Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer went first. Newsom's commutations are "mercy for the wolves," he said in a statement Thursday, before making the vow: "I, as the elected District Attorney of Orange County, have, and will, continue to pursue the death penalty."

Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer Issues Statement on Governor Newsom's Commutation of All Death Sentences in California Click here for full release: https://t.co/x65hY8Hlvx SANTA ANA, Calif. - Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer issued the following... pic.twitter.com/xWsH1Y8eby

— OCDA Todd Spitzer (@OCDAToddSpitzer) November 5, 2026

Newsom's own letter leaves them that opening. The commutations do not repeal the death penalty, so prosecutors can still seek it in new cases, as the Mercury News noted. San Mateo County District Attorney Stephen Wagstaffe, whose office is seeking death against the man accused of killing seven farmworkers at a Half Moon Bay mushroom farm in 2023, told the paper he was "disgusted." "It is contrary to two separate votes of the people of California," he said. "What he's done today is specifically undemocratic and serves his own personal philosophy."

The bigger question is whether the commutations survive at all. The state constitution bars a governor from commuting the sentence of anyone convicted of more than one felony without the California Supreme Court's approval, which covers 382 of the 548 cases , and the governor's office says none of the commutations take effect until those legal steps are done. That is where prosecutors are looking. San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan said her office is "researching any lawful remedies" for victims' families, who she said were "deprived of any input."

San Diego County District Attorney @SummerStephan issued the following statement on Governor Gavin Newsom's commutation of all death sentences in California: pic.twitter.com/cAW314gNmZ

— SD District Attorney (@SDDistAtty) November 6, 2026

Victims' rights are the likeliest line of attack. San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson said Newsom ignored Marsy's Law, the victims' rights guarantees in the state constitution: "I am not aware of any victims' family members receiving notice of these commutations from the Governor." He singled out Kevin Cooper, convicted of murdering Josh Ryen's family and his friend Chris Hughes and leaving Ryen for dead. Cooper maintains his innocence, and Newsom ordered an independent investigation of his case. "Josh has never received a call from Gavin Newsom," Anderson said, calling the commutations "arrogant and political showmanship."

Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho made the voters' case. A blanket commutation stands "in direct conflict with the will of California voters," he said. Californians have twice rejected abolishing the death penalty and in 2016 reaffirmed it through Proposition 66 , the measure meant to speed up executions, Ho noted. It also ignores "the voices of victims who have waited decades for justice," Ho said.

A statement from Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho. pic.twitter.com/NuspYtYFci

— Sacramento County DA (@SacCountyDA) November 6, 2026

Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was kidnapped from her Petaluma home and murdered in 1993 by Richard Allen Davis, fears the commutations are a first step. "We're all looking at the prospect of potentially them getting out someday, because they're one step closer now," he told the Mercury News. Spitzer made the same argument, pointing to state parole regulations that took effect Oct. 1 and, he said, make thousands of inmates serving life without parole eligible for parole. The governor's office says the commutations release no one and make no one eligible for parole, and that the commuted prisoners are excluded from the parole board's new commutation and resentencing rules.

Not every prosecutor objects. Santa Clara County District Attorney Jeff Rosen called the commutations "the right thing to do," and Contra Costa District Attorney Diana Becton said they would "save California taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars." The state has also set aside $239 million to turn San Quentin, home of the old death row, into a rehab center , as we reported.

Newsom leaves office in January and is weighing a 2028 presidential run. California has not executed anyone since 2006, and his successor, Xavier Becerra, has said he will extend the moratorium on executions Newsom imposed in 2019.

scraped.h1: Berkshire's Post-Buffett Era Gets Off To Rocky Start As AI Bets Stumble
scraped.body_text:
With Warren Buffett gone for not even a year, Berkshire Hathaway is already facing questions over its investment decisions. Under new CEO Greg Abel, the conglomerate has made a multibillion-dollar push into artificial intelligence, only to see some of its biggest bets stumble as enthusiasm for the technology fades, according to Bloomberg .

In his first year at the helm, Abel has committed $10 billion to Google parent Alphabet and another $930 million to Italian technology group Bending Spoons, marking a shift from Buffett's traditionally cautious approach to technology investments.

But the timing has raised concerns. Alphabet shares have fallen more than 24% since June, slipping below Berkshire's purchase price, while Bending Spoons has also retreated following an initial rally.

CEO Greg Abel

Still, analysts say Abel may be taking a longer-term view, much like Buffett did with his highly profitable Apple investment in 2016. With $365.5 billion in cash at the end of the second quarter, Berkshire has plenty of room to capitalize on lower valuations and expand its AI exposure.

Meanwhile, Berkshire's upcoming third-quarter earnings will offer a broader look at the conglomerate's performance under Abel. Solid US economic growth could support its businesses, although inflation and high fuel prices may weigh on retail operations.

Investors will also be watching Geico, where higher claims costs and advertising spending hurt recent profits, and railroad operator BNSF, which could benefit from stronger freight volumes and fuel surcharges.

Bloomberg notes that another focus will be share buybacks. Berkshire resumed repurchases earlier this year after a lengthy pause, but its stock has since climbed to record highs, potentially discouraging further purchases.

The results will offer an early test of Abel's leadership as he seeks to put Berkshire's enormous cash reserves to work while preserving the investment discipline that defined the Buffett era. He will have to do so in an era where Democrats now control a large majority of AI/data center planned capacity in the US...

Recall, under Buffett, Berkshire spent years building one of the largest cash piles in corporate America, more than doubling its reserves from roughly $150 billion at the end of 2021 to over $370 billion by late 2025.

Buffett largely resisted chasing soaring stock valuations, preferring to sit on the sidelines rather than overpay for investments. Now, less than a year after his departure, Abel is putting billions of those reserves to work in AI, with early results proving less than encouraging.

scraped.h1: Peltola Campaign Sues Alaska Over Rejected Absentee Ballots as Decoy Dan Sullivan Siphons Thousands of Votes
scraped.body_text:
The Peltola campaign sued Alaska over rejected absentee ballots as the decoy Dan Sullivan siphons thousands of votes.

The Associated Press reported that as of Saturday morning with 75% of the vote tallied, Democrat Mary Peltola is ahead of Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan by approximately 625 votes.

Peltola has 102,962 votes at 48.17% and GOP Senator Dan Sullivan has 102,325 votes at 47.88%.

The decoy Dan Sullivan has 3,600 votes at 1.68%.

The Peltola campaign’s scheme to siphon votes away from Senator Dan Sullivan is working.

Mary Peltola’s campaign is now suing Alaska for access to the rejected absentee ballots.

The Hill reported :

Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign is suing the state of Alaska to obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections, a new court filing shows.

Peltola’s campaign said they previously requested records of the rejected ballots on multiple occasions but were denied access.

“Plaintiff cannot ensure that its voters’ lawful votes were properly counted without knowing whose absentee ballots were rejected or questioned, and why,” the lawsuit reads. “Each hour and each day that Defendants deny Plaintiff the requested records to which it is entitled costs Plaintiff the opportunity to help ensure that qualified voters have their ballots counted.”

Peltola currently leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in the Alaska U.S. Senate race by just over 600 votes, but with approximately 30 percent of the vote still outstanding, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). No winner has been projected in the race as of Saturday morning.

The Division responded in a release on Friday, saying voters who have had their ballots rejected have not yet had access to the information, therefore, the campaign should not be able to have access yet either.

items.title: Democrats Eye Midterm Wins as a Path Around the Electoral College
