scraped.title: Democrats Eye Midterm Wins as a Path Around the Electoral College › American Greatness
scraped.description: New Dem majorities in five swing states could push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past the 270 votes needed to take effect.
scraped.h1: Democrats Eye Midterm Wins as a Path Around the Electoral College
scraped.body_text:
Democrats are looking to use their midterm gains to effectively sidestep the Electoral College before the 2028 presidential election.

The effort centers on the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, no matter which candidate carries their own state. Eighteen states and the District of Columbia have already joined, accounting for 222 electoral votes. The compact only takes effect once members reach 270, the same number needed to win the presidency.

Tuesday’s election gave Democrats full control of the governor’s office and both legislative chambers in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada. Several state lawmakers told the Times they have begun discussing legislation for the next session in hopes of getting it done before 2028. If all five join, the compact would cross the 270 threshold.

“This blue tsunami is really going to help push this forward across the whole nation,” Michigan state Rep. Carrie Rheingans told the Times.

Not every Democrat has embraced the idea. Nevada’s Democratic governor vetoed an earlier attempt to join the compact in 2019.

Legal experts expect a fight. Derek Muller, an election law expert at Notre Dame Law School, said, “It’s a very real possibility that enough states join this compact. There will be a lot of challenges.” Interstate compacts traditionally require approval from Congress and the president, he noted.

Supporters point to elections like 2000 and 2016, when the candidate who lost the popular vote won the White House. A June YouGov poll found 56 percent of adults believe the president should be chosen by popular vote.

Opponents warn the plan would hand presidential elections to the largest population centers and undercut the Founders’ design, which forces candidates to win support across a wide range of states rather than running up the score in a few big ones.

scraped.title: Left-Wing Activists Flood House Democrats With Calls to Dump Jeffries as Speaker › American Greatness
scraped.description: A Change.org petition against Hakeem Jeffries has topped 920,000 signatures, exposing a rift between Democratic lawmakers and their activist base.
scraped.h1: Left-Wing Activists Flood House Democrats With Calls to Dump Jeffries as Speaker
scraped.body_text:
Days after their midterm victory, House Democrats are being bombarded with phone calls and emails urging them not to make Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries the next speaker.

The pressure campaign reveals what Axios called a fundamental disconnect between House Democrats, most of whom are expected to back Jeffries, and at least part of their grassroots base.

One incoming Democrat has received about 150 calls, and a senior House Democrat reported more than 500 in two days, according to Axios reporting cited by Newsmax. “It’s our No. 1 issue, and it’s not close,” one House Democrat said.

Much of the outreach is tied to a Change.org petition started by Nicole Whitted that urges every member of the incoming Congress to vote against Jeffries in January. By Friday afternoon it had more than 921,000 verified signatures, Newsmax reported. The petition page discloses that Whitted is paid through Change.org’s ambassador program, a detail that has raised eyebrows on Capitol Hill. One House Democrat credited actor Mark Ruffalo, who shared the petition online, with driving much of the traffic.

Activists on the left have long been irritated by Jeffries’ ties to pro-Israel groups and corporate political action committees, and many argue party leaders have not done enough to resist the Trump administration. Ezra Levin, co-executive director of Indivisible, said Democrats “can’t go back to business-as-usual politics.” A Democratic chief of staff said many callers want Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland as speaker, though Raskin has shown no interest in running.

The campaign is unlikely to succeed. Jeffries formally announced his bid in a letter to colleagues Wednesday, no challenger has emerged, and no House Democrat has voted against him for speaker since he became leader in 2022. “Jeffries absolutely will be speaker,” said Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut.

Democrats will hold leadership elections Nov. 18 and 19, and the full House will vote for speaker when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3.

scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: What happens to the human soul when AI makes work optional?
scraped.body_text:
Allie Beth Stuckey asks pastor Jonny Ardavanis what Elon Musk’s AI utopia will do to people hardwired by God to work.

Tech entrepreneur Elon Musk has repeatedly predicted that a day is coming soon when AI and robotics will make traditional work optional in a utopian age of abundance, where humans will rely on universal high income while pursuing personal interests.

Trading the daily grind for a life of comfort and leisure may be compelling, but is it good for the human soul?

That’s the question Allie Beth Stuckey asked Stonebridge Bible Church Pastor Jonny Ardavanis, whose new book, “Get to Work: Seeing Your Daily Grind as God’s Good Gift,” explores why work is a divine gift rather than a burden to escape.

“I just think that’s going to be a horrible, horrible existence,” Ardavanis says of Musk’s AI utopia.

Regardless of one’s belief system, there’s an intrinsic understanding that work is a necessary part of the human experience, he argues, citing the oft-used expression “a job well done.”

“You mow the lawn, you see the stripes in your lawn, and you put your hands on your hips and you go, ‘There’s something Edenic about this,”’ Ardavanis says.

This sense of fulfillment, he says, can be traced back to the Garden of Eden, where Adam and Eve were first charged to cultivate and keep the garden as part of God’s original good design.

“Deep down, God has hardwired Eden into our souls, and we’re pining away to get back there,” he tells Allie, citing Ecclesiastes 3:11’s reminder that God has “set eternity in the human heart.”

But if AI removes the necessity of work, Ardavanis warns that the human heart, with its God-given orientation toward purpose and vocation, will wither.

“When a robot starts mowing your lawn, you know, you’re going to start to be stripped and starved of the opportunities to reflect God in that way. And I think it is going to be soul-crushing,” he says.

Work, he points out, isn’t just about doing; it’s also about thinking. When robots can think in our stead, what happens to the God-created mind?

“What does it mean to be made in the image of God? Well, it means we have a mind. It means that we are to engage that mind,” Ardavanis says. “Almost all of the instruction in the New Testament regarding the Christian life is what we do with our mind.”

“Your mind is God's gift to you, to employ it.”

This longing isn’t limited to believers. Even non-Christians recognize the irreplicable uniqueness of the human experience. Ardavanis points to globally famous actor Tom Cruise, who, in response to a question about AI’s impact on filmmaking, said , “There is nothing like human.”

“Even though Tom Cruise doesn’t know the God of the Bible, the God of the Bible has hardwired something into Tom Cruise’s heart,” he says. “We are to mirror and mimic God. When we do so, it gives us joy, and it gives us a level of purpose and meaning.”

“I’m looking into a world where people are excited about the absence of work, the three-day work week ... and biblically speaking, I think that that’s hard to reconcile with the fact that we’ve been given a mission by God.”

To hear more, watch the episode above.

To enjoy more of Allie’s upbeat and in-depth coverage of culture, news, and theology from a Christian, conservative perspective, subscribe to BlazeTV — the largest multi-platform network of voices who love America, defend the Constitution, and live the American dream.

BlazeTV Staff

scraped.title: Before AI takes a teacher's job, send it to the district office | Blaze Media
scraped.description: A teacher’s hunt for a payroll answer led through unanswered emails, two buildings, and a maze of offices. A chatbot could have saved the trip — and maybe a few salaries.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: Before AI takes a teacher's job, send it to the district office
scraped.body_text:
A teacher’s hunt for a payroll answer led through unanswered emails, two buildings, and a maze of offices. A chatbot could have saved the trip — and maybe a few salaries.

With shrinking enrollment and ballooning expenses, public school districts across the country are not only facing massive budget deficits but are also quickly losing the goodwill of the public.

Here in Texas, districts like Houston and Austin are seeing huge budget shortfalls. Around the country, school systems are on the path to bankruptcy yet have done little to cut spending.

So many meetings, conferences, and email exchanges could be phased out, leaving more time to actually teach students.

Many district leaders and their respective school boards seem to believe that these enrollment drops are nothing serious or that they can blame someone else for the problem and absolve themselves of responsibility. Consequently, instead of making significant spending cuts, they go on draining rainy-day funds or spending money they don’t have.

Worse still, the bulk of these expenses do not go toward hiring more teachers , but instead go toward administrative staff, extracurricular programs, curriculum and technology specialists, and countless office workers with undefined roles working in office buildings that the district inexplicably owns and maintains.

In the rare instances that cuts are made, it is mostly the teaching staff — that is, the actual people in the classroom working with students — who are affected.

Realistically, can anything be done to prevent these districts from imploding in spectacular fashion? Speaking as a teacher currently in the trenches, this might be a place where AI can reduce costs while boosting instructional quality.

I’m not talking about replacing teachers with AI-enhanced educational software, turning classrooms into computer lounges, and replacing principals with bored babysitters making sure the kids continue vegetating in front of their screens.

According to a recent essay in the New York Times, this is the bold new idea at Alpha private schools: “At Alpha, there are no traditional teachers, few books, and little paper. All of the academic lessons are delivered via apps, and students can earn lavish prizes for completing their work. Adults are present, but only as motivational guides.”

Predictably, this approach to education has mixed results. While the stronger students usually cruise through content and perform well on their standardized tests, the weaker students who need more help will often experience delays in their progress and opt out of the program altogether.

More importantly, it neglects the most important aspects of schooling: socialization and humanization. Education is as much about results as it is about relationships. Teachers do not merely dispense information to compliant drones who mentally download this information through note-taking and worksheets. Teachers are supposed to design their instruction around the needs of their students, govern their classes equitably, and connect the content of their subject to the world outside the classroom.

RELATED: The forgotten colleges that could restore hope to American education

Crisserbug/Getty Images

When this learning is outsourced to a computer and mediated through a screen, everything is reduced and flattened — of course, the superficial people in tech will mistake this for efficiency.

Separated from the outside world, students engage with material through drill-and-kill pedagogy, working through assessments that offer practice on state standards. While this works well enough for math instruction, it becomes far less effective in the sciences or humanities.

With all this said, there still might be a key role for AI in public education. While it can’t replace teachers, it can replace many of the people around them. And if used properly, it can also enhance the work that teachers do.

In terms of cutting down bureaucratic bloat, all districts, even solvent ones, could use a DOGE-style audit to identify useless positions, departments, and redundancies. There are countless individuals in a school district who could permanently disappear without anyone noticing. Many of them are collecting paychecks and later pensions for irrelevant work, but no one notices them because they are usually hidden.

Case in point: Years ago, I had a question about one of my paychecks. I sent out emails to the dozen HR people listed on the district website to see who could answer my question. When no one replied, I took a half-day off and drove over to the administration building to see if I could talk to someone face-to-face. Apparently, I went to the wrong administrative building and had to drive to the other one a mile away.

Once there, the receptionist directed me to a hallway on the fourth floor to look for a person who knew about paychecks. After wandering about for 10 minutes, I finally found someone who directed me to yet another person who finally had the answer to my question.

RELATED: AI doesn’t know you, but a good physician does

Moor Studio/Getty Images

Most public teachers have a story like this. Some random thing prompts them to take a journey through their district’s Kafkaesque bureaucracy, and then they realize just how many useless people are on the payroll. Today, most queries could be answered in a few seconds with a chatbot. Moreover, most duties done by non-teaching staff, like setting up schedules, organizing information, compiling data and documentation, and making presentations, could be done with AI.

Just as importantly, the people who work with students could accomplish far more with AI support. So many meetings, conferences, and email exchanges could be phased out, leaving more time to actually teach students. So many roles requiring specialized training and higher salaries could either be removed entirely or replaced by those with general experience and aptitude.

In such a system — which would resemble something like Singapore’s exceptional educational program — good teachers would be rewarded with more respect, authority, and income while administrators would function as their subordinates. Good teachers are far less replaceable than administrators, so they should be encouraged to stay in the classroom and help more students.

Like any large organization, most school districts have grown into something so unwieldy and chaotic that enacting meaningful reform is next to impossible. Those with the authority to do so are usually too incompetent and complacent to do anything, and those with competence and wherewithal to do something lack the authority. Meanwhile, taxpayers funding public schools tend to focus their ire on the people they can see and ignore the true source of the problem.

It may be difficult to imagine an alternative to the current dysfunction, but it can be done. And if done right, it will be a good thing for everyone involved.

Auguste Meyrat

scraped.h1: Elderly man on e-bike brutally beaten in unprovoked attack in broad daylight. Then Good Samaritan lends unexpected help.
scraped.body_text:
"I'm lucky to be alive," 77-year-old Herb Freeborn told WPVI-TV in the wake of a brutal, unprovoked attack he suffered just after noon Wednesday in Ridley Township, Pennsylvania, while he was riding his e-bike.

Ridley Township is just under 30 minutes southwest of Philadelphia.

'I ain't used to people helping me like that, you know.'

Freeborn told the station he was waiting to cross Chester Pike in the Crum Lynne section when a male approached him from behind and began punching him.

Surveillance video shows the suspect crossing through traffic and heading toward the victim before the attack, WPVI said.

"This guy came up behind me, started punching me and punching me," Freeborn recalled to the station.

WPVI asked him if the suspect said anything during the attack, but Freeborn said, "No, didn't say nothing, just came up to me and started hitting me."

The station said Freeborn suffered injuries to his eye and face.

RELATED: Laughing 'piece of s**t' thug caught on video punching victim in face as pair pass each other in Philly crosswalk

Surveillance video shows Freeborn managing to run from the attacker, WPVI reported.

At that point, one might expect the suspect to make off with the victim's e-bike — but he didn't.

The station said the suspect actually threw Freeborn's e-bike and walked away.

Surveillance video also captured a bystander — Danny Doyle — stepping in to help, WPVI noted.

Doyle told the station he saw the incident and went to assist Freeborn, grabbing the victim's e-bike and checking on his condition.

"At first I thought he was stealing his bike; that's why I went and grabbed it for him," Doyle recalled to WPVI.

Freeborn told the station that Doyle's actions meant a lot to him: "I want to thank him very, very much. I appreciate everything he done for me."

The elderly man then added a gut-wrenching admission WPVI: "I ain't used to people helping me like that, you know."

Ridley Township police released surveillance photos of the suspect and announced just before 4 p.m. Wednesday that he had been taken into custody.

Police on Friday didn’t immediately respond to Blaze News’ request for more information about the arrested suspect.

"If he did it to me, why wouldn't he do it to somebody else?" Freeborn asked the station.

Commenters under the police department's Facebook post about the incident didn't hold back:

Dave Urbanski

Sr. Editor, News

items.title: Democrats blamed Black and Latino voters for their loss in 2024, now they’re responsible for anchoring the nationwide “blue wave”
items.summary: In 2020, millions of working people mobilized to the ballot box and voted for Joe Biden, in hopes he would alleviate economic and political crises.

scraped.title: Democrats blamed Black and Latino voters for their loss in 2024...
scraped.description: Tuesday’s historic and sweeping electoral victories for Democrats across the country have put Trump and the Republican Party on the defensive going in
scraped.author: Deja Gaston
scraped.h1: Democrats blamed Black and Latino voters for their loss in 2024, now they’re responsible for anchoring the nationwide “blue wave”
scraped.body_text:
Tuesday’s historic and sweeping electoral victories for Democrats across the country have put Trump and the Republican Party on the defensive going into 2028. Democrats took back control of the House and Senate in a popular referendum on Trump’s billionaire-backed agenda responsible for eroding democratic rights and exacerbating the cost of living crisig. Not to mention helping U.S. oil industries make over $130 billion in profit from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and funneling billions into DHS to carry out mass deportations. Trump sits at the lowest approval rating before a midterm, with just 36% in support, while 62% of voters disapprove of his job as president.

Exceptionally notable was the mobilization of Black, Latino and Gen-Z voters who represented a large share of voters, contributing to Democratic wins in the House – key groups MAGA claimed they had made inroads into leading to their 2024 electoral win. Black and Latino voters represent between 9-10% of the total electorate yet 89% of Black Americans and 62% of Hispanic and Latino residents voted for a Democrat in this election. Seventy-two percent of people ages 18-29 voted Democrat while representing just 11% of the electorate. Sixty percent of people ages 30-44, 20% of the electorate also voted Democrat.

To contrast, polling data from the 2024 elections saw a decline in voter participation among these key demographic groups for the Democratic Party. Roughly 124 million people turned out for this year’s midterms, 12 million more than the 2022 midterms. Yet the voter turnout rate was still 63%, six points lower than in 2022. While the Democrats have taken back Congress, they remain deeply unpopular with a win that is a result of the anti-Republican, anti-billionaire sentiment.

Across the board, these swings back to blue should immediately disprove any racist or ideological caricatures made of voters across parties. These caricatures painted Black and Latino men as conservative Gen Z voters as susceptible to the “manosphere” and rural or non-college educated sections of the working class as prone to swallowing right-wing propaganda. These were all tropes the Democratic Party wasted no time in utilizing as the reasoning for their 2024 loss.

Following the loss of Kamala Harris in 2024, MSNBC host Joe Scarborough immediately sought to blame her loss on “racism” and “misogyny” among voters of color. Scarborough went as far to claim there “might be race issues with Hispanics that don’t want a black woman as president of the United States.” This posture from Democrat pundits was not only problematic, it purposefully inflamed tensions, which, while they do exist, are not a “fait accompli” negating the potential for multinational unity. Black and brown voters in that moment were patronized and scapegoated for the crises Democrats allowed.

While this narrative quickly spread in the days following the presidential race, it’s important to look back at the exit polls to uncover the reality:

Here is that same polling data broken down into gender by race:

While Latino men voted by 10 points more for Trump, the fuller picture of the results directly contrast the instigative statements. Between 2008 to 2020, Latino men and women supported the Democratic candidate in each presidential race. So what changed?

In 2020, millions of working people mobilized to the ballot box and voted for Joe Biden, in hopes he would alleviate the economic and political crises following the first Trump presidency. Biden ran on a platform that included aggressively tackling the COVID-19 pandemic where over a million Americans died, promised to rebuild the economy through the “Build Back Better” plan, campaigned to protect and expand the Affordable Care Act, provide a pathway to citizenship for 11 million immigrants and reform policing practices following the mass uprisings against racism and police brutality that same year.

Those same promises made on the campaign trail were quickly broken in the halls of Congress – even when Democrats had total control of both houses in 2021. COVID-era social programs such as the child tax credit, which helped to lower child poverty to 5.2%, the lowest on record, expired at the end of 2021. Child poverty more than doubled to 12.4% by 2022.

It’s in this context that the primary concerns for Latino men were the cost of living/inflation, steep housing and healthcare costs, and grim economic prospects for the job market in 2024. Democrats promised to address these working class burdens and failed. Trump came in on populist rhetoric to sway voters, while failing them too.

Latino men in that same polling overwhelmingly support progressive policies across issues. That includes reproductive health and the right to abortion access, increasing taxes on corporations, passing a new voting rights act and opposing mass deportations.

The new Democratic majority now has real power to roll out major legislation that doesn’t focus simply on reversing Trump’s rollbacks, but could push through important demands people voted for, including universal, single payer healthcare, the end to mass deportations and expansion of democratic rights.

Just a day after the midterm elections, Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries spoke on MS Now’s Morning Joe – the very same outlet chiding Black and Latino male voters – stating Democrats “would focus on getting things done rather than seeking revenge against President Donald Trump and his allies.” In other words, Democrats ran on affordability, not accountability. Harris just days before the midterms urged Democrats against pursuing a third impeachment on Trump. However, 90% percent of voters said government corruption was a key issue and a “crucial factor” in their votes.

The Democrats who are benefitting from mass discontent are already working to moderate their ceiling of what they’re “willing” to fight for, an unsurprising maneuver. It’s indicative of how despite the “blue wave,” the Democratic Party’s popularity only plummeted following the 2024 elections.

The potent rejection of Trump and the billionaire agenda comes on the heels of a wave of mass mobilization that has occurred since the beginning of Trump’s second term. The growth in opposition to ICE, the upward transfer of wealth from the “One Big Beautiful” Bill and the constant scapegoating of LGBTQ people and immigrants, all culminated in the historic general strikes of Jan. 23 and 30 .

That same momentum carried voters to the polls to make a resounding statement which was is more indicative of mass consciousness in opposition to the MAGA/billionaire agenda than a statement of support for the Democratic Party itself. After all, just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively following midterms.

The Democrats are already crediting their victories in several states, to the “ power of the moderate candidate .” The Democratic Party reflex has kicked in to undermine the real aspirations working people desire – economic stability, an end to the war machine and mass deportations, desires that surpass what the Democrats are willing to do when they have political power.

To defeat the right wing and ensure that popular demands expressed at the polls remain in the forefront, keeping up the pressure will be critical. The fight for working class political power must extend beyond the ballot box. There is a growing, positive view of socialism that is undeniable. The many progressive wins throughout the country reflect a desire for an alternative because the capitalist system can only reproduce more hardship and destruction.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

items.title: Debt, energy, war and the fight for socialism
items.summary: On present trajectories, the world is heading toward roughly $375 trillion in total debt by the end of 2026. For comparison, capitalism—taken globally and using generous arithmetic—generates perhaps $15–25 trillion in profit or surplus each year.

scraped.title: Debt, energy, war and the fight for socialism
scraped.description: On present trajectories, the world is heading toward roughly $375 trillion in total debt by the end of 2026. For comparison, capitalism—taken globally and using generous arithmetic—generates perhaps $15–25 trillion in profit or surplus each year.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
“They have no ideals to realize, but to set free the elements of the new society with which old collapsing bourgeois society itself is pregnant.”—Karl Marx, The Civil War in France

In the wake of the mass repudiation of Trump’s policies in the US midterm elections, a new stage of political and social conflict is set in the United States and around the world.

Working people seethe at rising costs, the lack of decent work and the rapid deterioration of healthcare, education and other social provisions essential to life. We watch with horror as wars in Gaza, Iran, Ukraine and Russia destroy human lives and whole societies, squandering trillions of dollars in the process. Presiding over it all is a class of billionaires dripping not just with avarice, but with outright contempt for human life.

But that which drives this crisis is not some fleeting mood of the capitalist class or temporary policy failure. As David North stated in a lecture delivered on the eve of the vote:

Whatever the outcome of tomorrow’s vote, policy will be determined in the final analysis by the crisis of the capitalist economy, by the disposition of a technology that is transforming the conditions of labor for the entire human race, by the drive of American imperialism to war and by the response of the international working class.

The direction of the world economy, and with it the politics of the ruling class, is increasingly defined by the intersection of three destructive processes.

First, the pile of debt undergirding global growth has reached astronomical proportions. On present trajectories, the world is heading toward roughly $375 trillion in total debt by the end of 2026. For comparison, capitalism—taken globally and using generous arithmetic—generates perhaps $15–25 trillion in profit or surplus each year.

Debt is a stock of financial claims backed by assets and future income, and much of it is continuously refinanced rather than paid off. But the comparison conveys the extraordinary scale of the claims that have accumulated against future production. Capitalism is mortgaging its future on an unprecedented scale.

And each year, more is added. Nearly $30 trillion in debt was added in 2025 alone. Debt is accumulating on a scale comparable to the annual expansion of the world economy itself. Interest payments on public debt alone have risen to $3.3 trillion. An ever greater stream of social wealth is sucked up and siphoned off to service the claims of banks and other creditors.

Alongside this is a second critical process: the rising cost of basic necessities and of the energy and raw materials on which economic life depends.

Diesel, a fuel essential to trucking, mining, agriculture, construction and manufacturing, has more than doubled in price for many users over the past year. European diesel futures traded between roughly $600 and $700 per tonne before the Iran war began in February. They now trade above $1,400 per tonne. These increases work their way through the economy, raising the cost of producing and transporting almost everything.

Natural gas prices, meanwhile, have tripled in Europe and Asia since the war began, with the United States relatively insulated. Similar pressures have appeared in jet fuel used by planes and the bunker fuel used by ships.

But the pressure extends beyond hydrocarbons.

Copper, a pivotal metal underpinning electronics, electrification, renewable energy and the infrastructure of AI, has also surged in price. Throughout much of the 2010s, it traded between roughly $2 and $4 per pound. It has recently traded above $6.50, reaching record levels.

Global food prices, meanwhile, remain dramatically above their levels of a decade ago. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s Food Price Index stood at 136 in September 2026, compared with an annual average of 91.9 in 2016—an increase of nearly 50 percent.

War, climate change, higher energy and transportation costs, and broader inflationary pressures are all to blame. For households already spending much of their income on food—grain, meat, cooking oils—it is a punishing drain.

But accompanying these two damaging processes—debt and inflation—is a third: war.

The war in Ukraine, the war in Iran, the genocide in Gaza, the fighting in Yemen, and beneath them all the mounting confrontation between China and US imperialism—these conflicts are increasingly intertwining and intensifying.

“Are we sleepwalking into World War III?” asked the Financial Times last month. In August, North described the growing conflicts as a “metastatic process” which “progressively transform[s] the world economy and every national state in preparation for the general conflagration toward which it tends.”

These three forces—debt, inflation and war—are increasingly connected expressions of the instability and crisis of the global capitalist economy. Each aggravates the others.

The wars in Ukraine and Iran and the fighting in Yemen have directly affected global energy, transportation and food prices. They have driven up the cost of fuel and agricultural production, spreading the pressure through industry and into household expenses.

By aggravating inflation, fiscal pressures and uncertainty, these wars have also contributed to rising borrowing costs, making it harder to keep the train of debt moving. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury has now reached a quarter-century high, moving past 5 percent and toward 6 percent. Higher interest payments demand still more money to service the debts already accumulated.

Meanwhile, financing the drive towards war requires enormous new expenditures, funded through a combination of borrowing and intensified extraction from the working population.

Global military spending increased by 41 percent in real terms between 2016 and 2025, while 2026 and 2027 are each expected to set new records. The Trump administration is demanding a $1.5 trillion military budget for 2027—an increase of roughly 50 percent.

Europe, meanwhile, is madly rearming for war with Russia. Germany alone plans roughly €1 trillion in military spending over the next five years, with annual expenditure rising to €168 billion by 2029, while the IMF calls for “deep cuts in the European model and the social contract” to accommodate the mounting fiscal burden.

But the connection runs in the other direction as well. Deteriorating economic conditions intensify the desperation among rival capitalist powers to control the energy, resources, markets and supply chains upon which their wealth and power depend. Each seeks to secure its own position at the expense of its competitors, even as the resulting conflicts damage the conditions of production on which they all depend.

The turn to war expresses the increasingly desperate struggle of these ruling classes to preserve their wealth and world position. They look to military power for a way out of the crisis. This is above all the course being pursued by the American and European ruling classes.

In Athens on October 7, Marco Rubio posed the question as “whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline,” calling for control over critical supply chains, economic and technological dominance and military rebuilding.

“We will make the Bundeswehr the strongest conventional army in Europe,” Chancellor Friedrich Merz declared in June 2025, justifying that goal with Germany’s size, economic strength and geographical position. At the Munich Security Conference in February, he explained, “competition policy is security policy and security policy is competition policy.” Germany’s economy is in a dire state, with high energy costs battering its industrial base and fierce competition from Chinese automakers threatening its once-dominant car industry.

And so the attempts to resolve one crisis ricochet to deepen the others.

Debt finances war; war raises the cost of necessities and of borrowing; and mounting economic pressure feeds an increasingly desperate struggle to secure control over the sources of global wealth.

The ruling class increasingly looks to artificial intelligence as a potential escape from this impasse. AI has generated enormous speculative valuations and investment, sustaining the appearance of renewed dynamism in an otherwise stagnating economy. But even as it revolutionizes production, it heightens the social contradictions of capitalism. The very advance hailed as a way out intensifies the crisis. Meanwhile, a new financial bubble has been inflated around it. It is only a matter of time before it bursts.

Who will pay for this astronomical debt? For this warmongering and rampant inflation?

The ruling class has its answer: social programs must be dismantled and hundreds of billions found for war, while private fortunes remain sacrosanct. Everything may be sacrificed to preserve and augment the wealth and power of those at the top.

Nothing remotely comparable is demanded of the immense private fortunes accumulated at the summit of society. Billionaire wealth has risen by more than 80 percent since 2020, reaching record levels even as austerity is imposed on the population. In California, a modest proposal for a one-time 5 percent tax on fortunes above $1 billion has already provoked more than $187 million in opposition spending, including over $102 million from Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone.

It is working people—the employed, unemployed and underemployed, across the world—upon whom the costs of these intersecting crises are being imposed.

They are squeezed harder every week, every month—at the grocery store, in their rent, at the gas pump and when the electricity bill comes due. Inflation means the erosion of life.

In Europe, Latin America, the United States and elsewhere, healthcare, pensions, unemployment benefits, support for families and virtually every other form of social expenditure become targets for cuts. Amid an already profound social crisis, everything afforded to the population is declared unaffordable. The debts accumulated by governments, banks and corporations, meanwhile, must be paid.

The mass youth protests in Europe and the midterm rebuke against Trump in the United States express deep popular opposition to this course. Working people are resisting the attempt to make them pay for the wars of the ruling class and the downward spiral of capitalism.

But these processes will not be halted by this or that ‘progressive’ candidate who remains fundamentally pledged to the continuation of the existing social order.

As the WSWS previously wrote :

In opposition to these forces, the working class must base its struggle on a strategy which is grounded on a complete break with finance capital. Anything less, no matter how “radical” it might sound, means subordination to its dictates.

The financial crisis cannot be resolved by adjustments, tinkering and bookkeeping measures. In the first place, the debt must be repudiated. It has been incurred to meet the interests of the capitalist oligarchy, not the working class.

The crisis of world capitalism offers its ruling classes no progressive way out. They turn instead toward war, even as its prosecution further destabilizes the capitalist economy upon which their own power rests.

In Ukraine and across the Middle East, warfare increasingly takes the form of economic attrition. Energy infrastructure, trade routes and productive capacity become military targets. The destruction of the infrastructure necessary to sustain civilian life becomes a means of exhausting an opponent’s capacity to continue the war.

Ukraine’s campaign against Russian refineries, for example, has driven Russian refinery throughput to its lowest level in more than two decades in 2026, with diesel production estimated by the IEA to have fallen nearly 30 percent. Dozens of warehouses and other commercial sites have also been struck. Russia, meanwhile, has increasingly targeted Ukraine’s power infrastructure. Russian attacks on Tuesday killed dozens and further damaged the grid as the region heads into winter.

This grinding stalemate, in which tens of thousands are sacrificed every month, increasingly turns on each side’s capacity to withstand prolonged economic and social destruction. American, Chinese and European war planners are studying its implications for future conflicts, including the possibility that a war over Taiwan could develop into a similar struggle of attrition.

The same logic is at work in Iran. The Trump administration and the Iranian government confront one another over who can withstand the sustained disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. For Washington and Israel, the failure to secure a decisive outcome creates pressure for further escalation. The United States is actively contemplating the use of its largest non-nuclear weapon on Iran.

In all cases it is working people who bear the cost of war.

Together, these convulsions express the historical exhaustion of capitalism. They emerge from contradictions accumulated over decades and intensified after the financial collapse of 2008. The vast expansion of debt and financial speculation that followed deferred the crisis while deepening the conditions that produced it: social inequality, economic instability and the struggle between the major powers over markets, resources and strategic advantage.

Capitalism as a system of organizing global social life has nothing left to offer the world. Nor can it secure its own future. Its attempts at self-preservation increasingly undermine the economic and social foundations of its continued existence. As Marx wrote, “The real barrier of capitalist production is capital itself.”

All roads here lead in one direction: the intensification of the class struggle.

Strikes and protests driven by soaring living costs, austerity and deteriorating working conditions are spreading across Asia, Latin America, North America and Europe; from truckers and healthcare workers to industrial workers and youth. The world is replete with signs of anger and refusal.

But the growth of opposition does not by itself provide a way out. So long as struggles remain divided along national lines and subordinated to the trade union bureaucracies, Social Democratic parties and their political satellites, they can be isolated and contained while the broader movement toward austerity and war continues.

The international character of the crisis demands an international response. Humanity’s accumulated scientific knowledge, technology and productive resources make possible a secure and dignified life for all, with shorter working hours and greater scope for human development. AI, automation and other developments can have a positive, revolutionary effect on humanity’s future.

But realizing these possibilities requires ending the subordination of production to private profit and the nationalist ambitions of the financial aristocracy. The productive resources of society must be placed under democratic social control and directed toward human need.

The struggle against war is inseparable from the struggle against the impoverishment of the working class. Both demand the independent political mobilization of workers, young people and the unemployed across all national borders. This movement must fight for an irrevocable break with finance capital and the expropriation of the financial aristocracy, whose wealth and power stand in the way of humanity’s further development. That is the revolutionary socialist program, and the only way through this historical impasse.

items.title: US midterm elections anticipate explosive growth of the class struggle
items.summary: The midterm elections expressed an immense growth of social anger over the cost of living, war, inequality and the assault on democratic rights that will not be contained within electoral forms and will erupt in the class struggle.

scraped.title: US midterm elections anticipate explosive growth of the class struggle
scraped.description: The midterm elections expressed an immense growth of social anger over the cost of living, war, inequality and the assault on democratic rights that will not be contained within electoral forms and will erupt in the class struggle.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Behind Tuesday’s midterm elections, which produced the largest defeat of a sitting president’s party in half a century, lies an immense growth of social anger over the cost of living, war, social inequality and the assault on democratic rights. That anger cannot and will not be contained within electoral forms. It will erupt in the form of the class struggle.

Three days after the vote, the process is already visible. At midnight Friday, the citywide contract between New York City and American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) District Council 37 expired. It covers about 90,000 municipal workers, including clerical staff, caseworkers, school aides, library workers and 911 operators. The deal it replaced, signed in 2023, provided raises of 3 percent a year and an $18 wage floor, $1 above the city minimum.

An $18 hourly wage comes to $37,440 a year for full-time work, before taxes. The median asking rent in New York City reached a record $4,199 a month in May, according to StreetEasy, or more than $50,000 a year. A city worker at the wage floor would have to hand over more than a full year’s gross pay to rent the typical apartment on the market.

These conditions are universal. In exit polls for the election, 90 percent of voters named the cost of living as a major concern, and those who described themselves as struggling financially swung by 60 points against Trump and the Republicans. Nearly 70 percent said the economic system favors the wealthy.

Friday’s jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed average hourly earnings up 3.1 percent over the year, while consumer prices rose 3.7 percent in the 12 months through September, driven by gasoline prices pushed up by the war. That is, real wages are falling. In the New York metropolitan area, prices rose 4.5 percent, and the official figures understate the inflation working people face on gas and food.

Mass layoffs are also on the horizon. Companies have cited artificial intelligence for 121,401 announced job cuts in 2026, about one in five of the total. A survey by the consulting firm Mercer earlier this year found that 99 percent of corporate executives expect AI to drive headcount reductions within two years.

On Wednesday morning, the day after Iowa elected a Democratic senator and governor, Deere announced the closure of its 115-year-old Ottumwa Works and its plant in Clarion. In Detroit, Dakkota Integrated Systems is shutting its instrument panel plant and eliminating 397 jobs.

The coming months will bring these conflicts to a head across every section of the working class. In New York, DC 37 joins the 40,000 subway and bus workers of Transport Workers Union Local 100, who have worked without a contract since May, while the Metropolitan Transportation Authority offers 2 percent raises and demands a doubling of health costs. In Boston, more than 4,000 nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have called an open-ended strike for November 12.

Graduate workers at Harvard have been on strike since October 27, and strike deadlines loom this month at MIT and the California State University. Tens of thousands of steelworkers at US Steel and Cleveland-Cliffs have worked without a contract since September 1. In New Hampshire, 250 grocery warehouse workers are on strike, and UPS is eliminating up to 30,000 jobs.

The Democrats have responded to the overwhelming opposition to Trump with calls for “bipartisanship” and “common ground.” This is motivated above all by the fear, shared by every section of the ruling class, of the growth of the class struggle. Tens of millions voted for higher wages, affordable healthcare, an end to war and an end to oligarchic rule. But the incoming Democratic House and Senate have been given their marching orders by Wall Street: Rescue the markets and fund war.

Whatever their posturing before the vote, the Democrats will be compelled to wage war on the working class. Who is to pay for a national debt approaching $40 trillion? How is the military budget to be raised to $1.5 trillion? The answer of both parties is the same, and a collision is inevitable.

This is already developing in the cities and states the Democrats run, including those governed by their Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) faction.

In California, Governor Gavin Newsom’s refusal to meet the demands of state workers provoked the first strike in the history of Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1000, by 100,000 workers, on October 21. In Chicago, overseen by Democrat Brandon Johnson, an ex-Chicago Teachers Union staffer backed by the DSA, the city and its school district face deficits of more than $1.5 billion. Plans for enormous cuts and “restructuring” are being announced as municipal elections get underway.

In Seattle, Mayor Katie Wilson, a self-described democratic socialist though not a member of the DSA, has proposed nearly $50 million a year in cuts while increasing police funding by $68 million. Firefighters packed the City Council’s budget hearing early last month to protest cuts that the fire chief said would take units out of service.

New York City itself is run by DSA member Zohran Mamdani, who has led the Democrats in forging a political alliance with Trump. Facing a projected budget gap of $7 billion to $9 billion next year, he has ordered two rounds of agency spending cuts and sued to block $10,000 bonuses for paraprofessionals under the Taylor Law, the state statute that bars public employees from striking.

In the developing collision, the trade union apparatus plays a decisive role in attempting to suppress the class struggle. Mamdani has also brought the union apparatus into his administration. Julie Su, who as Biden’s acting labor secretary helped block national rail and port strikes, is his “Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice,” and Jahmila Edwards, a top DC 37 official, runs his intergovernmental affairs office. If the Taylor Law is invoked against city workers, a member of the DSA will enforce it.

The United Auto Workers bureaucracy under Shawn Fain poured its resources into electing Democrats, in what Fain called its “biggest political program” in decades, while suppressing every struggle in the plants. At Bradford White, it isolated a 47-day strike and brought back the company’s terms four times until they were ratified. It has done nothing to fight the closures at Dakkota and Deere.

Teamsters President Sean O’Brien campaigned for Republicans, including Florida Senator Ashley Moody. The United Steelworkers just announced a tentative agreement with Cleveland Cliffs, which includes raises barely above the rate of inflation after keeping thousands of steelworkers on the job under rolling 48-hour extensions. Whether it backs the Democrats or the Republicans, the apparatus ties workers to the corporations and the state and blocks any independent movement of the working class.

Workers need organizations of their own: rank-and-file committees in every workplace, democratically controlled by workers and independent of the bureaucracy and both parties. The International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees (IWA-RFC) spearheads the fight to build such committees and to link them across workplaces, industries and borders.

The same process is unfolding internationally. In France, public sector workers struck nationally on Thursday. Spain faces a general strike on November 11, Ireland a public sector strike on November 12 and Italy a general strike on November 20, while the unions everywhere confine the struggle to one-day actions. Workers in every country confront the same crisis and the same demand that they pay for war through austerity.

The IWA-RFC advances demands based not on what the corporations and the city budgets claim is affordable but on what workers need: raises that make up for inflation and rise automatically with prices, guaranteed healthcare, no layoffs or closures and control over new technology by those whose labor it is being used to replace. In New York, that means committees in every city agency, prepared to defy the Taylor Law.

All of these struggles raise fundamental political questions. Equality and an end to the domination of society by the oligarchy cannot be won under capitalism. The DSA speaks for privileged sections of the upper middle class, which seek not to end the wealth of the oligarchy but a more favorable distribution of it within the top 10 percent of the population. Genuine socialism means the transfer of power to the working class, the expropriation of the ill-gotten wealth of the oligarchy, and the placing of the banks and giant corporations under the democratic control of the working class.

The decisive question is leadership. The radicalization expressed in the vote will not develop spontaneously into a conscious movement for socialism. That requires bringing this perspective into every struggle: exposing the role of the Democrats, the DSA and the trade union apparatus, building rank-and-file committees, and winning the most advanced workers and young people to socialism. That is the task of the Socialist Equality Party.

That anger cannot and will not be contained within electoral forms. It will erupt in the form of the class struggle.

items.title: Australia: Police with military weapons start patrolling NSW streets
items.summary: This historic turn is designed to create a threatening political climate, normalising the presence of heavily-armed police squads on the streets, with their weapons on visible display.

scraped.title: Australia: Police with military weapons start patrolling NSW streets
scraped.description: This historic turn is designed to create a threatening political climate, normalising the presence of heavily-armed police squads on the streets, with their weapons on visible display.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Under conditions of rising social discontent in Australia and globally, the state Labor government in New South Wales (NSW) is spearheading an unprecedented turn in policing operations, featuring officers carrying visible military-grade long-arms on daily patrols for the first time in Australian history.

This month, Premier Chris Minns’s government began taking the militarisation of policing to a new level, deploying its newly-established Armed Response Command (ARC) to patrol prominent public places in Sydney, including potential protest locations near the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House.

Officers are also cruising in purpose-built vehicles—BMW X5s and Toyota LandCruisers—fitted with technology to receive intelligence information from the command’s operations centre. Established at an initial cost of $94.3 million, the command is expected to comprise 250 officers by the end of 2027, with 28 civilian staff members.

This historic turn is clearly designed to create a threatening political climate, normalising the presence of heavily-armed police squads on the streets, with their weapons on visible display.

ARC officers are armed with shortened versions of the semi-automatic Australian Combat Assault Rifle, developed primarily for use in wartime battle. Measuring over 70cm long and with a range of more than 500 metres, they can fire 50 rounds per minute, raising the spectre of lethal shootings.

This is part of a wider response, brought forward amid explosive mass struggles by students and workers across Europe against war, re-militarisation, the soaring cost of living and the deteriorating conditions in schools and social services.

Minns has personally boasted of, and identified himself with, the new force. “The security challenges facing our state have changed, and our policing model needs to change with them,” Minns said when unveiling the ARC in early October, claiming it was targeting violent threats.

Last Sunday, NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley made a more revealing statement. She refused to rule out the ARC being deployed at protests. “If they’re required to be there because of the heightened risk, they will be,” she said. Catley claimed that police would make those decisions, but her green light for the use of the ARC at demonstrations itself indicates government pre-approval.

Catley added that the Minns government would “absolutely not” introduce regulation to define when and where ARC officers could be deployed. The government has rejected calls by Amnesty International to publish accessible rules governing when and where the ARC combat assault rifles can be fired.

Alongside the federal Albanese Labor government, the Minns government has a repressive record. It has been in the forefront of ramming through far-reaching anti-democratic measures, such as banning so-called “hate speech,” outlawing protests in declared zones and boosting police powers to issue “move on” orders and carry out searches and arrests.

Like Labor’s other police-state measures, the government and the corporate media have presented the ARC as simply a reaction to last December’s terrorist attack at Sydney’s Bondi Beach, where two alleged Islamic State gunmen killed 15 people at a Jewish community festival. But this cannot explain the large-scale mobilisation of heavily-armed police on the streets.

Moreover, many unanswered questions remain about how the two accused Bondi Beach perpetrators, a father and son, were able to carry out a reactionary atrocity despite being well known to the police and intelligence agencies.

The government’s intent is to intimidate—and potentially use lethal force against—demonstrations or other eruptions of opposition, not individual gunmen. That includes not only the continuing demonstrations against the US-backed Israeli genocide in Gaza and the occupied West Bank of Palestine, but any unrest, as in Europe, or rallies by striking workers.

NSW police commissioner Mal Lanyon last month declared that the ARC would have a dual purpose, that of deterring people who “incite hatred or cause fear,” as well as those “who wish to commit harm.”

This is line with the efforts of the political and media establishment to conflate opposition to the genocide in Palestine to antisemitism and to accuse Gaza demonstrations of causing fear in the Jewish population, even though the protests have been joined by many Jewish people who denounce the Israeli regime.

Over the past three years, the anti-genocide protests in Australia have been among the largest per capita in the world. In August 2025, 300,000 people took part in a march across the Sydney Harbour Bridge despite intensive attempts by Minns and the police to ban it.

After four decades of increasingly militarised policing in all Australian states and territories, primarily involving para-military riot and “tactical response” squads, the ARC represents a sharp further shift in police operations, designed to establish an intimidating presence on the streets.

Rather than acting as a “flying squad” or an on-call SWAT team, the ARC represents Labor’s adoption of US and European-style policing operations where military-grade firepower is a permanent open fixture in civilian areas, often backed by heavily-armed troops.

Already, over the past decade, existing units, such as Victoria’s Critical Incident Response Team (CIRT) and Public Order Response Team (PORT), have had access to military-grade, semi-automatic rifles. They are often deployed to visible positions outside designated major public events, but with their military-style weaponry mostly kept inside their vehicles.

In 2017, the previous Liberal-National government in NSW armed the Public Order and Riot Squad (PORS) with Colt M4 carbines. That was the first time in NSW history that such a squad was equipped with military-grade rifles.

Labor’s establishment of the ARC represents a doubling down by the Minns government on its already violent response to demonstrations.

In June last year, a large contingent of police, including the riot squad, set upon pro-Palestinian protesters in Sydney outside a factory listed as participant in Lockheed Martin’s construction of F-35 fighter jets, which the Israeli military has used to drop bombs on Gaza. Several participants were bashed, with one—former Greens election candidate Hannah Thomas—facing the possible loss of her sight in one eye as a result.

On February 9 this year, the Minns government authorised a violent police operation in Sydney against a peaceful protest opposing a visit to Australia by Israeli president and war criminal Isaac Herzog. A deployment involving hundreds of police culminated in cops indiscriminately pepper-spraying, bashing and charging at the demonstrators.

Widely-viewed footage on social media showed multiple assaults perpetrated by the police. Pre-dawn police raids were then conducted on the homes of alleged protest participants, charging them with offences such as refusing to obey police orders to disperse, affray, and assaulting or hindering police.

Labor Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had invited Herzog despite a United Nations inquiry finding that the Israeli president incited genocide in Gaza. That was a measure of the Labor government’s commitment to the US-Israeli war offensives and US militarism globally.

The introduction of the para-military ARC, alongside the far-reaching laws and measures imposed under the banner of combatting antisemitism, is another warning of the repression to which the Labor governments, as well as their Liberal-National counterparts, will resort, not only to threaten anti-genocide protests but to suppress opposition to war and militarism more broadly.

Over the past two decades, Labor also has backed legislation to enable the military to be called out to combat domestic unrest or alleged threats to designated infrastructure, giving soldiers unprecedented peacetime powers , including to use lethal force, detain civilians, issue directives and search people and premises. That is in line with the deployment of troops against demonstrators internationally, most recently in France and the US.

The strengthening of the police and intelligence apparatuses, alongside the military, will be directed against the working-class discontent and political disaffection that is brewing as the burdens of war are imposed on working people, via the soaring cost of living and cuts to essential disability, health, education and other social programs, while billions of dollars are poured into the military in preparation for war.

scraped.title: Announcing the English-Language Edition of "Socialist Strategy and Military Art" - Left Voice
scraped.description: Out now in English from 34 Press and Left Voice --- "Socialist Strategy and Military Art" by Emilio Albamonte and Matías Maiello draws on Clausewitz, Lenin, Trotsky, and Gramsci, rethinking revolutionary strategy and working-class hegemony for the 21st century.
scraped.author: Adrien Masson
scraped.body_text:
Out now in English from 34 Press and Left Voice — “Socialist Strategy and Military Art” by Emilio Albamonte and Matías Maiello draws on Clausewitz, Lenin, Trotsky, and Gramsci, rethinking revolutionary strategy and working-class hegemony for the 21st century.

Adrien Masson

First published in 2017, Socialist Strategy and Military Art by Argentinian Marxists Emilio Albamonte and Matías Maiello returns to the vital question of revolutionary strategy, an issue which seemed to lay dormant for decades. Following the work of important figures in the Marxist tradition, Albamonte and Maiello draw lessons from military theory and strategy — or the “art of winning” in Trotsky’s terms — to achieve working-class hegemony. Today we launch the English-language edition of the book, with an original prologue by the authors.

The fight for a socialist future is no longer a debate confined to the margins. It is expressed by a massive youth movement across Europe and general strikes in Italy, France, and Spain that put forward demands against militarism and the rising cost of living. In the United States, a new class consciousness is expressed by the rise of the DSA and the strike against ICE in Minneapolis.

These are trends that have been accelerating quickly since the 2008 financial crisis, which created a global economic downturn and marked the end of the “End of History.” No longer could the myth be sustained that the capitalist system would develop and expand without limit. What we saw instead was a world that has become racked by repeated crises, wars, climate change, campaigns against immigration, rising inequality, and an ascendant Far Right. But this new period has also brought with it renewed waves of class struggle, from Occupy Wall Street, to the Arab Spring, to the Yellow Vest movement in France, to Black Lives Matter, to the worldwide movement for Palestine. It is in this 21st-century context that new debates are emerging around the strategy these movements need to seriously confront not only capitalism’s morbid symptoms but the system itself.

Socialist Strategy and Military Art draws on the strategic thought of revolutionaries in the Marxist tradition across the 20th century, including Vladimir Lenin, Leon Trotsky, Antonio Gramsci, and Rosa Luxemburg, while seeking to apply their analysis in a non-dogmatic way to the conditions facing the workers’ movement today. The book also undertakes a critical examination of others claiming the banner of Marxism who are once again becoming a reference point for many on the Left, such as Karl Kautsy, Che Guevara, or Mao Tse-Tung.

Unlike many other books that have taken up the question of strategy in recent years, Albamonte and Maiello connect socialist strategy and military theory, engaging critically with the work of Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz. Though his relevance is often overlooked today, Clausewitz’s military writings were deeply influential for Marx and Engels and later studied by Lenin and Trotsky — not just in relation to the relationship between war and politics, but as a framework for thinking how the working class can conquer power. The authors investigate ideas like workers’ hegemony, the united front, soviets, and dual power as key elements of revolutionary politics.

As Albamonte and Maiello write in the prologue to the Spanish edition:

The world crisis will continue to increase and sharpen class struggle; the question is whether these opportunities are exploited to open the way to revolution and socialism in the 21st century or whether they will give rise to the triumph of the right and, eventually, fascism. This depends on the work of strategy. As Trotsky noted : “Had the Bolshevik party failed to carry out this work, there couldn’t even be talk of the victory of the proletarian revolution. The Soviets would have been crushed by the counter-revolution and the little sages of all countries would have written articles and books on the keynote that only uprooted visionaries could dream in Russia of the dictatorship of the proletariat, so small numerically and so immature.” This may be one of the main conclusions, 100 years after the Russian Revolution, for the new century that has begun. It is the starting point of the work that you find in your hands.

Although the book examines key lessons and political thought from the 20th century, these ideas are closely related to struggles taking place in our own time. The authors spend a significant portion of the book articulating a vision of working class self-organization, and the fundamental obstacle posed by the bureaucracies that control working-class organizations. They aim for the construction of a genuinely international revolutionary party, capable of preserving these lessons and guiding the working class towards its world-historic mission.

First published by Ediciones IPS and the Party of Socialist Workers ( Partido de los Trabajadores Socialistas ) in Argentina, 34 Press and Left Voice are publishing the English-language edition of this important work. You can order your copy now and we encourage you to share it widely. We offer our pages to debate its contents.

Left Debates

Leon Trotsky

Marxism

Party of Socialist Workers (PTS), Argentina

Strategy

Vladimir Lenin

In this episode, Tatiana Cozzarelli speaks to Andrew Feffer, author of Bad Faith: Teachers, Liberalism, and the Origins of McCarthyism. They discuss the Rapp-Coudert investigation and the anti-communist witch-hunt of the early 1940s — and the parallels to today's repression against the movement for Palestine.

Left Voice

A generation caught in global chaos is rising up in the face of a capitalist system that grows more corrupt by the day.

Julien Anchaing and Enzo Tresso

The war against Iran, differences over Israel, the culture war, and the battle to succeed Trump expose the tensions within a heterogeneous coalition. Behind the slogan America First, different factions compete to define the movement's direction and the strategy for maintaining U.S. hegemony.

Farid Reyes and Ezequiel Silva

In Los Angeles, a DSA-backed challenger leads the mayor favored by business. Statewide, billionaires are spending millions against a wealth tax. But Raman’s silence on Prop 40 and the DSA’s BDS controversy raise bigger questions about the left’s strategy inside the Democratic Party.

Tubman Amaru

November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike.

Damien Bernard

The Berlin Left Party's state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue.

Ari Aalto

October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis.

Juan Chingo

scraped.author: Damien Bernard
scraped.body_text:
November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike.

Damien Bernard

Public discontent was palpable, as the massive protests on October 17, 24, and 31 had already shown. But November 5 marked a leap forward, with nearly 1.6 million protesters, including 350,000 in Paris, according to the CGT labor federation. The mobilization was particularly strong in the major cities: 150,000 protesters in Marseille, 120,000 in Bordeaux, 100,000 in Lille, 80,000 in Toulouse, 55,000 in Lyon, 35,000 in Nantes and Rennes, 30,000 in Rouen, 28,600 in Grenoble, 26,000 in Caen and Strasbourg, 25,000 in Brest, 22,000 in Tours, and 20,000 in Orléans, according to the CGT.

The scale recalls certain days of the 2023 battle over pensions and reflects an outrage that extends far beyond young people and certain sectors of the workforce, sweeping across the entire country.

This widespread participation has led to major strikes across various sectors. At the SNCF (the French national railway company), strike participation was particularly high, ranging from 50 percent to 80 percent depending on the sector, according to management’s own figures.

In the national education system, according to the SNES-FSU union, 52 percent of secondary school staff joined the strike — marking the first majority strike since December 5, 2024 — compared to 38 percent on September 29. Having backed high school students since early October, education staff are thus taking their solidarity with young people a step further.

In the private sector, reports indicate that approximately 50 percent of refinery workers went on strike in Donges, La Mède, and Flandre. The striking workers’ main demands of the striking workers are support for young people and higher wages. Wages are also central for employees at Disneyland Paris, who took action on Thursday to demand raises that keep pace with inflation and lower gas prices.

This day marked a new phase in the convergence of the labor movement and the youth uprising. The latter remained a driving force behind the mobilization, with 1,000 high schools blocked or closed, according to student organizations. At universities, more than 50 campuses were already blockaded as of November 3, roughly half of all campuses, according to the same organizations. And on Thursday, numerous universities saw protests, blockades, and even occupations, such as Jussieu in Paris and Le Mirail in Toulouse.

This convergence was particularly evident in the rallies held across the country and called by interprofessional general assemblies. In Saint-Denis, at Paul-Éluard high school — where 80 percent of the staff were on strike to protest the administrative investigation launched after they opposed the intervention of the BAC (Anti-Crime Brigade) — strikers from the RATP bus depot at Barrage and students from Paris 8 University joined the rally organized by the city’s interprofessional union, before marching toward the Gare du Nord and then on to République.

About a hundred people gathered at 9 a.m. in front of the Châtillon maintenance depot to hear speeches and take part in a joint march organized by the Paris South Interprofessional General Assembly. In eastern Paris, hospital staff and social workers joined high school students and marched, despite police action that led to the arrest of an RP activist. These groups ended up at the head of the Paris demonstration, alongside anti-racist activists, drawing thousands of people around slogans calling for a “general strike” or opposing the Far Right, despite police repression.

The fight against repression has also been a major driver of this solidarity. In Montpellier, SNCF workers, hospital staff, teachers, and university students joined the picket line at Clémenceau high school at the call of the young people. Where police had deployed in large numbers every morning to break up the blockade, they withdrew when the workers and students arrived. In Le Havre, the arrest of four high school students on Tuesday strengthened ties with workers, and several demonstrations — some drawing as many as 1,000 people — were held to demand their release, joined by workers from CIM, Total, Sidel, Stillwater, and Safran. The issue is all the more pressing given that police violently suppressed the protests on Thursday, even charging the inter-union contingent in Toulouse and causing numerous injuries.

More broadly, however, this convergence rests on shared demands. At the Paris demonstration, teachers from Charlemagne high school accompanied their students in a show of support, saying that the students’ demands were also their own: “They want to improve our working conditions.” Wages, the high cost of living, public services, and the future of young people were common causes. In Sens, Lou, a high school student at the protests, summed up this link between generations: “I’m also fighting for my parents, for gas prices, for the cost of living — period.” All these factors could help build a genuine general strike, building on the momentum generated by young people, provided that the right plan of action is developed.

While the mobilization has taken on a new scale and shows a genuine desire to escalate the strike and build momentum, the government is seeking to regain control. On Thursday, Prime Minister Lecornu announced a “social conference” for Monday, responding in particular to a request from the CFDT, the largest labor federation. This initiative aims to steer the mobilization back into the realm of social dialogue, offering some concessions and relying on the union leadership’s willingness to negotiate.

This approach, which relies on the pressure of protests to secure some concessions, is a dead end for winning our demands, as the government’s proposals show, with an initial minimum wage increase of just a few euros. Meanwhile, CFDT General Secretary Marylise Léon is demanding a net increase of €100 in the minimum wage — which does nothing to address the “high cost of living” — and her CGT counterpart, Sophie Binet, is putting the onus on the government instead of calling for an escalation of the strike. What is needed is a battle plan equal to the moment, one that moves toward a general strike by bringing in sectors that have not yet joined the struggle and putting forward demands that inspire people to fight.

Grassroots organizing will be key to advancing this strategy, as Anasse Kazib explained ahead of the protest day. In recent weeks in Toulouse, more than 800 people gathered to prepare for the rolling strike and organize actions at Airbus, among sanitation workers, and at Tisséo (the public transit company); and on Thursday, the interprofessional bloc turned out in force at the demonstration.

In Bordeaux, students called for interprofessional general assemblies to join forces with the labor movement. All these initiatives serve as levers to fight for change and oppose the government’s attempts at negotiation; they should become concrete tools in the struggle, coordinate real sectors of society, help convey the radicalism of the youth to the workers, and combat repression. As a symbol of this potential, in Paris, the rally in front of the SNCF maintenance depot in Châtillon turned into a spontaneous march toward Montparnasse to confront Sophie Binet and fight for a general strike.

The strike rates reported in various sectors and the ties being forged with young people show that there is a foundation for moving this movement forward. Our strength lies in the streets, in workplaces, and in schools: we must use this mobilization to widen the movement. Now more than ever, we must set up interprofessional assemblies everywhere to organize joint actions, send delegations to workplaces, and bring new sectors into the strike.

The government is growing nervous; we must seize this opportunity to take the next step and organize a general strike capable of paralyzing the economy and imposing concrete demands, such as a net minimum wage of €2,000, a €400 raise for everyone, a ban on layoffs, major investment in public services, the repeal of Parcoursup (the French university admissions platform), the release of all detainees, and the government’s resignation.
