scraped.title: Germany’s Gen Z Joins the Revolt While Die Linke Forms Coalition with the Center - Left Voice
scraped.description: The Berlin Left Party's state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue.
scraped.author: Ari Aalto
scraped.body_text:
The Berlin Left Party’s state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue.

Ari Aalto

The Berlin Die Linke (Left Party) state convention this Saturday will most likely give a green light for coalition talks with the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. Since these two parties have already approved in principle, coalition talks will probably begin next week. The acceptance of the coalition agreement, which the negotiating teams are expected to submit around the beginning of December, will then be put to a vote by party members.

On the same day, the still somewhat vague youth phenomenon of GenZ regelt (“GenZ’s got this”) will also be mobilizing. Spurred by a massive movement in France, demands for youth protests in numerous German cities are circulating on social media. Because here too, many young people feel that they are growing up in a world that offers them nothing but wars and crises, while schools are crumbling and teachers are overworked. Even if the full impact is still difficult to predict, the strong response proves that there is also a generation in Germany that feels the need to take their future into their own hands and is prepared to take to the streets. This will continue to be necessary. Because the exploratory talks between the red-red-green coalition in Berlin promise only more of the same – social cuts, militarization, and police repression – rather than any real change.

Not all members of the Left Party are happy about the prospect of a red-red-green coalition governing Berlin. Even before the election, but especially since the preliminary and exploratory talks were announced, the Left Party Youth organization [‘solid], state and federal Palestine solidarity movements within the party, portions of the party’s grassroots organizations, and the network “Left within the Left” (LidL) have criticized the coalition’s participation in the government. And rightly so. The joint exploratory statement from the three parties suggests that the future coalition won’t even meet the Left Party’s one central campaign promise : a public referendum on expropriating housing from massive real estate concerns like Deutsche Wohnen & Co., Vonovia, Adler and Heimstaden. Draft legislation will not be presented to the House of Representatives until mid-2028, and it would only apply to housing with at least 10,000 units and would not even be implemented in the next legislative session. This leaves more than enough time for companies to restructure or for the SPD, together with the CDU at the federal level, to simply prohibit the socialization of housing . And as it is, all of the coalition’s projects are subject to strict funding approval.

Disappointing for many was the party leadership’s complete capitulation to a media smear campaign, primarily directed against pro-Palestinian factions within the party. Not only did they swallow the lie that the Left Party has a massive antisemitism problem, they also insisted upon a mechanism in the exploratory agreement that allows the SPD and the Greens to interfere in the Left Party’s internal democracy and demand expulsions if they so choose. And already, Vedi Emde, the Neukölln representative who won her direct mandate with 46 percent of the vote, is being threatened with expulsion from her parliamentary faction because of her stance on Palestine . However, the overwhelmingly strong election results of candidates who campaign on a pro-Palestinian platform demonstrate that, after three years of the Gaza genocide, a large portion of Berliners no longer accept the conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with antisemitism.

All of this shows that those in the Left Party who want to govern within a bourgeois state need to rely on media smear campaigns, other bourgeois parties, and the state apparatus itself (for example, the threat of contacting the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution) to discipline or eliminate opponents within their own party. However Elif Eralp’s recent scandal with Der Spiegel may have come about, the result was that, while she was forced to publicly humiliate herself this allowed her to clearly align herself with the press attacks against a Palestinian activist like Ibrahim Ibrahim—the only person in this entire affair who was actually attacked and threatened. These attacks, which the leadership of the Left Party joins in, are currently directed against anti-imperialist movements, but will soon target even those who oppose rearmament of the German state.

A demonstration against entering coalition negotiations on this basis will take place on Saturday at 11 a.m. in the Dong Xuan Center in East Berlin, prior to the party congress. The demonstration is being organized by, among others, the Internationalist Alliance, in which we as Klasse gegen Klasse (Class Against Class) are also involved, together with left-wing factions within the Left Party. Union members from the Berlin hospital movement are also planning a protest before the party congress, as the exploratory agreement makes no mention of the reintegration of the outsourced subsidiaries of the Berlin hospitals Charité and Vivantes.

The call to action from the Internationalist Alliance for the rally states , among other things:

The German state is militarily, politically, and ideologically complicit in the crimes of the Israeli state. […] Party chair Ines Schwerdtner promised at the ‘Together for Gaza’ demonstration on September 27, 2025, to stand with the Palestinians and to take action against both the genocide and the repression of the Palestinian movement. […] But for the leadership of the Left Party, opportunism and the pursuit of managing capitalism, together with the racist, genocidal parties SPD and Greens, means throwing Palestinian solidarity under the bus. […] This is particularly evident in their dealings with the Left Party in Neukölln, as well as the Federal Working Group (BAG) and State Working Group (LAG) for Palestinian Solidarity. […] They show once again that German militarization and imperialist ambitions in Southwest Asia, along with the maintenance of Israel’s settler colonialism, are a more important concern than the struggle for the political and economic rights of workers. […] To put this into practice, the Left Party now wants to strengthen the Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the police in coalition with the SPD and the Greens, in order to restrict our rights to demonstrate and freedom of expression using state power. Thus the party leadership betrays both voters and its own grassroots members in order to attack solidarity with Palestine supporters together with genocide supporters.

We call on everyone who recognizes the exploratory paper as an attack to join us at the rally: the Palestine solidarity movement; supporters of expropriating Deutsche Wohnen & Co.; students campaigning against arms research and their universities’ own complicity in genocide and apartheid; victims of racist and sexist police violence; and neighbors from Neukölln and Wedding. Let’s make the rally a place for networking and exchanging ideas on how we can fight for real change from the bottom up. Not by lazy compromise with capitalist government, but through mass mobilization, strikes, and blockades like those in France and Spain.

Whether the Left Party forms a coalition with the SPD and the Greens is a fundamental decision about its direction. Governing at any cost or building a militant opposition on the streets? This is a decisive question that separates party members by those who want to support the capitalist regime and those who want to fight it — even if they aren’t yet convinced that a revolutionary party, clearly distinct from reformism, is necessary. That is why we at Klasse gegen Klasse and Waffen der Kritik (Weapons of Critique) have tried, in recent weeks and in various ways, to gather forces for a clear rejection of the Left Party’s participation in government and for building a grassroots movement that can defend Palestine solidarity and actually enforce the expropriation of Deutsche Wohnen and similar companies.

As part of the Neukölln local group, we campaigned at the State General Assembly (LVV) of the Left Youth [‘solid’] at the beginning of October for a clear rejection of participation in government and for the active organization of resistance. [‘solid’] Berlin passed two important resolutions at this assembly: It reaffirmed the Berlin Left Youth’s position against participation in government with Greens and the SPD and emphasized “that renewed participation in government will have no positive effect on building a socialist party of resistance (which is what we need), but rather a negative one.” At the same time, the assembly expressed solidarity with all those affected by the smear campaign launched by the mainstream media together with the SPD and the Greens since the Left Party’s election victory in Berlin.

We promoted this same perspective at a large event organized by the “Left within the Left” network on October 13th, which drew nearly 200 participants , as well as at the plenary session of the “Left within the Left” network (LidL) on October 23rd, in grassroots organizations of the Left Party, and in the State Working Group (LAG) and the Federal Working Group (BAG) for Palestine Solidarity. Partly at our initiative, the BAG resolved at its meeting on October 25th to

call upon the members and delegates of the Berlin State Party Congress to mobilize and vote against the party’s participation in the government. It calls upon all left-wing members of the federal party, all left-wing currents within the party, and all socialist groups outside the party to fight for a joint socialist anti-government campaign.” This is because “the alliance with the SPD and the Greens requires abandoning a program that directly attacks the interests of capital.

Within the “Left within the Left” network, as well as in the LAG Palestine Solidarity, we have also proposed submitting a corresponding motion to the party congress against entering into coalition negotiations with the SPD and the Greens, and instead

advocating for the building of a militant opposition on the streets, in factories, schools, and universities. Only with mass mobilizations, strikes, and blockades like those in France or Spain will it be possible to actually attack the interests of capital instead of making weak compromises, to fully implement the expropriation of large real estate companies, to defend Palestine solidarity, and to repel the governments’ rearmament and austerity plans and the rise of the extreme right.

Unfortunately, many members of LidL and the LAG were concerned that such a clear rejection of participation in government would fail to garner a majority. Instead, the LAG adopted a motion demanding simply better results than those achieved in the exploratory talks as a basis for entering coalition negotiations. This logic inevitably leads to powerlessness, as it avoids clearly stating the cause of the party leadership’s concessions and betrayals—co-management of capitalism and participation in government—out of fear of being temporarily in the minority (which certainly reflects the balance of power within the Left Party, a predominantly reformist party where some sectors are becoming more radical in light of current events, but where considerable confusion still prevails, particularly regarding the question of class independence from capitalist parties).

But only by clearly stating it and disseminating it with the greatest effort will other sectors of the party be able to join this critique. By systematically refusing to speak out loud and clearly, these opposition forces risk becoming mere pawns of the left, serving only to promise that a different, somewhat less subservient, form of government participation might still be possible. We consider this a grave mistake, but we remain committed to the urgent need to unite all sectors within and outside the Left Party that oppose adapting to the SPD and the Greens and the perspective of simply managing the imperialist state. We invite all members of the Left Youth [‘solid], the SDS (the party’s Socialist-Democratic Student Association), and the Left Party itself who share this perspective to fight alongside us and join the “Left within the Left” network (click here for the Telegram channel).

We critically support a motion raised by the Left Youth [‘solid] Berlin for the state party conference, which rejects a coalition with the SPD and the Greens. However, we are critical of the motion’s proposal to elect a minority government comprised of the SPD and the Greens. This would ultimately amount to a “light” version of government participation, as it sacrifices the perspective of class independence just as much and generates the same pressures for integration and loyalty to the state. The only difference is that the left-wing representatives who would vote for a Green and SPD budget might feel they are getting off more lightly, since they are only complicit in the policies of the Greens and the SPD instead of supporting them themselves.

Also worth supporting are the motions by [‘solid] for the reintegration of outsourced subsidiaries, as in the case of the Vivantes hospitals, whose workers have struck for more than 60 days this year for this very purpose and were likewise sacrificed to the alliance with the austerity parties SPD and the Greens — against the sanctioning mechanism and expulsions from the parliamentary group, as well as for a six-week deadline between the conclusion of coalition negotiations and the members’ vote.

Even if the rejection of coalition negotiations by the party congress on Saturday seems unlikely, the fight for an opposition perspective is not over. We must use the time until the membership vote to raise awareness of this perspective. Anger over the media smear campaign and the spineless way the party leadership handled it is shared by many people both inside and outside the Left Party, who voted for the Left as a voice for the expropriation of large real estate companies and for a free Palestine. Many people are also justifiably disillusioned by the results of the exploratory talks, even if some still harbor some hope that at least expropriation might be achievable with a red-red-green coalition. Now it all comes down to engaging in dialogue with all these people and transforming their disappointment and anger into action.

We have to engage with them on why the disastrous outcome of the exploratory talks wasn’t simply an operational mishap that could have been prevented with a better negotiating team. The crisis of the German economic model means that even modest reformist policies have extremely limited room for maneuver. The only force that can compel the bourgeoisie and its state to make genuine concessions is the independent power of youth and workers. With the school strike against military conscription, a certain youth vanguard has emerged in Germany that recognizes that it must mobilize itself for its own defense. But the spark from the European mobilizations is also beginning to ignite even the heavy battalions of the German labor movement, as exemplified by the IG Metall shop stewards at Mercedes-Benz Untertürkheim . We have to strengthen these movements and unite them under a revolutionary program. That alone should be the linchpin of a truly socialist party – not pandering to the Greens and the SPD, not betraying every principle and its own party members just for a few government seats — where at the end of the day they will be forced to help manage the capitalist misery of social cuts and police violence.

There is still enough time before the membership vote to initiate discussions on this issue within all grassroots structures of the Left Party. To this end, the networking of the left wing must be strengthened: all members and branches that are critical of the coalition with the SPD and the Greens must now join the “Left within the Left” network (LidL). But above all, this discussion has to extend beyond party lines in order to truly mobilize all forces that, with the fiasco of the coalition negotiations, are beginning to recognize the limits of reformist government policies. These are the forces we can convince, based on their current experiences, to join us in intervening in the class struggle and to build a force of workers and youth independent of the state and the bosses.

For this reason, we are planning a defense rally with [‘solid] Neukölln in November, to which we want to appeal to everyone who is angry about the media smear campaign and disappointed with the party leadership, and who wants to build a strong opposition on the streets, in schools, universities, and workplaces. We invite all bodies of the Left Youth, the SDS, and the Left Party to do the same.

Because it’s clearer every day: the expropriation of large housing corporations that line the pockets of shareholders with our money and leave us to get sick in moldy apartments; the cutting of ties with institutions that actively promote murder, oppression, and displacement of our class siblings in Gaza and the West Bank; the abolition of military conscription; retirement at age 60; reduction of working hours to 30 per week with full pay; the disarmament of the racist and homophobic police; and the abolition of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution—no government can simply hand this to us; only we can fight for it ourselves. To realize this vision, we must now find as many allies as possible.

scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

National Bison Day recognizes an animal central to Indigenous culture and survival, as Tribal Nations continue efforts to restore buffalo herds, revitalize traditional food systems and strengthen tribal sovereignty.

Today is National Bison Day in the United States, observed annually on the first Saturday in November. The day honors an animal deeply revered by Tribal Nations — one that has sustained Indigenous peoples for generations, providing nutritious food, clothing, tools and materials for ceremonial and cultural practices.

In 2016, the American bison was designated the national mammal of the United States. Before westward expansion and mass slaughter decimated their populations, an estimated 60 million bison roamed North America, with the largest herds concentrated across what is now the central United States.

For generations, Native Americans throughout the Great Plains and other bison territories depended on the buffalo for virtually every aspect of life. The animal provided sustenance, supported tribal economies and held profound cultural and spiritual significance.

But that relationship was violently disrupted. By 1889, commercial hunting and government-backed eradication efforts had brought bison to the brink of extinction. Their near disappearance devastated Indigenous communities, disrupted traditional ways of life and contributed to the degradation of grassland ecosystems.

Today, Tribal Nations are helping lead the effort to reverse that history. Through conservation, herd restoration and Indigenous food sovereignty programs, tribes are bringing buffalo back to their lands — restoring not only an animal but also cultural connections, traditional food systems and an important part of their sovereignty.

Uplifting stories of Native traditions, language revitalization, and cultural innovation.

“The American bison is inextricably intertwined with Indigenous culture, grassland ecology and American history. While the overall recovery of bison over the last 130 years is a conservation success story, significant work remains to not only ensure that bison will remain a viable species but also to restore grassland ecosystems, strengthen rural economies dependent on grassland health and provide for the return of bison to Tribally owned and ancestral lands,” then-Interior Secretary Deb Haaland said in March 2023.

According to a report from Tribal Business News , the InterTribal Buffalo Council has transported more than 20,000 buffalo to Indian Country since its founding in 1992. As recently as 2024, approximately 25,000 buffalo lived on tribal lands, according to another Tribal Business News report .

Nationally, decades of conservation and restoration efforts have helped increase the number of wild bison in the United States from fewer than 500 to more than 15,000. The Interior Department currently manages approximately 11,000 bison in herds across 4.6 million acres of public lands in 12 states.

For Tribal Nations, however, the return of the buffalo represents far more than a conservation success. It is a restoration of relationships, traditions and food systems that were nearly destroyed. As buffalo return to tribal lands, they also help restore a measure of cultural continuity and Indigenous self-determination.

Levi “Calm Before the Storm” Rickert (Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation) is the founder, publisher, and editor of Native News Online. Rickert was awarded the Best Column Award in the print/online category... More by Levi Rickert

scraped.description: On Monday, Nov. 9, the U.S. Senate will vote on a bill that, if passed, could have far-reaching consequences for tribal preservation, sacred sites, and cultural resources across Indian Country. The Senate Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) aims to accelerate federal environmental review of project proposals. The bill proposes significant changes […]
scraped.author: Elyse Wild
scraped.h1: ‘An existential threat to Indian Country’ | Tribal Leaders Warn Bill Would Reduce Tribal Consultation, Destroy Sacred Lands
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

On Monday, Nov. 9, the U.S. Senate will vote on a bill that, if passed, could have far-reaching consequences for tribal preservation, sacred sites, and cultural resources across Indian Country.

The Senate Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) aims to accelerate federal environmental review of project proposals. The bill proposes significant changes to long-standing environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act. The bill was introduced in September, with no congressional oversight, public hearings or tribal consultation.

Advocates and lawmakers opposing BAAJA say that while the bill includes provisions that would advance clean energy initiatives, other provisions would devastate tribal sovereignty and environmental protections by allowing developers access to public lands for uranium mining, oil and gas pipelines, large-scale data centers, and more, without judicial review.

Your contribution is appreciated.

As well, it would narrow which projects receive review under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which mandates tribal consultation to determine how projects will affect areas of cultural significance to tribes.

At a virtual press conference held on Friday, Nov. 6, by conservation nonprofit Earthjustice, tribal leaders and advocates outlined their opposition to the bill.

All Pueblo Council of Governors chairman Joey Sanchez said the council is taking direct action and urged lawmakers to vote against the bill.

“APCG is headed to Washington, D.C., to make sure our voices are heard opposing this harmful legislation,” Sanchez said.

National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro (Pechanga Band of Indians) said many cultural and religious sites are outside reservation boundaries, making Section 106 crucial to protecting sacred lands.

“This is such an existential threat to Indian Country in the way that we try to protect our religion, our culture, our homelands,” Macarro said. “Having most of our land, having had it be stolen over the years, over the decades, over the centuries, there’s so much off our existing reservations and tribal lands.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., said that while permitting reform needs to happen to bring down the cost of energy, the bill would only do so at the expense of tribal sovereignty.

“So many of us want permitting reform, but we’re not going to do it by selling out and throwing under the bus Section 106 tribal consultation and these important environmental bedrocks, and that’s why I’m against this bill,” Leger Fernández said.

Native American Rights Fund staff attorney and Navajo Nation citizen Daniel Cordalis also spoke at the press conference, saying that BAAJA would roll back generations of hard-won tribal rights.

“Rights that we have fought for for generations, the bill, as written, blindly reduces and even stops the ability of tribal governments to participate as sovereign partners in federal decisions that can impact our legally protected rights in land, water and species interests,” Cordalis said.

While its rumored forthcoming amendments could ease the bill’s implications on tribal consultation, Macarro said they would fall short.

“The premise of the product is all wrong, and one of the reasons that it’s wrong is procedurally it is lacking in consultation with tribes,” Macarro said. “As leaders of tribal nations, sovereign leaders of tribal nations, we expect tribal consultation. That hasn’t happened, and a bill of this magnitude should not be the product of a rushed process at the end of a congressional session. It requires order and a deliberate process, where tribes have the opportunity to submit comments, not just on the fly.”

Elyse Wild is Senior Health Editor for Native News Online, where she leads coverage of health equity issues including mental health, environmental health, maternal mortality, and the overdose crisis in... More by Elyse Wild

scraped.title: Akwesasne community members fighting the opening of a Hyperscale data center - APTN News
scraped.description: A few minutes’ drive outside the borders of Akwesasne Mohawk Territory, industrial sites line the...
scraped.author: Savanna Craig
scraped.h1: Akwesasne community members fighting the opening of a Hyperscale data center
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

A few minutes’ drive outside the borders of Akwesasne Mohawk Territory, industrial sites line the perimeter.

One aluminum reduction and smelting site now operates as a digital currency mining facility.

The facility is set to expand, opening the doors to a new hyperscale data center. The center will be another facility on the list of many that border Akwesasne, Kanienʼkehá꞉ka territory.

A truck with three Kanienʼkehá꞉ka women drive past the facility. As they pass, a group of men nail up “no trespassing signs” along the facility.

“You’re on native land,” Dana Leigh Thompson shouts from the driver’s window. Thompson has been fighting to protect Akwesasne’s land, water and people for decades from outside corporate industry.

“We don’t care how many signs they put up [saying] no trespassing,” says Thompson. “This is our land. This is the land of the Kanienʼkehá꞉ka. Period.”

Three industrial and commercial sites are located near Akwesasne. In the United States these are known as Superfund sites.

The digital currency mining facility once operated as Reynold’s Metals. For decades, the aluminum reduction and smelting site released high amounts of toxic polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) into the environment.

A significant amount of U.S. Superfund sites are located on or near Indigenous land. Indigenous communities in North America are disproportionately exposed to environmental contaminants, including PCBs, according to a study from 2012 .

“There are 1,373 Superfund sites on or adjacent to indigenous communities in the United States,” says Thompson.

Two other Superfund sites line the border of Akwesasne.

The defunct General Motors site leaked aluminum die casting contributing to PCB contamination.

Thompson stands on her land, neighbouring the former General Motors site.

“What happens when a boat passes, all the water goes out, pulls it out, then it acts like a suction cup,” she explains, explaining that the pollutants are pulled from the site where PCB contamination is buried in the ground.

The third Superfund site, Alcoa Grasse River, discharged PCBs on the land and neighbouring wetlands from the 1950s to the mid 1970s.

‘Ranatakárias’

In July 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to accelerate federal permits of data center infrastructure. Within it, it states environmental reviews should be expedited to turn Superfund sites into data centers.

His efforts to expedite the conversion of Superfund sites into data centers, like the ones that line Akwesasne, has granted him the name “Ranatakárias” in Akwesasne.

“What that translates into is ‘town destroyer,’” says Thompson.

Now one of these sites will be expanding to develop a 1.5 million square foot hyperscale data center.

New York Digital Investment Group operates a digital mining facility on the old Reynold’s Metals site. The group has partnered with North Country Collocation Services to open the data center.

Wetlands surround the proposed three buildings that will inhabit the new hyperscale data center.

APTN News reached out to both New York Digital Investment Group and North Country Collocation Services for an interview request but didn’t receive a response.

Thompson is a mentor for the next generation. The next generation leading the fight against industrial and commercial sites from opening along Akwesasne are a group that calls themselves MUSH.

“We modeled ourselves after MASH, Mohawks Agree on Safe Health, which was created in 1981, during the height of all of the health effects and the environmental impacts that were happening to our people in the surrounding communities,” says Marina Johnson-Zafiris.

Johnson-Zafiris is a member of MUSH – Mohawks United Safety and Health – alongside Ronni Sunday.

The two focus their post-secondary studies on focuses related to their work at MUSH.

“I’m a masters student at Paul Smith College, studying natural resource conservation,” says Sunday, announcing to an audience.

The duo presented their work to an audience of students, researchers and students at the River Symposium, an event held in Cornwall, Ontario, to share knowledge of freshwater ecosystem conservation.

“I’m a PhD candidate at Cornell University in information science, where I mainly study work in developing technologies for land and water defenders,” says Johnson-Zafiris.

“Trump’s son is invested in these data centers big time,” Johnson-Zafiris says to the audience. “He made a statement, it was two or three weeks ago on National TV … he said, if you don’t want data centers, you’re going to be poor.”

Sunday and Johnson stand across from the lot set to be turned into the hyperscale data center.

While health impacts from PCBs are well-studied, the effects of data centers are not.

“When it comes to these data centers we don’t have cumulative long-term comprehensive research,” says Johnson-Zafiris.

MUSH specifies that their fight is against hyperscale data centers.

“We’re being very careful with our language in saying hyperscale data centers so that people can’t be like, ‘Well, you’re using a data center when you turn your phone on when you use Facebook,’” says Sunday. “We’re aware of that, but what we’re talking about is the scale of everything.”

Akwesasne is a border community, meaning the U.S.-Canada border runs through their territory. In May, the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne on the Canadian side put out a statement condemning and vocalizing concern over the building of this hyperscale data center along the border of Akwesasne. In October, the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe on the U.S. side formally published a press release opposing the Hyperscale Data Center from being built on or near their land.

APTN reached out to both councils for an interview. The Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe denied our request, and the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne never responded.

“They’re not really communicating with each other in the way that would kind of show a stronger stance against hyperscale data centers and also extractive industries,” says Sunday. “We’re just seeing one council saying something and the other one kind of following along behind them afterwards.”

Sunday says MUSH has been trying to get both councils to communicate on this issue together, “instead of just talking to me and Marina, and the rest of MUSH,” she says. She added that some elected officials from the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne have been attending some of MUSH’s information sessions. “But it’s two out of nine,” she said.

The group says they are not only fighting to prevent a Hyperscale Data Centering from opening on or near Akwesasne land. “What we’re hoping to do as MUSH, as a community organization, is not just focus it to a ‘not in my backyard conversation,’” says Johnson-Zafiris. “This shouldn’t be in anyone’s backyard.”

Next week the two will be traveling to Antalya, Turkey to attend the United Nations environmental forum COP31 alongside Indigenous Climate Action to raise global awareness around Hyperscale Data Centers.

Savanna has spent the last eight years reporting on policing, human rights violations, the silencing of the pro-Palestine movement and protests surrounding violence in the Middle East. She grew up in Toronto and began her career in Montreal reporting on Indigenous-led Energy East pipeline protests. Before joining APTN she was a freelance journalist for TRT World, Middle East Eye and The Breach.

scraped.title: “It’s all fake, It’s all rhetoric” MP Billy Morin says about Budget 2026
scraped.description: Conservative MP is not impressed with Budget 2026 and says 'I have crossed out destiny and put the masters of our deficit, debt, and deceit.'
scraped.author: Keelan Jacobs
scraped.h1: ‘It’s all fake. It’s all rhetoric:’ MP Billy Morin doesn’t have much good to say about Budget 2026
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Conservative MP Billy Morin during an Interview at APTN news Ottawa Bureau (November 06, 2026). Photo by: Keelan Jacobs/APTN

Conservative MP Billy Morin says Budget 2026 reveals a pattern of performative reconciliation that leaves Métis governments on the sidelines.

Morin, the opposition critic for Indigenous Services and former chief of Enoch Cree Nation in Alberta, went further while holding a copy of the budget.

“It is ironic that it says ‘Masters of Our Destiny,’ he said. “I have crossed out destiny and put the masters of our deficit, debt, and deceit. And when it comes to Indigenous people in particular, the deceit one really, I think, is highlighted.”

In Thursday’s budget, the federal government announced nearly $50 billion in spending over the next ten years, with $32 billion in new investments for First Nations housing and infrastructure.

“The prime minister said he was going to do $32 billion of investments, and he portrays that as new spending. I see very minimal new spending in that… All he did is keep the funding going. They had two options: cut it or keep it going. And they portray it as an investment or new funding. It’s not.”

APTN reached out to Indigenous Services Canada to ask whether the $32 billion announced in the budget was new spending or not. We were told that, at the moment, all questions related to the budget are to be directed to Finance Canada.

According to the department that responded after the story was published, “Budget 2026 newly allots $32 billion worth of new cash into community infrastructure that wasn’t previously there. This includes $1.3 billion of new money going towards First Nations off reserve, Inuit, Métis and modern treaty and self-governing partners to invest in affordable, supportive and transitional housing – which represents 10% of BCH’s [Build Canada Homes] new capital,” said the department. “How that money was derived or pooled is immaterial to the point, what matters is that community money that wasn’t available just yesterday now is – and is already flowing into Indigenous communities across the country.

“This is new money. Suggesting otherwise is patently false.”

Métis reaction

Manitoba Métis Federation president David Chartrand said Friday that his government was “appalled” by being left out of the budget.

“In recent years, Canada has finally started to address the long-overlooked needs of the Red River Métis in areas such as housing, early learning and childcare, and post-secondary education,” Chartrand said in a statement. “However, a significant gap still exists between our Nation and the general population. There’s no doubt our people will be angered that their needs have been dismissed by this Budget.”

The MMF noted that Métis appear only once in the 532-page document — “as part of the title for a piece of legislation, An Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families – a piece of legislation that Canada has claimed they do not have a mechanism to fund us for.”

“The hugely successful distinctions-based approach has vanished, and government is reverting to phrases like ‘Indigenous’ when, in reality, they mean First Nations and Inuit,” Chartrand said. “The Red River Métis pay billions in taxes in this country, yet we have been forgotten by this government.”

Read More:

Budget 2026 delivers $32B to First Nations, but Métis, Inuit largely left out

Manitoba Métis Federation ‘appalled’ they were left out of budget

The MMF said it had met with “numerous Ministers as well as the Prime Minister” ahead of the budget to discuss infrastructure, housing, health, and child and family services.

Morin said he understands the Métis questioning the government.

“How serious is this government about partnering with the Métis when they can’t even put them and acknowledge them in the budget? Morin said. “President Chartrand has every right to be appalled with this budget because every indication from this government is just like it treats First Nations people; it’s all fake. It’s all rhetoric and they don’t really mean it.”

Keelan is Anishinaabe from Walpole Island First Nation (Bkejwanong Territory). He graduated with an Honours B.A. In Political Science from the University of Toronto and follows the stories where power, money and public policy meet. Keelan has a strong interest in economics and finance, and is a lifelong hockey and sports fan.

scraped.title: Nearly half of the ballot measures that could affect Indian Country passed - ICT
scraped.description: Measures passed this midterm election cycle impact trans and 2SLGBTQIA+ rights, abortion access, environment and more.
scraped.author: Nika Bartoo-Smith
scraped.h1: Nearly half of the ballot measures that could affect Indian Country passed
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Nika Bartoo-Smith Underscore Native News + ICT

Voters across the country weighed in Tuesday on more than 140 statewide ballot measures. Across 17 states, 31 ballot measures were on the docket that had the potential to impact Native people and communities.

Of the 31 ballot measures, 15 passed.

Major themes of the ballot measures spanned across issues including voting rights, 2SLGBTQIA+ rights, abortion access, cannabis regulation, environment and beyond.

A number of laws aimed at limiting trans rights passed throughout the country, relating to students’ access to play sports, bathroom usage and gender-affirming care.

“I think it’s good to point out that many of these propositions did not come from the voters, did not come from the general population. Many of these were proposed by [the] establishment that was there,” said Jaynie Parrish, Navajo Nation, executive director of Arizona Native Vote.

Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington all passed these anti-trans ballot measures. All states with tribal nations and a high number of Native people.

“We already have some of the highest rates of violence against transgender and Two-Spirit people, and this kind of feeds a bit into that as well as underrepresentation in general for these communities that are under attack,” she said.

Voters in Arizona also voted to pass Proposition 318, a measure that changed private space access and sports eligibility requirements. Parrish said they were hoping it wouldn’t pass.

“But I think a lot of folks just didn’t quite understand what that measure meant, and I think it’s on the cusp of the wave of what we’re seeing across the country, and how there has been rhetoric and actions to really suppress our Two-Spirit, transgender relatives in any capacity,” she said.

Next door in New Mexico, voters passed a ballot measure to pay its state legislators.

“New Mexico was the only state in the country that did not pay its legislators a salary, and this affects who can serve in office, who this actually is accessible to,” said Angel Charley, who is Laguna Pueblo, Zuni Pueblo, and Diné.

Charley, a state senator in New Mexico, was one of four women of color who introduced Constitutional Amendment 4.

“When you think about who can actually serve their communities and serve them well, we need to pay our legislators to be able to do that,” she said. “It also opens up the possibility of running for office for someone who might not have thought about it before, so I’m thinking about young people, students, people right now who are working two or three jobs to make ends meet. Those are the kind of lived experiences that we need in government to change the system so it works for working people.”

It was a toss up between states with voter ID requirements on the ballots: Nevada and North Carolina both voted in favor of ballots requiring photo identification to vote. Arizona, California and Colorado voters voted against such measures, while Massachusetts will move forward with same-day voter registration.

Voters in Arizona voted against Proposition 144 that would require a government-issued ID to vote and that only U.S. citizens can vote in the state.

“With [Proposition] 144, we already know that Arizona already has some of the most restricted laws already when it comes to voter ID,” Parrish said. “So, for us that have been in this work, as organizers and as part of our team, we’re well versed to see what voter suppression looks like in many of these legislative pieces, and so for us, that’s what it amounted to was another measure to try to make it harder for our people to vote.”

This is a developing story and will be updated as ballots are counted.

Below are the results and updates for the 31 ballot measures in 17 states.

Idaho

Both states with measures on the ballot that would have restricted the authority to legalize and grow marijuana voted against those measures.

scraped.title: 'Wear your big earrings. Let out your loudest lili and let’s go’ - ICT
scraped.description: Peggy Flanagan, the country’s first Native woman U.S. senator, pledges effort to roll back Medicaid cuts and ensure the Indian Health Service funding
scraped.author: Kevin Abourezk
scraped.h1: ‘Wear your big earrings. Let out your loudest lili and let’s go’
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Kevin Abourezk ICT

Newly elected Minnesota U.S. Sen. Peggy Flanagan, the first Native woman to serve in the upper chamber, said Wednesday that she looks forward to restoring Medicaid funding cuts, ending the Iran War and ensuring Indigenous people have quality healthcare as promised to them by the federal government.

“I am running on caffeine and adrenaline and tremendous amounts of gratitude to the people of Minnesota,” she said Wednesday during a virtual press conference. “I think we had a tremendous result last night in Minnesota but also all across the country.”

“I am thrilled that my sister Deb Haaland was elected governor of New Mexico last night,” she said, noting that Haaland, Pueblo of Laguna, is the first Native woman elected governor of a state. “I’m just very hopeful about the future as we head into 2027: holding the Trump administration accountable and also working hard to make sure that people can afford the lives they want to live. … I am honored and so very humbled to be the first Native American woman elected to the United States Senate.”

Flanagan – an Anishinaabe Kwe or Ojibwe woman – said her first priority would be to restore Medicaid funding that President Donald Trump’s administration cut, as well as banning prior authorization, which is a practice employed by many insurance companies in which they require customers to get permission before getting healthcare procedures done or risk not having those procedures covered. Flanagan said she also supports Medicare for all.

She said ending the war in Iran will be a priority and working to reduce the rising cost of gasoline, a problem she attributes to the war. She offered stern words about the Trump administration’s decision to send thousands of ICE agents into Minnesota earlier this year.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

“We have been impacted so deeply here in Minnesota by the chaos, the terrorization, the scooping people up simply based on the color of their skin, including members of the Native community here in Minnesota, and the fact that they’ve been allowed to kill two Minnesotans with zero accountability whatsoever,” she said. “I think that is the message that I will be bringing to Washington, D.C. – that people want accountability.”

Flanagan said she was honored to see Michael Fairbanks, chairman of the White Earth Nation of which she is a citizen, and a drum group perform an honoring song for her prior to her victory speech Tuesday night.

“I absolutely understand the responsibility that I have as an Anishinaabe Kwe, as a member of the United States Senate, to ensure that we are working to make sure that the federal government upholds treaty rights and trust responsibilities, and frankly, that should be the floor,” she said.

“The significance of this moment is not lost on me, and I’m really hopeful for what we can do.”

She said she also looks forward to working with Wab Kinew, premier of Manitoba and Canada’s first First Nations provincial premier, to renew ties with Canada following the political turmoil that she said Trump’s tariffs and aggressive rhetoric have caused.

Kinew congratulated Flanagan on her win early Wednesday morning in a social media post:

“Congratulations MN Senator-Elect Peggy Flanagan and all the Democrats for absolutely dominating Trump in the midterms! I look forward to working together to lower costs on both sides of the border by ending the war in Iran (gas & diesel prices) and the Trump tariffs (the price of everything else).”

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“The American people have delivered a resounding rejection of the President’s actions over the past two years,” Kinew wrote. “Canadians are ready to rebuild the relationship and strengthen our economies.”

Flanagan said she’s hopeful that her win would inspire other future Native leaders who can now see the possibility of fulfilling their own political ambitions.

“Although it took 250 years for a native woman to become a United States senator, I certainly know that the next Native woman … elected to the US Senate, it will happen much faster,” she said. “We won’t have to wait for 250 years, and it gives me a lot of hope.”

Looking forward, she said she plans to seek a seat on the Senate Indian Affairs Committee and will work to ensure the Indian Health Service is fully funded, and she offered some words of comfort for Mary Peltola, who is Yupʼik and the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Alaska, whose tight race with incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, has yet to be called.

“The election night in Alaska lasts a little bit longer than it does in other states,” Flanagan said, referring to the challenges in counting votes in Alaska, where rural villages, including many Native villages, struggle to transport ballots, often by airplane, to the state capital of Juneau. “I know that she has run a really strong campaign and I look forward to that outcome, and I’m excited about the possibility of having two Indigenous women serving in the U.S. Senate together.”

She encouraged Native people all over the country to celebrate her win with her in whatever way they choose, and she thanked the many Indigenous women who have supported her throughout her life and political career.

“I would encourage all the aunties to wear your biggest earrings possible today,” she said. “Everyone should feel like they are a part of this. I exist because of the love and support of the Native community here in Minnesota, and I’d say even more specifically, the urban Native community here, and yeah, rock your ribbon skirt. Wear your big earrings. Let out your loudest lili and let’s go.”

Kevin Abourezk is a longtime, award-winning Sicangu Lakota journalist whose work has appeared in numerous publications. He is also the deputy managing editor for ICT. Kevin can be reached at kevin@ictnews.org. More by Kevin Abourezk

scraped.h1: ICT NEWSCAST: What do midterm results mean for Indian Country?
scraped.body_text:
ICT

The ICT Newscast for Friday, November 6, 2026, covers voting trends and cultural opportunities in Minnesota and Arizona. Check out the ICT Newscast on YouTube for this episode and more.

With historic wins for Native Americans from Peggy Flanagan winning the senate in Minnesota to Deb Haaland taking the governor’s race in, ICT partnered with FNX for three hours of live coverage on election night, November 3. Check out the recording at www.sdlkfsdf ; Moderator Antonia Gonzalez talks with Mark Trahant, Chris James and Mike Stopp about what’s next.

Leaders across the country speak up about what voting means for tribal nations. From local races to the national stage, representation is key.

Since 2018, ICT has tracked Indigenous candidates during presidential and midterm elections. The first-of-its-kind database was started by former ICT editor Mark Trahant, Shoshone-Bannock, in 2016. The number of Indigenous candidates this year has increased by nearly 400 percent, when compared to 2016. Advance Native Political Leadership’s Jordan James Harvill, Cherokee and Choctaw, gives his analysis on this year’s elections, and Iowa state legislature candidate Jessica Lopez Walker, Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska, talks about the importance of representation in public office.

Voter registration is down across the country, but precipitously in Indian Country. From non-standard addresses to remote regions counting on mail-in ballots, fighting for the right to vote is important.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

The Phoenix Art Museum recently unveiled their largest acquisition of Native American art in the Museum’s history. Gifted from the William P. Healey Collection of Native American Art, the collection features work by 99 Indigenous artists representing 44 tribal nations, including Jaune-Quick-to-See Smith, Cara Romero, Harry Fonseca, Kay WalkingStick, and T.C. Cannon. The exhibition is available to see through July 17, 2027.

The Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community hosted its annual powwow August 14–16, once again featuring the traditional moccasin game. The tribe revived the moccasin game tournament to help pass the tradition on to youth, a group often left out of the practice in the past. Coordinator Sunka Ska said that inclusivity matters, since today’s young people will one day be responsible for carrying the tradition forward.

View previous ICT broadcasts here every week for the latest news from around Indian Country.

scraped.title: Idris Elba is set to star in and direct new action-comedy ‘In Laws’
scraped.description: Idris Elba will star in, direct, and produce the upcoming action-comedy “In Laws,” playing a blacklisted secret agent.
scraped.author: Janeé Bolden
scraped.h1: Idris Elba is set to star in and direct new action-comedy ‘In Laws’
scraped.body_text:
The “Luther” star will play a disgraced secret agent in the upcoming buddy comedy, which is expected to begin filming in 2027.

Idris Elba is preparing to flex his comedic muscles in a new project that will put him both in front of and behind the camera.

The Golden Globe-winning actor is set to star in and direct the upcoming action-comedy “In Laws,” according to an exclusive report from Deadline . The film, which is expected to begin production in Spain in March 2027, will mark Elba’s fourth feature as a director.

Elba will play Carson Hughes, a blacklisted secret agent who gets an unexpected opportunity to redeem himself. But there’s a catch. He’ll have to work alongside a younger, by-the-book rookie agent to stop a deadly plot.

As the unlikely partners race against time, their differences threaten to derail the mission. Adding to the chaos, the two discover they have a wedding neither can afford to miss, assuming they can survive working together long enough to get there.

For Elba, who has spent much of his career playing intense characters in projects ranging from “Luther” to “The Wire,” the film offers an opportunity to explore a different side of his talents. Elba will produce the film alongside Gina Carter through their production company, 22Summers.

“Gina and I are really excited to make movies that make people laugh, and there’s nothing I love more than a great buddy comedy,” Elba said according to Deadline. “It’s a genre I’ve always loved, and one we’re excited to bring our own spin to.”

Jeffrey Greenstein of A Higher Standard and Mark Fasano of Nickel City Pictures are also producing. Greenstein co-wrote the screenplay with brothers Eshom and Ian Nelms, based on an original script by Adrian Speckhert and Cory Hughes. Additional casting is underway.

Although audiences know Elba primarily for his acting, he’s been steadily building his directing résumé. He made his feature directorial debut with the 2018 crime drama “Yardie,” and his upcoming film “Above the Below” is scheduled for release Dec. 4.

A post shared by Lionsgate (@lionsgate)

He’s also attached to direct an untitled Apple Original Films project featuring Wunmi Mosaku and Charlie Cox, expected in 2027.

Meanwhile, Elba and Carter’s 22Summers recently completed production on another installment of the actor’s popular “Luther” franchise for Netflix, titled “Luther: The Day Will Come.”

With “In Laws,” Elba appears ready to combine his action-star credentials with a little more laughter, and this time he’ll be calling the shots

scraped.title: Lil Jon opens up about his final conversation with son Nathan and learning to grieve: ‘It’s okay to cry’
scraped.description: Lil Jon opens up about final conversation with late son Nathan, DJ Young Slade, and how he's learned to navigate grief after his son's death.
scraped.author: Janeé Bolden
scraped.h1: Lil Jon opens up about his final conversation with son Nathan and learning to grieve: ‘It’s okay to cry’
scraped.body_text:
Lil Jon is opening up about one of the most painful experiences a parent can endure, sharing intimate details about the loss of his 27-year-old son, Nathan, and the final conversation that has brought him some peace.

During a deeply emotional appearance on CNN’s “All There Is with Anderson Cooper” podcast , released Friday, Nov. 6, the rapper and producer reflected on the accidental drowning of his son , a DJ known professionally as DJ Young Slade, in February. He also spoke candidly about the challenges of grieving while trying to remain strong for his family.

One of the most poignant moments came as Lil Jon recalled a conversation with Nathan just before his disappearance. The two had discussed the young man’s ongoing health struggles, and Lil Jon admitted he had been frustrated that his son hadn’t followed through on some of his suggestions for relief.

After discussing the exchange with his therapist, the rapper realized Nathan needed to feel that his efforts were being acknowledged. He called his son back to apologize.

“I said, I’m sorry. Said, I see you and I hear you,” Lil Jon recalled, explaining that he wanted Nathan to know he recognized how hard he was trying.

It would be their final conversation.

Lil Jon later learned from Nathan’s best friend that his son had been overjoyed by the phone call and had excitedly told his friend about his father’s apology.

“So it makes me feel at peace to know that he left feeling loved by me,” Lil Jon said.

Nathan went missing near his Georgia home in February and was subsequently found in a pond. Lil Jon told Cooper that his son’s death was ruled an accidental drowning, emphasizing that it was not a suicide.

The days leading up to the discovery were agonizing. Lil Jon recalled visiting Nathan’s home after learning he was missing and feeling that something was terribly wrong.

When authorities eventually recovered his son’s body, the loss was overwhelming.

“I always thought that he would be burying me,” he told Cooper.

A post shared by All There Is with Anderson Cooper (@allthereis)

The rapper described the difficulty of making funeral arrangements for his only son, including choosing a casket and serving as a pallbearer. He explained that carrying Nathan to his final resting place was an extension of the responsibility he had felt as a father since the day his son was born.

In the months following Nathan’s death, Lil Jon found himself navigating grief while preparing for a world tour with Pitbull. Performing offered a welcome connection to audiences and an opportunity to experience joy, but it also became a way to avoid confronting his pain.

During a recent EMDR therapy session, he said he finally recognized how much he had been holding inside.

As the oldest child in his family, Lil Jon had grown up believing it was his responsibility to be the strong one, a role he continued to play through the deaths of his parents and eventually his son.

“I kept myself so busy this year that I didn’t let myself mourn,” he admitted.

That realization has changed the way he approaches grief and the example he wants to set for his young daughter. Rather than allowing sadness to define her memories of him, he said he wants her to see him laughing, loving her mother and embracing life.

Throughout the conversation, Lil Jon also shared the many ways he continues to honor Nathan, whose love of music began in childhood. He recalled enrolling his son in DJ lessons at age 11 after recognizing his natural talent and watching him develop into an artist in his own right.

Today, Nathan remains part of every performance.

Lil Jon wears a shirt bearing his son’s logo, carries a commemorative coin engraved with their pictures and speaks to Nathan before taking the stage. He also got a tattoo of his son’s signature, mirroring a tattoo Nathan had gotten of his father’s autograph.

The rapper said those rituals help him maintain a connection to his son, even as he continues to struggle with the permanence of the loss.

“It’s not hard to live. It’s just hard to live without,” he told Cooper.

The conversation also touched on another unexpected source of grief. While researching his family history for his memoir, “I Only Shout So You Can Hear Me,” released Oct. 20 through Black Privilege Publishing, Lil Jon discovered at age 53 that the man who raised him was not his biological father. Both men have since died, leaving him unable to ask the questions that surfaced after the revelation.

He described the discovery as mourning the life he had believed he knew, another experience that has forced him to reconsider what it means to process loss.

Despite everything he has endured, Lil Jon said sharing his experiences has become part of his purpose. After spending much of his career protecting his privacy, he now hopes that speaking openly about grief can help others who are struggling.

His message is simple: Don’t suppress the pain, and don’t stop living.

“It’s okay to cry,” he said. “It’s okay to let whatever you’re feeling come out.”

“We have to keep living, even though we’ve lost, we have to keep living for them.”

scraped.h1: ‘I ain’t trying to see her like that’: Raamla Mohamed on writing Jax’s lowest moment in ‘Reasonable Doubt’
scraped.body_text:
‘Reasonable Doubt’ creator Raamla Mohamed breaks down the intention behind Jax Stewart’s addiction storyline in season 4.

Creator Raamla Mohamed cringed at the thought of seeing her beloved character Jax Stewart lick the remnants of a pain pill off of a public bathroom sink in “Reasonable Doubt.” But she knew that discomfort was part of the uncomfortable reality of addiction.

“I’m a fan of the show, right? So I was like, I ain’t trying to see her like that sink. Oh my god!” Mohamed said in an exclusive interview with theGrio. “But for me I’m like, it does really get us to understand where she is, and to be honest, if you hadn’t seen something like that before…seeing the behavior it had to feel bad.”

For the “Reasonable Doubt” creator, showrunner, and executive producer, the addiction storyline in this season felt inevitable. In fact, it’s a topic she always knew she wanted to explore through the show. And while in earlier seasons it is blatantly shown through Jax’s father, Eddie (played by Richard Brooks), and her client, Ozzie Edwards (played by Kyle Barry), Mohamed has teased the prominent lawyer’s addictive personality throughout the past three seasons.

“Even in the pilot, Jax asks for some Ambien when she needs to sleep, and we see her smoke cigarettes. She has an addictive personality. So obviously, then with the trauma of being shot, it felt like an inevitable storyline, “ she explained. “It’s not until you really see it through Jax that you see that it can happen to you.”

While some social media users have shared mixed feelings about seeing the show’s leading lady fall into the cycle of addiction, others have applauded the how Jax’s storyline this season exposes one of the realities of being a “high-achieving” Black woman.

“In my mind, an addict is in an alley, smoking crack. And I think that, unfortunately, that is kind of how we think of Black people, if they’re addicts… It’s also what we’ve seen on television,” Mohamed shared. “But the truth of the matter is that now we are also part of a high-functioning community where there are lawyers, doctors, plenty of people who do well and become addicted to [substances].”

“So it’s not about how strong you are or how smart you are,” she added.

And part of the reason Jax’s storyline hits so hard that it is almost hard to watch at times is a result of the work done behind the scenes. Just as Mohamed has been intentional about creating a world that feels unapologetically and authentically Black on and off-set, the “Reasonable Doubt” team has been intentional about spotlighting the realistic escalation of addiction through careful research, bringing in Black addiction consultants like Dr. Candice Washington, and having an on-set mental health coordinator at all times. This is paired with the creative decisions amplifies the layered truths of addiction and how it impacts not only addicts but also their loved ones.

This is especially seen in the show’s explosive episode 7, which Mohamed wrote and Anton Cropper directed. Beyond the dialogue, Mohamed said she wanted it to feel “silent and intense,” which explains the decision to feature very little music in the episode, aside from Beyoncé’s “Save the Hero” closing it out.

While not all viewers can relate to the specifics of Jax’s trauma and addiction, many Black women can relate to the weight that she’s carrying. Like many Black matriarchs, Jax is balancing showing up for everyone professionally and personally and keeping up with an image people have grown to know. Jax is the dependable one, the strong one, the one who can solve any problem and still come out of the trenches looking flawless. But this season, viewers are getting a front-row seat to what happens when you spend so much time running and maintaining everything but your mental health.

“There are two lines in the season so far that I think are the most important,” Mohamed shared. “The first is from episode three, when Jax tells her therapist she’s tired of being sad. [She’s like] I’m over it. I just want to be the baddest bitch in the room. The second is when she says, ‘I’m tired of being strong; it’s exhausting.’ To me, that’s a bit of the arc. It’s like, I want to be strong, and then it’s like, oh gosh, it actually is exhausting.”

Which is why sometimes you need to tell yourself to “sit down,” the same way Lewis told Jax to and the same way our parents did when we were kids. Though this season is uncomfortable, Mohamed hopes it reminds women to that it’s okay to slow down.

“You don’t have to keep chasing more of the things, “she reminds us. “I think as women, it’s hard every day we always feel like we’re failing at something. But look around and see what you have, and [ask yourself] what you really want and what you need.”

As far as Jax, the “Reasonable Doubt” creator, described her future as “aspirational.”

“I know that there were people who were questioning this journey, but I hope that by the end of episode [7], and definitely by the end of the season, that it’ll make sense [to them].

items.title: Dear, Black Male Educators: Keep the Promises You Made to Yourself
items.summary: As we look ahead to American Education Week, here are five suggestions for current and aspiring Black men in education from someone who has spent more than three decades fighting for our voices to be heard.Read more...

scraped.title: Black Men in Education: Keep the Promises You Made to Yourself
scraped.h1: Dear, Black Male Educators: Keep the Promises You Made to Yourself
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

As we look ahead to American Education Week, here are five suggestions for current and aspiring Black men in education from someone who has spent more than three decades fighting for our voices to be heard.

By

Sharif El-Mekki

Published

Getty Images stock photo

During the Black Men in Education Convening this November, more than a thousand Black male educators will gather in Philadelphia to discuss how to shape the next 100 years of education and confront some of the toughest questions facing Black educators today.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

We know that Black men account for only 1.3 percent of U.S. public school teachers . Black teachers reported the highest morale of any racial group in Education Week’s 2024 survey: +5, while that measurement for teachers overall stood at –13. Teachers of color were also more likely to plan full classroom careers in Educators for Excellence polling. Yet in 2021–22, 9 percent of Black teachers left teaching, versus 7 percent of white teachers .

We love this work, but too many of us still leave before we are ready .

As we look ahead to American Education Week, which honors public school educators and the importance of public education, here are five suggestions for current and aspiring Black men in education from someone who has spent more than three decades fighting for our voices to be heard.

1. Move as a team and study together.

Teachers improve faster where collaboration on instruction is stronger . Find at least one colleague. Meet every two weeks with student work in hand. Name a goal for your students and one for yourself; then hold each other to both. The promises we make to the communities we serve include the ones we make to ourselves.

Black educators have long worked this way. In 1854, young Black men in Philadelphia, Octavius Catto among them, built the Banneker Institute —a literary society for original lectures and essays. The Fellowship began in that spirit, with seventeen of us at a West Philadelphia restaurant. Some of us were thinking about leaving. Most of us stayed.

Those of us who lead classrooms and schools are Black intellectuals, and our work is praxis, what our revolutionaries called theory and practice. Read something together, try it with children, and check whether it changed what they learned.

2. Treat your health as a practice, in community.

Black men in the U.S. had a life expectancy of 71.3 years in 2024 , nearly eight years below the national figure. Our Center is working with Philadelphia’s Department of Public Health on those disparities among Black men who teach.

For most of my career, I would have declined or ignored the opportunity to discuss my health in a group (or at all). I recently joined a Pahara Institute vitality group, and for the first time saw health as something I practice with others. Get the annual physical, know your blood pressure and blood sugar, protect your sleep, and move most days with a brother.

Audre Lorde, living with cancer, wrote that “caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation, and that is an act of political warfare.” Self-care that keeps us able to serve is just.

3. Let your grief and your wounds be met.

In 1992, I was shot . City victim services called, and I ignored them. I don’t need that, I told myself. Maybe I didn’t. I had my faith, family, and friends. I had a beloved and loving community.

My Mama died in 2020. Six years later, I am still learning a grief I never felt prior to her passing. My faith teaches me that the end is not the end, and I believe it. Food still has not tasted the same. I miss her. I can see now that losing her may be keeping me from serving at the level I expect, so I am looking for a grief counselor. For decades, I offered grieving students an empathy I would not offer myself. If you have been grieving alone, take “the call” this time.

Some of our wounds come from schools and districts. It is often assumed we come to school for healing. More likely, we arrived whole, and thirteen years of schooling battered us. Then comes a trifecta: that trauma, racism in the wider world, and racism on the job, from hiring to being passed over. We are asked to be the heavy or enforce policies that are ineffective at best and harmful at worst, and even choosing whether to resist weighs on us. Take stock and address it without wounding others. Sometimes, hurt people hurt people, and our students should not bear that.

4. Know your worth, in name and in dollars.

I started teaching at $26,000 a year and opted out of the district’s 401(k) because I figured I could not afford it. No one had that conversation with me. It cost me. We should keep pushing, with allies like the Teacher Salary Project , for higher pay for all teachers, especially in hard-to-staff schools. Learn about retirement, debt, and savings, and teach each other.

Learn what the profession calls the skills you already have. Building culture and community in a classroom is expertise. Black male teachers spend more time mentoring and counseling students than teachers of any other group, and colleagues send us their students. People call it an invisible tax. It ain’t invisible. We will always help, and coaching others should also be paid work while we remain teachers of record. We can do some of this while still leading classrooms. After all, not all of us need to rush into administration.

5. Build the skill, the mindset, and the will, with humility.

Our children need our love, and they also need us to teach superbly and move with humility. I have seen us act haughtily, certain, and wrong. Being a Black man does not make any of us an expert on every Black child, across generations, neighborhoods, and bodies. Humility and the wisdom to know what we do not know usually win out. Sharpen one skill this year, ask a colleague to watch, let students know what you’re working on, and ask them in a few weeks if they’re noticing any difference. Keep this up, and check whether students are learning more.

In 1896, Mary Church Terrell gave the National Association of Colored Women its motto: lifting as we climb . Our first invitation to young people is the classroom itself. When students spend their days in classrooms full of curiosity and love, intellectually challenged, culturally affirmed, and dedicated to their success, they can picture coming back to lead one. Model that first. Then ask them to join us .

Wherever you teach, start Monday. Find your colleague. Make the changes you have been avoiding. Our children are counting on the promises we keep.

Mama often reminded us of a Farsi saying: shoma harakat, khoda barakat. You move, and God blesses the movement. Pray while you row. Most days, you have to pick up the oars.

Sharif El-Mekki is the founder and CEO of the Center for Black Educator Development and founded The Fellowship: Black Male Educators for Social Justice. A former Philadelphia teacher and principal, he has spent more than three decades in education.

scraped.title: TikTok Creators Over 40 Sharing Real-Life Advice for Gen Z
scraped.h1: 13 TikTok Creators Over 40 Delivering Real-Life Advice Young People Actually Need
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

While TikTok was built on dance crazes and trends, there has been a rise in seasoned experts sharing real-life advice with young people navigating a crowded digital world.

By

Mahalia Otshudy

Published

Screenshot: TikTok

In 2020, TikTok kept young people distracted from the horrors of COVID-19 and the boredom of a worldwide lockdown with dance trends, hilarious memes, and fashion content. Now, as many Gen Zers settle into adulthood and build lives of their own, new content is gaining traction: real-life advice from creators over 40. Doctors, lifestyle experts, and more are breaking through the digital noise with tips to help Gen Z navigate every aspect of their lives.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

If you’re looking to refresh your TikTok feed with seasoned experts, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite creators who can help.

Cardiologist Dr. Yele Aluko cuts through the social media noise with advice on optimizing heart health, including symptoms you shouldn’t ignore and foods and drinks that can increase your risks for heart attacks.

Thanks to beauty filters and an influx of fillers and cosmetic procedures aimed at young folks, the message to keep all signs of aging at bay makes growing older seem daunting. Through her lifestyle content, the stylish Mia Maugé helps Gen Z see why maturing is a privilege and a beautiful journey. One look at her gorgeous grey hair will make you want to break up with your colorist immediately.

Related: Gen Z: Here’s The Life Advice You Need to Hear in Your 20s

Dr. Lee Warren is the content creator to turn to for simple yet fascinating facts about brain health and how to rewire your mind to work for you, not against you. The brain surgeon and bestselling author serves as a valuable resource for an anxious generation.

Stanley Tucci is not just a versatile, Academy Award-nominated actor; he is also a wizard in the kitchen, whipping up simple yet delicious dishes that can impress any dinner guest. His TikTok page is a calm, comforting space that breaks down five-star recipes into five simple steps.

Gen Z is the next generation preparing to enter the housing market. Although Carmen Renee’s content targets folks over 40, her videos serve as textbooks for Gen Z on how to host, set up a home, and do it all while looking chic.

It seems that with every TikTok scroll, a new health craze pops up, often without science-backed evidence that supports it. Plastic surgeon Dr. Anthony Youn analyzes viral health claims and breaks down the facts and fiction for his audience.

Author and lawyer Mel Robbins hosts a podcast that frequently features experts in fields such as health and relationships. As a self-help author, Robbins also offers a wealth of knowledge on how to change your life day by day.

Dr. Jessica Shepherd is helping women understand what is happening to their bodies as they age. As a menopause and perimenopause expert, her page is loaded with advice on how women can make sense of the symptoms and take better care of themselves.

Since 2020, working from home has become increasingly common, often leading to missed physical activity and poor posture while hunching over a computer. As a physical therapist, Dr. Josh shares quick, easy daily exercise habits to help you stay in shape.

While the internet is filled with makeup tutorials, former celebrity makeup artist Erica Taylor shares Hollywood tips to help folks look and feel their most glamorous. In her videos, viewers learn how red-carpet makeup relies less on wizardry and more on refined techniques anyone can master.

During lockdown, Tabitha Brown became TikTok’s favorite auntie. Through her page, she has embraced many Gen Z followers, providing life advice and encouraging words to help folks get through their week feeling a little lighter.

Beyond the silver screen, Reese Witherspoon is diving into novels and building a book-loving community that discovers stories together, making reading a hobby that is fun, relaxing, and cool again.

If you’re looking for tips on how to age gracefully, Dr. Chisom Ikeji has you covered. As a geriatrics and critical care physician, she shares expert advice with folks looking to take preventative health measures.
