scraped.title: Here are The Biggest Flipped Seats of Midterm 2026 – The Root
scraped.h1: Here are The Biggest Flipped Seats of Midterm 2026
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Candidates made history in the 2026 midterms, breaking barriers and flipping Republican-held seats as Democrats reshaped the nation’s political landscape.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

(Photo by Megan Varner/Getty Images), (Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images), (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

The 2026 midterm elections produced a sweeping political shake-up, with Democrats emerging in control of both chambers of Congress. Keisha Lance Bottoms, Cyril Jefferson and James Talarico were among those making headlines as historic races turned into victories. But alongside the national party shift came another significant development: Black candidates secured landmark victories across the country.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Several contests also resulted in Democrats taking seats previously controlled by Republicans. Here are the major flips reported by the Associated Press.

High Point, NC, Mayor Cyril Jefferson defeated Republican incumbent Addison McDowell to flip the district McDowell once carried by more than 38 points in 2024. His election to the U.S. House of Representatives marks a significant change in the district’s congressional representation.

Western Michigan saw a historic change as Democrat Sean McCann defeated eight-term Republican incumbent Bill Huizenga to represent Michigan in the U.S. House. His win puts the district in Democratic hands for the first time in nearly 100 years, adding another longtime Republican seat to the Democratic column.

North Carolina saw a major political shift as Democrat Lakesha Womack unseated Republican incumbent Tim Moore, capturing 51.1% of the vote. After Moore won the district by roughly 16 points in 2024, Womack’s victory turned a previously Republican-held seat in the U.S. House blue and changed the district’s political landscape.

RELATED : New Doc Takes a Look Inside the Texas Colonies Built By Black Americans After Slavery

Indiana’s 5th District delivered one of election night’s surprises. Democrat J.D. Ford defeated Republican incumbent Victoria Spartz, who had won reelection by more than 18 points in 2024. It was a major turnaround in a district Republicans expected to hold.

Georgia just elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as its first Black governor and the first Black woman governor in American history. Her victory ended nearly three decades of Republican control in the statehouse. More than a simple party flip, it marked a historic, barrier-breaking milestone in U.S. politics.

Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Greg Abbott, becoming Texas’ first Latina governor and the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990. In a state Republicans had dominated for decades, this was a generational political shift and a historic breakthrough for Latina representation.

Aaron Ford defeated Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo, becoming Nevada’s first Black governor. His victory added another Black governor to the nation’s political landscape and flipped a Republican-held governorship. The significance extends beyond Nevada: Black political leadership is no longer an exception in gubernatorial politics.

Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson, flipping Iowa’s open Senate seat. A former Paralympic basketball player, Turek becomes the first former Paralympian elected to the U.S. Senate. Iowa also elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 2008.

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley made history as Wisconsin’s first Black governor. His win flipped the Republican-held office and placed a Black executive at the helm of a critical presidential battleground state. Representation and political geography collided in one consequential victory.

Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, becoming Ohio’s first Democratic governor since 2006. Her victory ends two decades of Republican gubernatorial control and gives Democrats another major Midwestern governorship. It’s a significant reversal in a state that has moved toward Republicans in recent presidential elections.

Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins, ending her decades-long Senate career and flipping a seat Democrats had not won since 1988. The result is particularly significant because Collins had repeatedly survived Democratic challenges in a state that votes Democratic in presidential elections.

Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Republican Roger Marshall, making history in a state that had not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932. That’s nearly a century of Republican dominance in Kansas’ Senate representation interrupted by one election.

James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, giving Texas Democrats their first Senate victory since 1988. He also became part of a broader Democratic breakthrough in statewide Texas politics, alongside Gina Hinojosa’s gubernatorial victory. Two statewide victories in one election fundamentally changed the state’s political narrative.

Former governor Roy Cooper defeated Republican Michael Whatley to claim North Carolina’s open Senate seat. Democrats hadn’t won a Senate race in the state since 2008, or an open Senate seat since 1974. That’s a 52-year drought for open-seat victories finally ending.

Dr. Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, flipping a South Carolina Senate seat held by Republicans since Strom Thurmond switched parties in 1964. She also becomes the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate. A remarkable breakthrough in one of the South’s most reliably Republican states.

Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Jon Husted, reclaiming an Ohio Senate seat after losing his previous reelection bid in 2024. The former senator’s return flips a Republican-held seat and restores a familiar Democratic figure to Washington. A comeback with real consequences for Senate control.

Penny Brown Reynolds defeated Republican Tim Fleming, becoming Georgia’s first Black secretary of state and the first Democrat to hold the office in nearly 20 years. A former judge and Biden administration official, Reynolds’ victory marks a historic breakthrough for Black women in statewide elected leadership.

scraped.title: JD Vance Tries to Take Credit for Accomplishments That Weren’t His, and Mamdani Buries Him in 9 Seconds Without Saying a Single Word
scraped.description: Critics accused Vice President JD Vance of claiming credit he didn’t earn after he touted lower crime and investment in the state on X. On
scraped.author: Shelby Erdman
scraped.h1: JD Vance Tries to Take Credit for Accomplishments That Weren’t His, and Mamdani Buries Him in 9 Seconds Without Saying a Single Word
scraped.body_text:
Critics accused Vice President JD Vance of claiming credit he didn’t earn after he touted lower crime and investment in the state on X.

On Monday, Vance posted about the Trump administration’s achievements in New York.

He called the post “The Trump Administration Delivers for New York,” and he captioned the message, “We’ve got your back, New York!”

He falsely claimed President Donald Trump is responsible for multi-billion-dollar investments in the state, a major drop in the crime rate and protecting jobs.

Vance took credit for “SAFER COMMUNITIES,” WORKING FAMILIES TAX CUTS,” AND “HISTORIC INVESTMENTS.”

Boost Mobile Employee Screams ‘Rape’ at Black Customer Who Keeps Telling Her Not to Touch Him

‘You Don’t Need to Do That!’: Louisville Father of 9 Offered to Pay for a Boy’s Snacks. Seconds Later, He Was Shot in the Chest

The only problem? It’s not completely true, and X posted a community note under the post challenging part of it.

Vance claimed credit for a 48 percent drop in crime, 337,000 protected jobs, and $472 billion in state investment.

An X Community Note said some investments extended beyond New York and lacked direct ties to the Trump administration.

“Several figures here aren’t federal results or NY-specific. The $472B combines US wide pledges: Micron’s $250B is nationwide (NY site $100B) Anthropic’s $50B covers TX and NY. The 48% murder drop is from NY’s state run GIVE program (28 departments, Jan – May 2026),” the note said.

The huge drop in crime is due to New York’s Gun Involved Violence Elimination, or GIVE, initiative, which involves 28 police departments. Other achievements happened under New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and clearly Vance distorted the investment gains with inflated math

By falsely trying to take credit for some of these achievements, Vance got on the wrong side of Mamdani. The mayor quickly responded to Vance’s message with one of his own, and he didn’t write a single word.

He posted a hysterical nine-second video meme above Vance’s post. It shows a man in a fluorescent work vest pretending to hold back a subway train, then ushering people on and off the train before signaling to the conductor that the train is ready to go.

The post went viral, racking up almost 50 million views.

Social media had a field day, with commenters mocking Vance and calling him out for his falsehoods.

“This has to be the most brutal ratio in the history of this site,” an X user observed.

Another hilariously reposted Mandani’s video clip showed Vance as the man guiding the train with the caption, “Mamdani owns you, bum.”

Others agreed. “Taking credit for something someone else has done is INSANEEEE.”

This poster summed it up: “Lmao no way you just took credit for this man’s hard work.”

Trump and his Republican cronies were desperate in the final hours before Election Day on Nov. 3. Trump spent weeks campaigning in red states where he easily won the 2024 election.

Now, just two years later, Republicans are struggling in what should have been easy re-election races, tied to an unpopular president and his even more unpopular policies.

At stake is control of Congress. Polls and experts expect Democrats to take back the House, and they also believe they have a shot at a Senate majority.

https://t.co/nNSc9S9Gr2 pic.twitter.com/IEZtA9oAdK

We hope this story was worth your time. For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run. We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us. Our readers did that.

Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

We know a request for support isn't why you came here. But without readers choosing to fund this work directly, the depth of reporting we can do at home and abroad shrinks along with everyone else's. If you're not in a position to give, that doesn't change how much we value you as a reader.

If you are able to, a recurring contribution does more for us than a single one-time gift, because it lets us plan the next investigation instead of just the next invoice. It takes about 30 seconds, no long form, no account. Thank you for continuing to support independent journalism and freedom of the press.

Atlanta Black Star is a narrative company. We publish narratives intentionally and specifically to enlighten and transform the world.

Contact us: [email protected]

scraped.title: 'It's Like a Vacation': Russell Wilson Sets the Bar High Ahead of Baby No. 5 as Ciara Gushes Over His Delivery Room Routine
scraped.description: Russell Wilson’s wish for baby number five, affectionately known as “Cinco,” has officially come true! Three years after expressing his desire to expand
scraped.author: Sharmaine Johnson
scraped.h1: ‘It’s Like a Vacation’: Russell Wilson Sets the Bar High Ahead of Baby No. 5 as Ciara Gushes Over His Delivery Room Routine
scraped.body_text:
Russell Wilson ’s wish for baby number five, affectionately known as “Cinco,” has officially come true!

Three years after expressing his desire to expand their family, the former NFL star and his wife, Ciara, are preparing to welcome another addition.

Many wonder how the singer balances motherhood, marriage, and her thriving career while continuing to expand her family. Ciara has made one thing clear: having five children isn’t just Russell’s dream. It’s hers, too!

The couple announced the pregnancy in September with a social media post showcasing Ciara’s growing baby bump .

The couple announced the news in September with a social media post showing Ciara’s growing baby bump , giving fans a glimpse into the next chapter of their love story.

‘That Ciara Prayer Still Going Strong’: Russell Wilson and Ciara Shut Down the ‘Gram on Their Seven-Year Wedding Anniversary with New Photos

‘Definition Of Love’: Ciara Pulls at Heartstrings with Reaction to Russell Wilson’s Retirement — Proving Why They’re the Internet’s Favorite Couple

Since then, the excitement surrounding the newest addition has continued to build as the family prepares for its latest bundle of joy.

During a Friday appearance on “ Today with Jenna & Sheinelle ,” the “Goodies” singer opened up about her love for motherhood and how having a supportive husband makes the journey even more rewarding.

“I’m an only child, so I want a big family. I love being a mom. It’s my favorite job in the world,” Ciara shared.

The multihypenate also opened up about embracing life at 41. Ciara said she feels more empowered than ever as she prepares to welcome her fifth child.

“I just turned 41 w-o-n, okay, so I feel really good. It was hard for me to say 40, you know that, but now I’m embracing every part of my journey. I feel so empowered. We’re on our fifth baby, 41, and I’m feeling younger than ever. I am really excited,” she said.

And when it comes to welcoming a new baby, Russell knows exactly what his wife needs.

Rather than leaving Ciara with an ordinary delivery experience, he makes it his mission to create a comfortable, relaxed environment where she feels celebrated.

“He makes the process fun for me. It’s like a vacation. He gets into it. He has, like, the twinkle lights in my room that I love. He hooks it up. He has the Apple TV,” she revealed.

She said Russell goes above and beyond to make sure she is calm, cozy, and at peace with each delivery.

The couple are already raising four children: Future Zahir, Ciara’s son from her previous relationship with rapper Future, and their three children together, Sienna Princess, Win Harrison and Amora Princess.

The excitement wasn’t limited to the parents, either. When it came time to share the big news with their children, Ciara and Russell made the announcement a family moment to remember.

They initially set things up as a family photo opportunity for the grandparents.

But instead of an ordinary picture, Ciara had the children count to five in Spanish before revealing her baby bump. The surprise quickly turned into an unforgettable moment filled with excitement and joy from everyone.

Ciara once prayed for a husband, and judging by how things are going, that prayer came with a few extra blessings. But it seems motherhood remains one of her greatest joys.

During a May 10 interview with Angie Martinez, Ciara opened up about the qualities she wanted in a husband.

She said faith, discernment, and wisdom topped her list. She also wanted a man who genuinely loved children, knowing he would need to embrace her son.

Ciara added, “I prayed for a man that was worldly as well. Because I love to explore so someone that was gonna edify my world, that was important to me. I was ready to level up!”

Between a husband who goes above and beyond to make the delivery experience special and children who are just as excited about their newest sibling, it’s clear that baby Cinco is already surrounded by plenty of love.

Ciara & Russell Wilson on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle. 🎥: @NBC @JennaSheinelle https://t.co/FOUeHaWBLg

scraped.title: 'Why Would You Say That?!': Gym Rat Thought He Could Get Away with Racist Remark, Then He Learned a Hard Lesson
scraped.description: An unidentified man is being lauded for his brave defense of his daughter. A video uploaded to X on Oct. 31 may be thin on details, but it’s having a
scraped.author: Grace Jidoun
scraped.h1: ‘Why Would You Say That?!’: Gym Rat Thought He Could Get Away with Racist Remark, Then He Learned a Hard Lesson
scraped.body_text:
An unidentified man is being lauded for his brave defense of his daughter.

A video uploaded to X on Oct. 31 may be thin on details, but it’s having a significant impact on viewers.

In the brief clip, the father is enjoying a workout at a gym when another man makes the kind of offhand racist remark that can leave a lasting sting.

The man quipped, “Well, at least you weren’t born Black.”

The father wasn’t about to let the clueless comment slide. Clearly upset, he repeatedly yelled, “My daughter’s Black! Why would you say that, bro?”

Apparently unfazed, the man snarked, “I’m going to hold your hand, and we’re not gonna fight.” But that didn’t go over well.

‘You’re Going to Jail!’: Mother Gets Swarmed by Cops at California Pumpkin Patch After Sitting at Table Woman Was Saving for Relatives

‘You Don’t Need to Do That!’: Louisville Father of 9 Offered to Pay for a Boy’s Snacks. Seconds Later, He Was Shot in the Chest

Though the footage went haywire at this point, the audio made it clear that the two tussled off camera.

By the time the clip ended, the man had apologized, but the father remained upset.

He warned: “You’re lucky I don’t smack a weight over your head.”

The confrontation was another reminder that even in the most mundane circumstances, Black people are made to feel othered.

As one commenter said on X: “This is an example of how prevalent racism still is in society, that he would say that so casually, and expect a stranger to feel the same way he feels about Black people!”

Many people heaped praise on the father for standing up for his daughter, even though she wasn’t there.

“You could hear the hurt in his voice,” one person wrote. “And that smirk…definitely set him over the edge. True definition of being an ally and standing for what’s right.”

Another chimed in: “I appreciate and love that he defended his daughter’s honor, even with his daughter not being there to be directly confronted or insulted. Now that’s what real men and real fathers do. Salute.”

🚨 A racist at a gym told a white man "at least you weren’t born Black," not knowing the man he said it to has a Black daughter. "WELL, AT LEAST YOU WEREN’T BORN BLACK." The man with the Black daughter confronts him, and things blow up. He then apologizes: "I apologize, I didn’t mean to insult you." No gym, city or official response has been confirmed. All that’s known is what the video shows. He said it to the one man in the room with a Black child. Is an apology after getting caught enough, or should the gym ban him?

scraped.title: As Mississippi Counts Vote, Ballot Monitors Say They’re Being Shut Out
scraped.description: From inaccurate meeting times to wrong locations, volunteers say they are navigating confusion while trying to ensure a transparent counting process.
scraped.author: Aallyah Wright, Jasmine Williams, ‘Sipp Talk Media
scraped.h1: As Mississippi Counts Vote, Ballot Monitors Say They’re Being Shut Out
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

Photos by Eric Truman-Reeves for ‘Sipp Talk Media

CANTON, Mississippi — It took Natt Offiah an hour to realize he had arrived at the wrong location to monitor the provisional and absentee ballots in the Mississippi U.S. Senate race. He drove to Madison County Circuit Clerk’s Office on Wednesday, but the building was under construction.

After a phone call, Offiah, director of organizing for the People’s Advocacy Institute, and his colleague finally reached the temporary clerk’s office. They were redirected again, shared Offiah, still unable to locate officials.

At the next building, one woman said, “I haven’t seen them in an hour or so,” before directing the organizers down a hallway.

Offiah said he banged on the door, to no avail. The duo sat outside the room for 45 minutes before heading back to the front desk. A receptionist then told Offiah about two dozen staffers had left 15 minutes before his initial arrival.

No one could provide him any information on when they would return to continue counting votes.

“There is no standardized process for counting. Each county can pick and choose when they want to start counting. So, we’re running into this runaround issue,” Offiah said.

His experience mirrors the dozens of other volunteers who say they didn’t sign up for chaos and confusion, but to protect the democratic process. Some — who reported their concerns in group chats shared with Capital B — say they’ve been denied a seat to observe the process, while others struggle to find information.

With the nation’s close eye on Mississippi, advocates say it’s even more critical to ensure election officials “do the right thing.” Voters have been on edge since Election Day, waiting to see who will become the state’s next U.S. senator.

Despite no early voting or online registration, turnout and absentee ballots have surged. As of Nov. 6, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.

Yet, there are still thousands of mail-in and affidavit ballots outstanding .

LEFT: Complicating Mississippi’s vote count is there is no uniform process on how officials conduct affidavit ballot counting. RIGHT: Erin Shirley Orey takes notes as affidavit ballots are counted.

Issues like voter ID laws and inoperable machines have fueled delays, said Lydia Grizzell, policy and advocacy manager of ACLU of Mississippi.

“It is appalling the number of issues that we’ve seen and we had on Election Day, and now we’re seeing the extension of that post-Election Day in a way that is not great,” she said.

The Mississippi secretary of state’s office did not address the monitors’ allegations of being shut out of the vote counting process, but told Capital B the public is entitled to be present for the counting of ballots, the process where election commissioners announce which affidavit ballots are accepted or rejected, according to state statute. This does not include the preliminary work commissioners do to determine a voter’s eligibility.

There is no uniform process on how officials conduct affidavit ballot counting. In some counties, where ACLU dispatched attorneys, election officials had a closed door process, Grizell added.

“ The best thing that we can do is have people watching, witnessing, and doing their best to gather as much information as possible as to what is happening,” she said.

Volunteers across the state are being deployed in a widespread effort prompted by several grassroots organizations. The NAACP has also deployed national legal, policy, and field staff to the state to make sure every vote is counted.

Both candidates sent their own groups to monitor the process and assembled a group of lawyers who are prepared to take legal action if necessary. Lawyers for Hyde-Smith sent a letter to election commissioners requesting “immediate separation, secure custody and preservation of all affidavit ballots.” Following Hyde-Smith’s legal team’s response, Colom’s legal counsel sent a letter to all 82 counties, calling the GOP senator’s demand unlawful.

Ahead of the election, thousands of Mississippians were moved to inactive status because the secretary of state’s office paid $50,000 to use unverified data from credit bureau Experian to clean out voter rolls. Secretary of State Michael Watson told Mississippi Today that the rollout of the commercial data was “wildly successful.”

This unprecedented number of inactive voters led to more affidavit ballots, prolonging the count, Tarekegn said. These ballots must be “cured”, meaning to correct issues with voter identification or mail-in ballots, by Nov. 10.

Organizers also pointed out that Mississippi’s outdated voting system exacerbated the counting issues. With no early voting, most ballots come in on Election Day. This overwhelms the system. Still, Tarekegn praised Mississippians for the high turnout.

“Mississippi is one of the hardest, if not the hardest, state to vote in,” she said. “We’re truly talking about probably more than 90% of the people having to show up on Election Day between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. to cast their vote.”

On Election Day, Rachel Madden was the 20th person in line at her precinct in DeSoto County. After an hour’s wait, she was told she had been made inactive and needed to vote by affidavit.

“She just told me that my name wasn’t in the system, and I was like, ‘Well, that doesn’t make any sense,’” Madden said.

She hadn’t changed her address, so she was confused why she had been flagged as inactive. The poll worker assured her, “It’s not a big deal, you’re like the second person this has happened to,” she said.

She said she was instructed by the poll worker to go to the courthouse to “cure” her ballot after being given a form. She made the 25-minute drive to the courthouse, where the employee informed her she had been inactive since May by District 1 Election Commissioner Laura Edler because of Madden’s supposed move to nearby Memphis, Tennessee.

Madden says she never moved anywhere. Her address was corrected in the system and she received a new voter card.

She recalls she then called to ensure her ballot was accepted. She said that an employee told her they would not be taking any more calls about affidavit ballots for the next 10 days, which would put Madden outside the deadline of ballot curing.

“I was like, in 10 days, it’s not gonna matter,” Madden said. “Even in person that day, they were not helpful. If I had not insisted, I don’t think they would have done it. I just don’t think that’s fair or right.”

Edler did not speak to any individual’s standing, but told Capital B that when the commission receives a change of address from the secretary of state’s office, then the voter will be notified and must rectify the issue or remain inactive.

Ballot monitors say it’s also been difficult to do their jobs.

In DeSoto County, Kelly Jacobs, a local organizer, said District 4 Election Commissioner Sissie Ferguson prevented her from watching as election officials presorted ballots and checked names.

The day after the election, Jacobs said she stopped by the election’s commissioner office, but learned they had changed locations. She then traveled to the police department, which directed her to the new location.

After being barred from entry, Jacobs called an attorney, who affirmed her rights, but officials continued to block her from observing, she said, which she captured on video. Commenters on the video state that they were allowed access to observe vote counting in other counties.

On Nov. 5, around noon, the public was able to monitor the process, but by then, the process had already started, she said. Jacobs is not confident officials will follow the law.

“Why did I have to go and complain? If not for my complaint, they would still be all locked up [in the room],” she said. “There’s five election commissioners. Why would none of them know the open meetings law?”

Ferguson did not respond to Capital B’s request for comment. However, commissioner Edler said no one has been denied access. As of the afternoon of Nov. 6, she said there’s “a room full of people” who were actively watching the process.

In Lee County, about 100 miles away, a monitor reported that an official told them a count wouldn’t happen until “later this week or early next week,” according to a group chat shared with Capital B. Another volunteer was told it would occur on “Thursday morning” with no additional details.

Offiah, although still battling frustration and confusion, said he is looking forward to continuing the good work with the community.

“As a lifelong Mississippian, I am used to us living in a legacy of constantly fighting back, and this is just in alignment with our legacy,” he said. “And people ask folks from Mississippi, why do we live down here? Why do we stay out here with everything that we’re facing?”

He added: “But we’re fighters, and we won’t ever stop fighting.”

Aallyah Wright is the rural issues reporter for Capital B. From farmers to land fights to health care and jobs, her reporting explores the issues that matter most while celebrating culture and joy. Follow her on Bluesky @aallyahpatrice.bsky.social and Instagram @journalistaallyah. More by Aallyah Wright

scraped.h1: These divers are killing a beautiful coral to save Brazil’s marine life
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

RIO DE JANEIRO — Beneath the surface of Brazil’s coastal waters, a silent invasion is transforming marine ecosystems.

Sun coral (Tubastraea coccinea and Tubastraea tagusensis), an invasive coral native to the Indo-Pacific, is spreading along Brazil’s coastline, threatening native species.

First seen in Brazil in the 1980s, attached to an offshore oil platform in Rio de Janeiro state, sun coral has since spread rapidly. Estimates suggest it can expand at 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) rate per year and is now found along approximately 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) of the Brazilian coast.

Without any natural predators to keep it in check, sun coral can quickly dominate rocky reefs, outcompeting native species for space. It also releases chemicals that harm neighboring corals, including Brazil’s native brain and star corals.

The consequences ripple through the entire ecosystem. As sun coral takes over, small reef-dwelling organisms can disappear, and fish populations may decline. Research suggests that once sun coral covers 45% of a rocky reef, its ecosystem may already be profoundly altered.

But Brazil has been fighting back. In 2018, the country created a National Plan to prevent, control and monitor the invasion, bringing together scientists, conservationists and public authorities in an effort that could offer valuable lessons for other countries.

On the front line is Adriana Gomes, a marine biologist with Brazil’s Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation (ICMBio). Alongside a team of volunteer divers, she is removing sun coral colonies one by one from the waters surrounding the Cagarras Islands, a protected marine area just 5 kilometers (3 miles) off Rio de Janeiro’s iconic Ipanema Beach.

Home to an extraordinary diversity of marine life, the archipelago has been designated a Hope Spot — a place recognized as critical to ocean health.

Watch our video to follow their underwater mission and discover what it takes to protect Brazil’s marine biodiversity.

Next week, the U.S. Senate is set to debate and vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) ( S. 5653 ), a compromise permitting reform deal. Ahead of the planned vote, David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s Climate Program, issued the following statement:

“We appreciate the effort and care Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich put into reaching a compromise to facilitate the buildout of desperately needed clean energy and protect ratepayers from Big Tech’s voracious data center binge. The bill’s provisions on transmission and ratepayer protections are strong and sorely needed, and they ought to be enacted. Unfortunately, the bill’s drawbacks are greater, more immediate, and more certain.

“The bill seriously weakens the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act and guts the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. It fast-tracks the permitting of all manner of projects, then makes it virtually impossible to regulate or arguably even enforce existing rules against them, without an act of Congress. Among other effects, the bill will open the door to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a hasty and reckless buildout of data centers powered by fossil gas. And the bill would make it significantly more difficult to moderate, regulate, or alter these actions later, regardless of what public health , climate destruction, or public sentiment demand. The bill also includes massive giveaways to the mining industry.

“There is also the question of President Trump’s implementation. We do not trust that he will abide by the letter or intent of the law. Regardless of what the law says, we expect him to spend two more years on his reckless and costly fossil-fuel building spree while working to block clean energy. Under BAAJA, his actions will form most of the baseline by which courts assess whether future administrations are discriminating against a given form of energy.

“In the November 3 elections, voters across the country resoundingly rejected data centers. This is not the time to pass a bill that enables Big Tech to charge forward with them, powered by fossil fuels , over the objection of local communities.

“No less important, the makeup of Congress will change substantially in January. It is likely a much better deal can be reached then—one that enacts the laudable and important provisions in this bill, and more, without so many sacrifices.”

scraped.author: Jessica Kutz
scraped.h1: The Navajo Nation Just Elected Its First Woman President
scraped.body_text:
The Navajo Nation isn’t alone. The Seneca Nation of Indians also elected its first woman president this week.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

This story was originally published by The 19th .

Crystalyne Curley is set to become the first woman president of the Navajo Nation, the largest reservation by land mass in the country.

Curley, who also held the distinction of being the first woman to serve as the Nation’s council speaker — the head of its legislative branch —when she was voted by council members to fill that role in 2023, has worked on issues related to water rights, uranium contamination and voter rights.

In another first for tribal governments, the Seneca Nation of Indians in New York also elected its first woman president, Tina Abrams. She previously served two terms on the Nation’s council.

While Native women made history for their tribes in this election, it is not uncommon for women to hold top positions in tribal nations. Activist Wilma Mankiller was appointed as principal chief of the Cherokee Nation in 1985, the largest tribe in the country by tribal enrollment numbers. Though there is no official data on women’s representation in tribal governments, the nonprofit RepresentWomen found that in 2020 at least 78 tribal nations had reached or exceeded gender parity in their legislatures.

Curley’s campaign website lays out her vision as president, including prioritizing behavioral health services, affordable housing programs, workforce development and protecting Diné culture and sovereignty, among other initiatives.

Leading up to the election, Curley told Indian Country Today , a nonprofit news outlet, that she brings her perspective as a mom to the position. “I want to make sure that our children have a safe future, a safe home where they feel they’re proud of who they are,” she said.

By Navajo Nation election law, the results are considered unofficial for ten days after November 3rd. With an 1115 vote count difference between them, Curley’s opponent Justin Jones has not conceded and says he’ll launch a legal challenge over the results, according to the Navajo-Hopi Observer.

The Nation, which has the second largest number of enrolled tribal members nationwide, spans northeastern Arizona and parts of New Mexico and Utah.

scraped.description: “The Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” reads the petition.
scraped.author: Jon Queally
scraped.h1: Petition Urging Dems to Reject Jeffries as House Speaker Passes 1M Signatures
scraped.body_text:
“The Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” reads the petition.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

An online petition that demanding that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) not be the next Democratic Speaker of the House has hit one million signatories on Saturday as the clamor for a leadership change within the party explodes after historic midterm wins driven by populist demands.

As of this writing, the Change.org petition — titled “ House Democrats: CHOOSE A NEW SPEAKER ” — has 1,007,831 verified signatories, with the number rapidly rising.

While the final totals are not yet established, Democrats emerged from Tuesday’s elections with at least 254 seats in the next Congress, reclaiming the majority from the Republicans who currently can count on just 162 seats when new members are sworn in come January.

While Jeffries is clearly the presumptive choice for Democrats, and he formally put himself in the running on Wednesday with a letter to all members, outside progressives have voiced serious opposition given his failure to embrace many of the positions — including backing Medicare for All , taking on entrenched corporate power , and restricting military assistance to Israel over its genocide in Gaza — that have animated voters nationwide this election cycle.

According to the petition:

We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment.

The Speaker has enormous influence over the direction of the House, including its legislative priorities and agenda. Before casting their votes, representatives should closely examine Jeffries’s public record, policy positions, campaign donor record and leadership … and listen to constituents who do not want him elevated to Speaker.

This is not a foregone conclusion. There is still time for other Democratic members of the House to step forward and seek the nomination for Speaker, someone whose priorities more closely reflect the voters who hope to elect the Democratic majority.

We are calling on every member of the incoming 120th Congress to vote against Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker in January 2027 and choose a different candidate.

Axios reported Friday that members of Congress have been “inundated” with calls urging them not to elect Jeffries and suggested that some of the hesitations are not just among progressives.

The outlet reporting interviewing “nearly a half-dozen incoming House Democrats in deeply red seats Thursday who declined to state a firm position one way or another on voting for him.”

Sign this petition if you want a new speaker of the house. https://t.co/G88VLySjsQ

As Corbin Trent, the former top aide to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) who now runs a progressive organizing outfit called A Fight Worth Having, wrote in a column published at Common Dreams on Friday, “the Democratic leadership we have today is completely ill-suited for this moment. They do not have the vision for what it’s going to take to rebuild the trust the American people have lost in their government, their institutions, and the Democratic Party itself.”

“Democrats have spoken loudly and clearly that they want new leadership,” Trent said of the election. “Unfortunately, too many of the people in Washington aren’t listening.”

While the large Democratic majority in the House makes it easier for Jeffries to maneuver leading up to the leadership vote, and given that no challenger has stepped forward to take him on directly, the betting money is still safe that Jeffries will be the next Speaker of the House.

But the public push denouncing him as the wrong choice of leadership in a moment where Democratic voters are clearly demanding — and expecting — a much bolder agenda, the pressure may yet have an impact on his calculations.

scraped.title: AI Companies Are Preying on Under-Resourced Schools, Students Say
scraped.description: Poorer schools are being lured into spending their limited funds on AI tech in the face of chronic understaffing.
scraped.author: Finley Williams
scraped.h1: AI Companies Are Preying on Under-Resourced Schools, Students Say
scraped.body_text:
Poorer schools are being lured into spending their limited funds on AI tech in the face of chronic understaffing.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

When high school librarian Tara Donnelly talks to her classes about how AI has changed online search, she always starts with one question: “What is Google’s main goal?”

Students generally reply, “give you information,” or “tell you the answers to things” — until someone hits the nail on the head and ventures, “Make money.”

Donnelly, a member of the AI working group in the Chicago Teachers Union, says Google is one of many tech companies that are centrally motivated by profit, despite purporting to serve other aims. As AI developers like Microsoft and OpenAI push to integrate their products into U.S. schools and pupils’ lives more broadly, Donnelly said she believes that students are entitled to a clear understanding of the forces shaping their education.

“The ed tech industry is profiting off of running a race with school districts to see who’s going to adopt their chatbot or whatever their tech piece is, and it’s forced on students,” Donelly told Truthout . “Students should have the opportunity to refuse to use AI if they want to. They deserve to have the whole picture and not just to be the money-maker for these ed tech pieces.”

“Students should have the opportunity to refuse to use AI if they want to.”

Indeed, experts, education advocates, and students interviewed by Truthout portrayed a bleak reality in which desperation creates pressure for marginalized students to use AI, and for under-resourced schools to adopt it as a surface-level solution to structural problems like chronic underfunding and understaffing. Many education policy analysts say that in the absence of conclusive evidence that AI improves learning outcomes, companies’ pitch of AI tools as an educational cure-all distracts from more pressing needs: holistic, culturally responsive education that prioritizes human interaction and productive struggle.

Donnelly — an educator at Foreman College and Career Academy, a predominantly Latine school on Chicago’s Northwest Side — said she thinks about these concerns specifically in the context of racially equitable schooling.

“Whenever we’re talking about education, we’re talking about students of color. We always have to be very intentional about, how is this going to affect these students and what do we need to do differently? ” Donnelly said.

Yeisbel Peña, a Latino high school senior in Boston who is interested in computer science, said it’s possible for young students to use AI to advance their thinking. But “raw education — just one-on-one, [the] old type of education — is the most appropriate way a person can actually engage and learn,” he said.

“When you have AI, it just says ‘yes,’ constantly. Any question you ask, it’ll probably just tell you yes,” Peña told Truthout. “It won’t give you complexity. And I believe that that complexity that you get from being in a classroom with a teacher … without it, you’re kind of just limiting yourself.”

Still, he said that in the absence of well-staffed after-school homework help, students at his charter school, which mostly serves students of color, often turn to chatbots instead. Peña described classrooms with only one teacher to assist 10 or 20 students.

“All of them trying to get one-on-one help, it definitely gets very diluted,” Peña said. “So you definitely don’t get the best quality of help.”

In Raleigh, North Carolina, Sacdiya Rashid, 17, said she sometimes chooses to turn to chatbots, which have helped her understand difficult math problems. Though she said that students can harm their learning by becoming over-reliant on the technology, she believes there are commercial influences at play beyond any individual student’s choices.

“I think these AI companies are trying to benefit off of students, like, struggling students,” she told Truthout.

“I don’t think we should really blame students for these AI companies and [the] narratives they’re trying to push. Because I think it just hurts the students,” Rashid said.

Indeed, students at Donnelly’s school in Chicago nominally have access to after-school tutoring, but the primarily immigrant, first-generation and high-poverty student body was hit hard by “Operation Midway Blitz,” President Donald Trump’s anti-immigration raids in the city last year. Because of that, Donnelly said, “There’s not a lot of after-school life within the school.”

“So it’s tough to get extra help,” she said. “In my experience here, it’s more that they’re using [AI] to do the work for them, because they either don’t have time or maybe aren’t understanding it as well as they need to.”

Even as AI chatbots and other AI-enabled ed tech tools spread rapidly in U.S. schools — through both formal and informal avenues — there is extremely limited evidence supporting the conclusion that this technology supports student learning.

Stanford University’s AI Hub for Education within the SCALE Initiative seeks to find and disseminate equitable education practices through research. The organization earlier this year conducted a meta-analysis of K-12 education studies to evaluate the presence of causal evidence indicating AI’s impacts on students’ educations. Lily Fesler, a senior research associate at SCALE, told Truthout that although causal evidence is the only way to concretely judge the technology’s effects, “it’s really hard to conduct randomized control trials, quasi-experimental studies, so there just aren’t a lot of those studies right now.”

Still, senior technologist at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Equity in Civic Technology Project, Hannah Quay-de la Vallee, told Truthout that poorer school districts may still be coaxed into spending their limited funds on unproven technology. In August, the Center for Democracy & Technology published a report examining how administrative AI use could potentially cause disparate impacts in schools, violating students’ civil rights — for example, AI content filtering on student devices could block material related to immigration or sexual orientation, or AI-enabled predictive analytics designed to identify “at-risk” students could mistakenly flag students of color.

“In a school with more resources, more unrestricted resources, they have more avenues for saying, ‘Well, we want to accomplish X goal, and we could do that with AI, or we could do it by hiring more staff, or we could do it with enrichment programs’ or whatever it may be,” said Quay-de la Vallee. “In other cases, you’re going to have schools that have funding that has to be spent on tech.”

At the start of September, New York City Public Schools banned classroom AI use for K-8 students. Shortly after this, the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) announced a policy limiting AI use for all of its roughly 370,000 students. In Chicago, advocates have pressured Board of Education candidates to pledge their support for an AI moratorium.

In interviews with Truthout , activists named ChatGPT, Gemini, and Amira Learning (an AI-enabled reading program) among the tools they’ve seen appear in their schools, both formally and informally.

Across the country, parents, teachers, and students have grown apprehensive of modern technology’s potential adverse effects on student learning and well-being, and suspicious of Big Tech’s motives.

Indeed, recent reporting has revealed tech companies’ decades-long concerted effort to embed themselves more deeply into U.S. schools.

Among many examples, journalist Natasha Singer cites Google’s push to “[hook] students early on services like Gmail and Chrome. The real revenue, made from amassing consumers’ data and showing ads based on their online activities, would come later.”

Google’s narrative that one-to-one tech programs would enhance student learning had considerable buy-in; schools have spent tens of billions of dollars on Chromebooks and other ed tech programs and devices since the tech wave began. Schools’ adoption of Google products only accelerated during the pandemic, when Chromebooks seemed essential to distance learning.

“It feels very predatory to be coming to the most under-resourced schools and communities and trying to sell these things.”

The Trump administration, for its part, has encouraged the wholesale adoption of AI throughout the economy, and particularly in U.S. schooling; in 2025, Trump signed an executive order designed to promote AI education and integration for youth and teachers across the country. A new opportunity to create lifelong customers has emerged, and tech companies are vying to become the dominant AI peddler.

Trump-era AI industry lobbyists continue to exert their influence over U.S. politicians, promoting anti-regulatory views and sidelining the counsel of academics and impartial researchers. The goal is to underplay AI’s potential risks and externalities in every aspect of contemporary life.

Silicon Valley, Singer writes, is exercising its power — and “the public education system, hungry for resources to improve opportunities for students, has become an avenue for multitrillion-dollar companies to enact their agendas.”

Parent and educator activists with the Los Angeles chapter of Schools Beyond Screens and New York City’s AI Moratorium Coalition told a similar story, in which cash-strapped public schools feel they have little choice but to invest in technology.

“Everyone is stretched so thin. Education is so deeply devalued and de-professionalized and defunded. We are all so desperate to the point where, when a sales pitch comes in, someone is willing to just shake hands and sign the contract,” Alisha Maynoush Mernick, an organizer with Schools Beyond Screens LAUSD, told Truthout . “It feels very predatory to be coming to the most under-resourced schools and communities and trying to sell these things, and trying to frame it as giving out of their own goodwill.”

AI Moratorium Coalition steering committee member Kaliris Salas-Ramirez described the bind in which schools and educators sometimes find themselves: “If we don’t have the opportunity to invest in that human capital — because it’s going to take too long, because we can’t find the teacher, because we can’t find the interventionist — then [people say], OK, well maybe this could be the next best thing.”

Mernick sees a bigger issue in AI and ed tech adoption.

“This is just one symptom of a much, much larger problem, which is that when we underfund public schools, we are creating an opportunity for companies to swoop in. That’s privatization in a nutshell,” Mernick said. “It really is just funneling public taxpayer money out of public institutions and into corporate pockets.”

For Rashid, the Raleigh senior, AI tools that don’t improve student learning have no place in the classroom.

“It doesn’t really help the student, and it’s only really so that AI companies can kind of line their pockets,” she said.

scraped.title: The GOP’s post-midterms scramble is pure “Survivor”
scraped.description: JD Vance’s radical honesty is straight out of the season 51 playbook.
scraped.author: Gabriella Gladney
scraped.h1: The GOP’s Post-Midterms Scramble Is Pure “Survivor”
scraped.body_text:
Mother Jones illustration; Chuck Snyder/CBS/Getty; Robert Voets/CBS/Getty; Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty

The show Survivor is currently airing its 51st season, and you might think that after 25 years of television, every kind of strategizing and maneuvering has already been tried. But this fall, one contestant is making an attempt to manipulate his fellow contestants in a different way: by using honesty.

Conventional Survivor strategy entails keeping your cards close to your vest, lying to people’s faces so that your target doesn’t see the vote coming. But current contestant Devin Way’s strategy is to appear trustworthy so that he can more easily deceive down the line. “My whole thing now is weaponized honesty,” Way said at the start of the second episode, after ending up on the wrong side of the vote.

Another scramble is taking place after a different kind of vote: After the Republican Party suffered historic losses across the country this past Tuesday, many prominent GOP figures are scurrying to mitigate the damage. Texas Senator Ted Cruz went on X to call the results “a blue tsunami” and “a Watergate level repudiation.” House Speaker Mike Johnson, who told CBS in October that if Republicans lost the majority, “my intention is to stay and serve,” told his staff Wednesday morning that he won’t run for minority leader . And President Donald Trump admitted his war in Iran hurt Republicans—though he insisted, “ if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again .”

Vice President JD Vance has taken a page straight out of the Survivor season 51 playbook. On Wednesday, he posted a roughly 600-word diatribe on X that has the veneer of an honest assessment of why so many voters turned on the GOP. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote. “Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.” Donald Trump Jr. reposted it with three 💯 emojis .

But where was all this honesty before election night? In September, as missile strikes on Iran continued, Vance told reporters, “I wouldn’t call it a war right now.” In mid-October, he said at a CBS town hall that in “some ways” the US had “won decisively.” His honesty showed up only once it was useful, which makes it look a lot like a manipulation tactic, especially from a man widely seen as Trump’s potential heir .

At the first tribal council this Survivor season, Devin Way put everything out in the open. (Warning: spoilers ahead.) As everyone around him whispered about last-minute plans, he made it known that he planned to vote for his tribe-mate Jenna, but was blindsided himself when his ally Aaliyah left instead. His strategy, meant to show his tribe-mates exactly where he stood, mostly gave them what they needed to plan around him.

Vance and the Republican party are trying a similar sleight of hand: appearing to show the American people where they stand in hopes of winning them back. But as Tuesday’s outcome made clear, the American people aren’t buying it.

scraped.title: Three states where the midterms could unleash a new era for clean energy
scraped.description: Trifectas in Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin are a big deal for climate action.
scraped.author: Jake Bittle
scraped.h1: Three States Where the Midterms Could Unleash a New Era for Clean Energy
scraped.body_text:
Supporters of Wisconsin Democratic governor-elect David Crowley watch early election results at the campaign's election night event on November 03, 2026, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. John Moore/Getty

This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

When Trump was elected in both 2016 and 2024, promising to make the federal government hostile to climate action, many climate advocates insisted that state and local governments would take up the mantle of pushing for clean energy. That’s the thesis of the “ America Is All In ” coalition, which brings together cities and states that have vowed to uphold America’s “climate commitments…[i]n the absence of federal leadership.” The unspoken caveat in these claims is that the states leading the way on climate policy are concentrated in a few liberal parts of the country, like New England and the West Coast.

The Democratic Party’s historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could change that. Democrats have secured control of both state legislative chambers and the governor’s mansion—also known as a “trifecta”—in Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, three states that have spent years or decades under Republican or divided control. The three states have also lagged in their support for clean energy. Democrats also restored trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan, and Nevada this week, but those are states where they last had unified control earlier this decade.

“It is impossible to overstate how monumental these results are,” said David Weiskopf, the senior policy director at Climate Cabinet, a nonprofit that works to elect climate-focused candidates and pass state climate policy. He said that the six states where Democrats have secured trifectas would be one of the world’s largest emitters if they made up their own country, rivaling Canada and Saudi Arabia. “This is just a massive opportunity to make progress.”

Here’s how the election could open up the floodgates for new climate policy:

Compared to its neighbors in the Upper Midwest, Wisconsin has been far less ambitious when it comes to ditching fossil fuels in its power sector. While Michigan and Minnesota have both passed laws that mandate that the states get all their power from clean sources by 2040, Wisconsin set a measly 10 percent renewable electricity standard more than two decades ago. It blew past that goal but never set a new target. Unlike most other states, it doesn’t even require utilities to plan for what kinds of power plants they want to build. The state gets a larger share of its electricity from coal than its immediate neighbors.

Renewable energy advocates in the Badger State believe they can make some short-term gains with Democrats’ first trifecta since 2010. Erik Kanter, the policy director for the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin, said he believes that the new Legislature can agree on the “low-hanging fruit” of making utilities plan for the future, which he said will nudge more of them to build renewables rather than extending the lifespans of gas and coal plants. The Wisconsin Legislature failed this year to pass a law that would require data centers to source their power from clean sources, and Kanter expects such a measure to pass once Democrats take control. The Legislature will also likely renew programs like Knowles-Nelson, a longstanding fund for parks and ecosystem preservation, which once enjoyed bipartisan approval but has lost support from Republicans in recent years.

Weiskopf, of Climate Cabinet, believes that even more ambitious moves are in the offing. He expects Wisconsin’s new class of legislators to pursue a 100 percent clean electricity standard, filling what he calls a “Wisconsin-sized hole” in the Upper Midwest. Not only would that help to phase out coal in the state, it would also make it easier for neighboring states to meet their climate goals, since the whole region shares the same interconnected power grid.

The Pennsylvania Senate has long been known to Democrats as the place where climate policy goes to die. Even though the party managed to flip the lower house of the Legislature a few years ago, Republican leaders in the upper chamber often refused to bring climate bills to a vote . The Keystone State’s status as a large producer of both natural gas and coal also made it difficult to secure agreements within the Democratic Party on clean energy proposals.

“You don’t want to let yourself fully imagine what it can be, because you’ve been let down in the past,” said Lindsey Williams, a state senator who represents a swath of the Pittsburgh metro area. “Now we’re in that moment of, wow, there’s so many things that we can accomplish.”

Every year since 2019, Williams has introduced a bill that would establish mandatory energy and water efficiency standards for appliances like ovens and showerheads, a measure she said could save consumers millions of dollars a year. The legislation has never moved forward—but she thinks it will in next year’s session.

She hopes Democrats will use their first trifecta since 1993 to advance a full-scope climate agenda. In addition to passing laws that would allow community solar and warehouse rooftop solar , Democratic lawmakers also want to pass a funding package for struggling mass transit systems like Philadelphia’s. The $1.5 billion infusion would help prevent the transit “death spiral” for those systems and would reduce reliance on gasoline-powered cars.

The state’s reelected centrist governor, Josh Shapiro, appears to be on board with at least some of these proposals. Although he withdrew the state from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative , a Northeast-wide carbon pricing system , he has promised to create a similar cap-and-trade system for Pennsylvania itself if he can get legislative support. He has also named funding for mass transit as a leading item on his agenda for the new legislative session next year. But Democrats will have to be careful: While they will now control both chambers, they’ll have slim majorities in each, and may have just a narrow two-year window to pass climate policy before one flips back.

“We need to be brave and lead,” said Williams. “Yes, what are the low-hanging fruits, but what are the big ambitious things that we can get done this session?”

The last time Democrats had a trifecta in Arizona, the Grand Canyon State, was in 1966, decades before the general public was even aware of global warming. The state has ample sunshine and wind, so its renewable energy industry has grown quickly over recent years , and its grid is cleaner than in regions like the Midwest. Furthermore, the many newly built suburbs of the Phoenix metroplex tend to be heated with electricity rather than natural gas . Yet Republicans in the state Legislature have all but banned climate and environmental policy, prohibiting the state government from regulating greenhouse gas emissions or energy use, and numerous climate and water bills have failed in recent years.

Lauren Kuby, a longtime Democratic legislator who represents the Phoenix suburb of Tempe, says she and her colleagues have a long wish list that spans several issues. Their first order of business is to reform the Arizona Corporation Commission , the state’s utility regulator, which Kuby says has been slow to embrace new technologies like solar and wind even as developers seek to build more of them. Legislators want to pass a law that would direct the commission to make utilities invest in solar, batteries, and “virtual power plants,” or networks of homes and businesses that coordinate their energy usage. As part of the reform, they might even change the commission’s name, taking out the “corporation” and replacing it with “public utilities.” The two Democrats who appear set to win seats on the commission will make these reforms easier to push through.

The Legislature could also break long-standing logjams on the crucial issue of water—a scarce resource in a desert state where climate change is worsening droughts. Kuby and other senators have been trying for years to pass a bill that would regulate groundwater pumping in the state’s rural areas. These areas are home to massive dairies and alfalfa farms like Riverview and the Saudi-backed Fondomonte , which have been blamed for sinking land and dried-up residential wells. The bill has failed in several legislative sessions , but Kuby believes that some form of regulation can pass in the coming year, bringing an end to the water free-for-all in the desert areas outside Phoenix.

“That has been languishing and has not been heard in the Legislature, even though we have agreement from a lot of Republicans on water and environmental protection,” said Kuby. Of the trifecta, she said, “It’s a game-changer.”

items.title: Voting While Disabled Needs to Get Easier

scraped.title: Voting while disabled needs to get easier
scraped.description: Midterm voters faced a cascade of challenges to voting access in both red and blue states.
scraped.author: Julia Métraux
scraped.h1: Voting While Disabled Needs to Get Easier
scraped.body_text:
Mother Jones illustration; Bryan Dozier/NurPhoto/AP

Disabled people faced a myriad of hurdles to voting during the midterm elections, reflecting both apathy in accommodating marginalized people across the country and voter suppression in states that have sought to deliberately throw up physical and bureaucratic challenges to the process.

“Disabled voters are unable to access the right to vote in every state, in many circumstances, in every county, at every polling place,” said Casey Doherty, a policy analyst for the Center for American Progress’ Disability Justice Initiative . Around 40 million disabled Americans are eligible to vote.

That includes attacks on mail-in voting, which Doherty said effectively disenfranchise many disabled people, especially immunocompromised and otherwise Covid-cautious potential voters who may be hesitant to go to a potentially poorly ventilated polling location. But access issues extend to every stage of the voting process, Doherty noted, including in registering to vote and receiving voting materials on time.

Many states attacking mail-in voting have legislated some exemptions for disabled people, who tend to break evenly along party lines. But some disabled voters, including many I spoke to, are surprisingly likely to emphasize voting in person—in part out of concerns that mail ballots, even if sent back on time, won’t be properly counted.

That’s especially true for voters in a state like Georgia, which months after the 2020 presidential election made it a felony for certain people to return a ballot on another voter’s behalf; many disabled voters seek ballot assistance at polling places and by mail. And, especially in the South, people may have to travel further to vote, with ABC News finding that in the wake of the Supreme Court’s 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision, which weakened voting protections, around 2,700 polling locations closed over a period of a decade.

A 2024 report by the US Election Assistance Commission and Rutgers University found that 14 percent of voters with disabilities faced issues with voting in the 2022 midterm elections, in comparison to 4 percent of non-disabled people, and that more people faced accessibility issues voting in person than voting by mail.

“The most common reported difficulties among in-person voters with disabilities in 2022 were difficulty waiting in line, reading or seeing the ballot, writing on the ballot, and getting inside the polling place,” the report reads. In the run-up to the 2026 elections, even more voting restrictions were deployed by states that have taken advantage of the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act—some forcing disabled people to re-register, sometimes in person, and others slashing the window of time in which they can vote.

Voting accessibility has improved overall across the past two decades, the report noted, with more ramps at voting locations and accessible voting machines. “The improved accessibility reflects funding…for accessible voting systems, improvements to polling places, poll worker training, and increased information about voting accessibility for individuals with disabilities,” the report says.

But where problems still exist, the only remedy is often to file individual complaints under federal or state disability laws, a hurdle that has historically limited enforcement of accessibility statutes and makes it more challenging to expand voting accessibility specifically.

As I reported in 2024 , many polling places, particularly in the South, are in churches—but places of worship are exempt from the Americans with Disabilities Act when not acting as a polling location, which leaves few options when they’re inaccessible. And according to a Ballotpedia analysis, the average level of reading expertise needed to correctly parse the average ballot measure in 2026 was that of a graduate student, posing clear challenges to some disabled people, including would-be voters with intellectual disabilities.

Failure to accommodate access needs while voting can vary immensely. One Deaf voter in Georgia told me that she had been repeatedly instructed not to use an electronic device she requires for captioning. In New Mexico, a woman with severe ME/CFS reported that her county clerk’s office said it never received her absentee ballot request, forcing her to obtain a sworn statement from her doctor attesting to her disabilities in order to receive a last-minute one—another obstacle significant numbers of disabled voters wouldn’t be able to clear. A chronically ill Illinois voter asked for a chair while waiting in line, but inadequate staffing at the polling place meant she had to lug it through the line herself as it moved.

Maria Town, president and CEO of the American Association of People with Disabilities, reported not being able to vote privately on Election Day in Maryland’s Prince George’s County, where the only voting table without long lines at her polling place lacked a privacy screen that matched the height of her mobility scooter, “preventing our ballots from being anonymous,” Town said.

“Polling places should be provided with more privacy shields as a temporary accessibility remedy for voters who may need to vote in a different configuration than a typical booth,” Town said.

Justin Salas, who is blind, wanted to access a sample ballot for his area before he went to vote on Election Day, but the ballot on his county’s election website didn’t work with a screen reader. Salas, who lives in Nevada, said he’d been reprimanded intensely for using a magnifying tool on his phone to vote in the 2024 primary elections, and wanted to iron out problems in advance. But the county never got back to him with a resolution.

“I just wanted to be an informed voter,” Salas said, “and I was not an informed voter.”

In Riverside, Missouri, Patrisha Gillette set out to use curbside voting. Gillette lives with lupus and small fiber neuropathy, both of which contribute to mobility issues. But signs at her polling places directed prospective voters to go inside to inquire about curbside voting.

“I’m like, ‘You’re kidding, right? You want me to come inside to then ask you if I can vote outside, and then get back into my car and pull around’” to vote, Gillette said.

That obstacle, Gillette said, could easily deter other disabled and aging people who want to vote in the state. (The Missouri Secretary of State did not reply to a request for comment.)

“I worry about everybody who it’s just too much [for],” Gillette said, who was able to find a phone number for her polling location—though it wasn’t readily available—eventually online. “Then they leave and don’t end up voting.”

“There’s a failure of empathy and lack of understanding on the state and local government level as well as the federal level,” Salas said. “It doesn’t matter if it’s left or right or center; people seem to think that the accessibility issue can be blown off.”
